en: Now begins the second chapter.
1. The Section on Pervasion (Sarvagatatva-adhikaraṇa).
In this quarter (pāda), he primarily demonstrates the application of words characterized by indicative marks (liṅga) to Viṣṇu.

He shows what is to be established in this quarter in order to prove both the distinction between the preceding and succeeding quarters and their unity as a single coherent whole: "By indicative marks," etc.

The property that causes the inference of the *liṅga* (the mark) is its "self" (*ātman*). Those [words] for which that [property] is the basis of their application (*pravṛttinimitta*) are described as such [i.e., "having that as their self"].
This is because of the metaphorical treatment of non-difference between the cause (*nimitta*) and that which possesses the cause (*nimittin*).
Thus it is stated in the *Sudhā*.
Alternatively, the word "ātman" may have the sense of essential nature (*svarūpa*). In the previous interpretation, its application to that which establishes the self is figurative (*gauṇī vṛtti*).
But in the second [case], there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*); this is the distinction.

The suffix *ka* is used in its own sense (*svārthe*). Thus, the meaning is: those words which, by means of a pervaded property (*vyāpyadharma*), indicate the property-bearer (*dharmin*), and which are etymologically derived (*yaugika*) at first sight.
The phrase "of words well-known elsewhere than Viṣṇu" should also be supplied [with the word] "of words";
the meaning is: of those that consist of a single nominal stem and of those that consist of the co-occurrence of multiple words.
"[Application] to Viṣṇu."

"Manifests" (pradarśayati) means that the author of the Sūtras establishes, in an eminent manner, that the subject matter has Viṣṇu as its ultimate referent— this being understood through both the technical sense of "great yoga" (mahāyoga) and the conventional usage of the learned (vidvad-ruḍhi).
The meaning is that he proves this preeminently.

In the Vaiśvānara section, the phrase "primarily" was stated in order to exclude the charge of non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) resulting from the fact that the reconciliation (*samanvaya*) was carried out by way of names alone.

Thus, the intention is that even there, because the reconciliation of many signs (*liṅga*) is effectively accomplished primarily through the reconciliation of names, there is no lack of pervasion. [The text continues: "Brahman is all-pervading."
Thus, the omnipresence of Viṣṇu has been stated;
and that same [omnipresence] is perceived in the case of Āditya through such passages as, "Of this very one, that Āditya is the essence" (Ai.Ā. 3.2.3).
Although there is no need to demonstrate the intermediate connection (*avāntara-saṅgati*) between the final section of the previous chapter and the first section of this chapter,

nevertheless, because such a connection is possible here and because the result must necessarily be stated, the author demonstrates the connection with the preceding section and the subject matter (*viṣaya*) etc., with the intention [of doing so]. The meaning of the statement "Brahman" is that the all-pervasiveness (*sarvagatatva*) of Viṣṇu without limit has been declared therein.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "And that..."
The word "that" recurs, and the phrase "it has been said" also persists; and thus it is stated:
"Brahman is all-pervading."

Thus, that which was described as "thatness" (tattva) belonging to Viṣṇu known as Prāṇa—that very state of being a constituent part of Him, which is included within His omnipresence and consists in His abiding in the hearts of all living beings—is stated in that same *Aitareya* [Upaniṣad]: "For the Bahvṛcas meditate upon Him alone when [the hymn] is recited; the Adhvaryus [meditate on] Him in the fire;
the Chandogas [meditate on] Him in the Mahāvrata [rite]; [they meditate on] Him in this earth, Him in the sky, Him in the wind, Him in space, Him in the waters, Him in the plants, Him in..."

The meaning is that [the word] "this" (etam) refers to what has been stated in the subsequent sentence: "In the lords of the forest, this; in the moon, this; in the stars, this; in all beings, this—this alone they call Brahman.
To the question "What follows from that?", he states the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) along with its reasoning: "And that... (tacceti).
The word *ca* is used for emphasis.

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), [the following is included]: "One should know that he who is this bodiless self consisting of intelligence (*prajñātman*) and that which is yonder sun are one and the same;
therefore, for every person, there is a sun... the sun is the self of the moving and the stationary... him."
The passage beginning with "In all beings" (Ai. 3.2.3) is taken here;

the citation of "of that" (tasya) and so forth is made because it is necessary to provide the object to be referred to by the word "this one" (etam), and also for the purpose of demonstrating the argument of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa).

And thus, since the state of abiding in the hearts of all living beings— which was stated by the subsequent sentence "as this" (yathaitam)— is understood to belong to that very Sun (āditya) because it was the subject of the preceding sentence beginning with "of him" (tasya),
therefore, that previously mentioned state of being the Truth (satyatva) must also belong to him alone;
it does not belong to Viṣṇu— such is the construction.
In this prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), "being that" (*tatamatva*) is intended in its restricted sense of being present in all beings.
Nor should it be said that such a view fails to raise the objection regarding the unlimited omnipresence favored by the proponent of the final position (*siddhāntin*);
for in the prima facie argument, [it says] "this very one."

By this restrictive determination (*avadhāraṇa*), since there is an exclusion (*ākṣepa*) of anything other than Viṣṇu, its connection is shown to be one of exclusion (*ākṣepikī-saṅgati*); furthermore, the subject matter, the doubt,
and the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) supported by reasoning— that it is something other than Viṣṇu who resides within all living beings— are thereby demonstrated.
This is established; the meaning of the scripture is as follows:

"Of him"—of the aforementioned "this" one named Saṃvatsara, the four-faced Brahmā—Pradyumna, who bears the name Āditya due to being the beginning of all, the most pervasive, and the controller, is the *rasa*, that is, the essential core.

One should know that this single form exists in two places: that which resides in the human body, which—by virtue of abandoning the material body—is bodiless, the "conscious self" (*prajñātman*), consisting of knowledge and uncontracted (*aniruddha*);
and that which is situated in the sun, Pradyumna. One should understand that these two forms are one.

Therefore, because of the identity of Aniruddha and Pradyumna who reside in that Sun, the Sun "becomes" (bhavati)— that is, it becomes manifest— “toward every person” (puruṣaṃ puruṣaṃ prati), meaning it faces each individual.
If it is argued that [the Self] exists in all persons, like the saying "there is a well in every house," [the text replies:
"[He is] the Self of the moving" (*jagataḥ*)— that is, of the animate— and "of the stationary" (*tasthuṣaḥ*), that is, of the inanimate.

The one who performs the taking up and so forth is ‘asūryaḥ’; Viṣṇu, who is to be attained by the wise (sūri), ‘āprāḥ’— that is, he filled completely— the heaven, the earth, and the intermediate space.
The words beginning with "etam" are each connected with the locative case endings;
thus, "the Bahvṛcas," meaning the followers of the Ṛgveda, [say] "for this very one."

Indeed, they investigate— that is, they know— this very Viṣṇu, who has entered the sun as the Puruṣa, within the "Great Uktha," meaning within the thousand Bṛhatī verses named the Great Uktha, regarding that deity;
[they are] the Adhvaryus.
The followers of the Yajurveda deliberate upon the deity of the bricks used as means for the piling of the fire-altar (*cayana*) in the context of the "Agni" [section];
the *Chandogas*, that is, the followers of the Sāmaveda, [deliberate] in the context of the "Mahāvrata."
They deliberate upon the deity of that hymn named after it:
[is it] "in this" earth, or "in heaven" in the intermediate space such as the wind and so forth, or likewise "in all beings"? It is this very same one.
The meaning is that the wise declare [Viṣṇu] to be pervading within all living beings (*sarvaprāṇiṣu*).

Although the word "in all" (*sarveṣu*) alone would have sufficed, the further mention of "in beings" (*bhūteṣu*) is intended to indicate that what is meant here to be established is simply His existence within the elements (*bhūta*).

The sense of the remainder of the sentence is: "They call this very Viṣṇu, who resides in all beings, 'Brahman' in the primary sense, because He is full of attributes and because He is all-pervading."
In the *Sthānādhikaraṇa-ṭīkā*, however, it is explained thus: "In all beings—that is, in the locations such as the eyes and so forth—they declare this one alone, Brahman, who is full of attributes.

The opponent (pūrvapakṣin), however, thinks that for this very [Brahman], the well-known year under discussion, the well-known Āditya, the Sun, is the *rasa*—meaning the essence or the presiding lord (*adhipati*).
Therefore, he said:
Sūtra—Oṃ.
Because the teaching is established everywhere.
Om.
Now, he introduces the aphorism that establishes the final conclusion with the words "ataḥ" (therefore).
Thus, because there is a logical connection (*saṅgati*) and because an objection (*ākṣepa*) exists, Bādarāyaṇa spoke the following reply in order to resolve it; this is the meaning.
He recites that very *sūtra*: "In all cases," [referring to] "That which is this bodiless, conscious Self" (*Ai. Ā. 3.2.4*).
By such statements as these, it is Nārāyaṇa alone who is spoken of everywhere.

Here, with the intention of carrying forward the word "tat" (that) from the *Samanvaya-sūtra*, changing the gender, and supplying the word "ucyamānam" (being spoken of), he explains the portion of the proposition: "sa yaśca... (He who...).
The word "by the sentence" is to be understood as the ellipsis;
for although one should have said "by [the passage] beginning with 'of this very [ātman], that...'", [the author has used the term "vākya"].
Because it is a preceding statement;

nevertheless, since that [statement] was introduced for the purpose of demonstrating the arguments of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), it was set aside, and the phrase beginning with "That which is this bodiless self consisting of intelligence" (*sa yaścāyamaśarīraḥ prajñātmā*) was stated specifically to indicate the statement that demonstrates the arguments of the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

In reality, however, the presentation of the phrase "sa yaśca" (he who... is not intended merely as a demonstration of reasoning, as is the case with the phrase "tasyaitasyāsau" (of that very one...).
Nor is it intended merely to indicate the subject matter;

rather, it should be understood as follows: because the subject-sentence was not previously cited, this [verse] is for the purpose of providing the means of referring back to that sentence via the word "this" (etad), and for the purpose of demonstrating the reasoning for being inherently bodiless (*aśarīratva*), which is unique to this [subject] and not shared by anything else.
‘Everywhere’: this refers to Nārāyaṇa alone, who is said to be present within the hearts of all living beings. By the use of the word ‘Nārāyaṇa’—it is as stated:
“Whatever exists in this entire world, whether it is seen or even heard...”
Pervading all that is within and without, Nārāyaṇa remains.
Thus, this statement is also included.

And by that [statement], since the word "everywhere" (*sarvatra*) in the Sūtra is used in a restricted sense and intends precisely that [the Self] resides within the hearts of all beings, the doubt that it might exist elsewhere outside [the heart] is dispelled.
"That alone is the supreme Brahman for the seers" (Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad 1.6).
He explains the causal portion of the phrase "that which is the supreme Great Brahman" with the words: "That very [Brahman]..."
This has been explained in the *Jijñāsā-naya*.

For the purpose of making known the non-difference between Īśvara and Brahman, there is the connection of the *Bhārata* statement—“He who is the supreme great Brahman, he who is the supreme ultimate resort”—with the subsequent sentence: “Of those names of that Lord of the World, the foremost of the worlds, who is the supreme great Brahman and who is the supreme ultimate resort.”
"Who indeed is superior to Vāsudeva, who is designated by the word 'Brahman'?
For he alone is complete with all qualities, whereas others [are so called] only figuratively.
This is because the well-known designation "Brahman" is taught in reference to him alone. //1//
The *Smṛti* devoted to Vāsudeva-Āditya states:
"Other than Vāsudeva"—that is, other than Kṛṣṇa—who else could be the primary denotation of the word *brahman*? None at all;
rather, he alone is the primary denotation.
Why? Because "he"—Vāsudeva—is full of all qualities, whereas others are incomplete;
therefore, [it might be argued that] "all individual souls (jīvas) are indeed Brahman."
To the question "How so? regarding this and other such points, he says: "other than that."
The meaning is that living beings other than Vāsudeva are designated by the word "Brahman" only figuratively— that is, in a non-primary sense— and not in its primary sense.
The word "iti" [indicates] that the phrase "in sentences" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
By this, it is shown that the term "everywhere" is also connected with the word "cause."
And likewise, in all the cited passages, there is "the teaching of the word 'Brahman' which is well-known"— that is, understood through conventional usage— "to that very one," namely Viṣṇu alone.
The meaning is that [the Self] is heard of as being omnipresent in all things.
By the phrase "in that very [Self]," it is stated that there is no room for [any other] hearing [of a different entity].
By this [is meant the passage]: "That which is this bodiless, conscious Self" (Ai. Ā. 3.2.3).

By such statements as these, and by the remainder of the section in the *Aitareya Āraṇyaka* (3.2.3), "In all beings, they call this very one Brahman," it is Nārāyaṇa alone who is described as being present within all beings everywhere, and not Āditya or others.
Why? Because [the text says], "they call this very one Brahman."

Thus, the meaning of the Sūtra has been stated: because the term "Brahman," which is well-known from the Śrutis and other sources as being uniquely established in Nārāyaṇa, is taught in reference to the entity that pervades all beings; [this is] "from the Śruti.
Sū - Oṃ.
And because the intended qualities are established.
"‘He who is unheard from here... (Ai. Ā. 3.2.4), etc.

Having introduced the sūtra which establishes that Viṣṇu alone possesses the all-pervasiveness mentioned here by means of another argument, he cites the very scripture cited therein: “vivakṣita... and so forth;
by the word "etc.," [the passage] ‘unmoved, unmeasured, unbent, unseen, unknown, undirected’ is included.

"The remainder of the passage, 'One should know that the inner person within all beings is the equal Self—the hearer, the thinker, the seer, the advisor, the proclaimer, the knower, and the perceiver' (Ai.Ā. 3.2.4), is to be understood.
The word "ityādi" (and so forth) is a term with its third case ending elided.
The phrase "this is intended [by the author]" connects with the words of the sūtra.
For this very reason, the *Tattvapradīpa* states that there is a unification (*ekībhāva*) between the sūtra and the bhāṣya.
By this, it is indicated that the word "by the scripture" (*śrutyā*) is to be supplied as a supplement to the sūtra.
The particle *ca* serves both to aggregate the previously stated reasons and to indicate emphasis.
Since there is a desire to speak regarding that which is fit to be spoken,
they are "intended to be spoken" (*vivakṣitāḥ*), meaning they are fit to be spoken or, alternatively, they are those that will be explained hereafter.

Alternatively, it may mean "those which are the objects of the purport of the Śrutis," as stated in the *Tattvapradīpa*: "The author of the Sūtras employed the word *vivakṣita* (intended) in order to refute those who claim that the Śrutis lack purport regarding the qualities of Brahman.
The term "everywhere" (*sarvatra*) is understood to carry over [from the previous context].

The word "gone" (gate) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. And thus, in all cases, it refers to those things intended by the scripture which are fit to be described as being established in the omnipresent,
or which are about to be described hereafter by the scripture as being established in the omnipresent, or which have become the objects of the scripture's intended meaning.

The meaning of the Sūtra is stated as follows: because qualities such as the non-hearing [of the mantra] and others, which pertain to the collection [of attributes], are appropriate for Viṣṇu alone and are logically possible only in Him—and because they are not possible elsewhere—Nārāyaṇa alone is the one spoken of everywhere.
That Viṣṇu who was introduced [in the previous Sūtra] is "therefore" (ataḥ).

It is pervaded by the qualities of place and time; for this reason, based on the etymological explanation of the verbal root *at* as "continuous movement" (*sātatyagamana*), there is also the statement: "Therefore, it is called *santata* (continuous)."
Alternatively—the meaning of "atistṛtīye" is "in an excess beyond the third," that is, in a superior degree.
"Aśrutaḥ" means incapable of being heard by any means whatsoever;
[the Lord] hears His own Self by Himself through His own sovereignty.
According to the Vedic scripture: "He does not dance before you" (Ṛgveda 10.112.9).
"Agataḥ" means not attained; or, because He is full, He is known as the Self of all.
Because He is not an object of mentalization for the sake of the entire self, He is "amataḥ."
"Unbowed" means devoid of a leader— that is, independent;
"unseen" by anyone through direct perception, because of being complete in every respect.
For this very reason, it is "unknown in its entirety," meaning not known in its specific details;
it is "uncommanded," meaning devoid of an instigator, or alternatively, not enjoined by others.
He says "the hearer" (*śrotā*) to show that others do not possess hearing and so forth in their entirety as He does, nor are they such that others have not heard from them themselves;
[the word] "hearer" means one who simultaneously acts as a listener with independence.
‘Mantā’ means the independent thinker of all things;
the independent seer of all things.
‘Ādeṣṭā’ means the director who effects the assignment [of functions].
‘Āghoṣṭā’ means one who speaks correctly;
‘vijñātā’ means one who knows specifically,
one who knows preeminently.
The "Person" who is "within," that is, dwelling inside, "of all beings," that is, of all living creatures.

The meaning of the Śruti, according to the perspective of Viśveśvaratīrtha and others in the *Tattvapradīpa* commentary on the *Aitareya-bhāṣya*, is that one should know the Self as "Full," "Equal," "Uniform," and as the "Agent" of taking up [the body] and so forth in every respect.
For He possesses qualities such as being "unheard of" (*aśruta*), based on such scriptural passages as: "O Viṣṇu, no god was born, nor is one being born [equal to You]" (Ṛgveda 7.99.2).
Now, one might ask: how is it known that these qualities—such as being "unheard of"—stated in this Śruti reside in Viṣṇu? To this, he says: "For He... (*sa hi*).
The word "hi" signifies well-known fact. The meaning is that Viṣṇu, by means of such statements as "He is not [perceived] by you," is well-known as possessing qualities such as being beyond hearing.
The intention is that in the Śruti, the word "by the ear and so forth" (*śrotrādinā*) must be supplied as an ellipsis.
Although, since "non-existence" (*atatva*) is mentioned first in the Śruti, one ought to say "possessing qualities such as non-existence" (*atatvādiguṇa*).

Nevertheless, because that [all-pervasiveness] has the nature of being omnipresent and is thus established as residing in Viṣṇu, it would be unestablished [for the opponent]; and since Viṣṇu is already well-known as possessing the quality of all-pervasiveness, it would be improper to refer to it as something already established. Therefore, it was stated "because it is not heard [in that context]" (*aśrutatvāt*). Alternatively, in the formal argument: "Viṣṇu possesses the quality of all-pervasiveness, because of such scriptural texts as *'Not yours, O Viṣṇu...'* (Ṛgveda 7.99.2)," the quality of all-pervasiveness (*atatva*) is what is to be proven; and regarding that, [the text says] "*'Not yours, O Viṣṇu... [implying it is not limited].
In such passages, because [the Lord] is not mentioned and because there is no connection with a logical reason, it is said that He is "unheard" (*aśruta*) and so forth:
"He is the Sun, He is Vāyu, He is Indra; He is the Unheard, He is the Unseen—He who is Hari, who is the Supreme, who is Viṣṇu, who is Ananta."
Thus, in the Caturvedaśikhā, [verse] 2.

Since the fact that Viṣṇu is not explicitly heard [as the subject] in the scriptural passage beginning with "Not those," and so forth, is not immediately apparent, he cites a clear scripture for this very purpose, saying: "He.
He who is the "Savitṛ," the creator of the universe, is Hari alone.
He who is "Vāyu," the deity whose nature is strength and knowledge, is the Supreme, the Paramātman alone.
He who is "Indra"—possessing supreme sovereignty—is Viṣṇu alone, not the well-known [deity] and others.
He who is "unheard" and "unseen" is the infinite and immeasurable Hari alone, and no other; such is the meaning.

Alternatively, the meaning is that he who is well-known as denoted by words such as "Hari" and so forth is precisely the same one denoted by words expressing qualities such as "the Impeller" (Savitṛ) and so on;
thus [ends the phrase] "and so forth."

Since it is stated in the *Caturvedaśikha* and other texts that "He who is unperceived," and so forth, the logical connection (*anvaya*) is that for this reason as well, He alone possesses the attributes of being unperceived and so on.
Nor should it be argued that the individual soul (*jīva*) is meant because of the word "sun" or because of qualities such as "consisting of sight.
For, just as from the word "Brahman" and by means of marks such as being unperceived, Viṣṇu is declared to be all-pervading; [so too here].

To the objection that, because of the word "Āditya" and because [the self] possesses the characteristics of all living beings, why should Āditya or all living beings not be omnipresent, he says: "And not so."

The meaning is as follows: from the word "Āditya" in the passage "Āditya is the essence," and because [the qualities] such as "consisting of sight" are well-known in the context of omnipresence in the Śruti text, "The Self consists of sight, consists of hearing, consists of the Vedas, consists of mind, consists of speech" (Ai.
Ā. 3.2.1), [these qualities belong] to the individual soul (jīva) by virtue of its identification with a body whose nature is the eyes and other organs of cognition.
The word "and" (*ca*) serves to aggregate the reasons.
By the term "living being" (*jīvaḥ*), the word *śārīra* (embodied) found in the aphorism is explained, according to the traditional teaching (*smṛti*):
"Both are declared to be embodied—the living being (*jīva*) and likewise the Supreme."
Furthermore, because the individual soul (jīva) identifies with the body, its possession of a body is logical.
The singular number used for "the jīva" intends to refer to the collective whole.
Moreover, the word "and" (ca) in the phrase "and the jīva" is to be construed with the preceding term.
Therefore, the proposition regarding the sun is subsumed;
"pervading everywhere" is the ellipsis [to be supplied].
Thus, it is connected with the statement that "it should not be so spoken."
Sū - Oṃ.
But because of the impossibility [of it], he is not the embodied soul. Om.
Because it is simply impossible for one [self] to reside within all bodies. // 3 //

When the question arises as to why it should not be stated, the Sūtra is presented; since the portion concerning the proposition (*pratijñā*) has already been explained by the introductory commentary (*avatārikā-bhāṣya*), he explains only the part concerning the reason (*hetu*): "Because of the impossibility" (*anupapatteḥ*).
This [reason] is understood by modifying the text to read "of each individual soul" (*ekasyaikasya jīvasya*).
"[In all bodies]" (*sarvaśarīra*)...

The meaning is that it is because the existence [of the self] in the entire body is untenable, precisely because it would contradict the logical consequence that every living being would experience identical enjoyment.
The word "eva" (precisely) implies that one need not seek any other reason, such as the absence of a factor that would cause otherwise.
By the word "eva," the particle "tu" found in the Sūtra is explained.
The impossibility [of this] has been established with its reasons in the *Ṭīkā* itself.
Sūtra: Oṃ.
And because of the designation of action and agent. Om.
"He praises himself to another," and so forth (Ai. Ā. 3.2.3). // 4 //
Setting forth a sūtra that refutes the omnipresence of the embodied soul by means of another argument, he cites the very scripture employed therein: "Karma... etc.
This [particle] "ca" emphasizes the state [of being], and it signifies conjunction;
[it refers to the fact that] "the embodied one has been mentioned everywhere."
Thus, these three words follow by way of modification.

And so, in the Aitareya Śruti, regarding the act of praising in the phrase "he praises this Self to another," the embodied living being (jīva) is the object (*karman*) of that action in the expression "he [praises] this Self. This refers to the previously mentioned and all-pervading [Self].
And because he is designated as the agent in that very [action], and because there is a rule that two agents in a single action are generally distinct,
and because there is no cause for an exception, the meaning is that the term "embodied one" (śārīra) is not used in all instances.
However, in the *Tattvapradīpa*, by virtue of the word "and" (ca), [it refers to] "for another" (parasmai).
Thus, it has been stated that the intention is expressed by the designation of "giving" (*sampradāna*):
"he [who gives] this Self"—
the Supreme Self characterized by qualities such as consisting of sight— to another.
"To one who is unworthy he speaks" means he teaches; for him, "the Vedas have their milk milked out," which means they become devoid of fruit.

The phrase "and so forth" (*ityādi*) is to be construed with the preceding sūtra according to the previous method. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the [passages] mentioned in the *Ṭīkā*—namely, "He knows himself" (*ātmānaṃ veda*) and "He who has abandoned the friend who knows the truth, for him there is no portion even in speech" (*yastityāja sacividaṃ sakhāyaṃ na tasya vācy api bhāgo asti*; Ai.Ā. 3.2.4)—are included.
And the statement cited in the *Tattvapradīpa* is also taken here:

"He who has abandoned"— that is, he who knows otherwise— the "friend," Hari, who knows the accumulation of karma (*karmasañcaya*) and is his companion because of their dwelling in the same place, [out of] affection.
"In his speech"—that is, in the study of the Vedas and so forth—there is "no portion," meaning there is no fruit; rather, there would be hell. Sūtra: Oṃ.
Because of the distinction in sound.
"‘They call this very one Brahman’ (Ai. Ā. 3.2.3).
As for what was stated—that from the word ‘Brahman’ it follows that Viṣṇu alone is omnipresent—that is incorrect."

Since the word "Brahman" can also apply to the individual soul (jīva), one might object that it is not grasped [as referring to Brahman] because its application to the soul is secondary (amukhya). However,
this objection is invalid, because it is possible to accept even a secondary meaning on the strength of subverting factors such as the soul's being "consisting of sight" (cakṣurmayatva) and so forth.

Nor [is it the case that] the individual soul (jīva) is not [the subject] because of the sublation mentioned in the second sūtra, for in the Gītā it is heard that the soul has not been heard [by all]: "Even having heard this, no one indeed knows it";
and because what was stated in the third [sūtra] applies equally even to Viṣṇu.

Nor can it be [the case] because of the sublation by the statement in the Fourth Chapter regarding its consisting of sight and so forth; for one and the same thing can logically possess both the status of object and agent. Anticipating this objection, he presents the sūtra that dispels it and cites the very scripture contained therein: "By the word... (Śabda...).
The commentary is connected with the aphorism (sūtra).
Thus, in the statement "They call this very one Brahman," the word "Brahman" under discussion functions as the reason [for the identification] because of its specific distinction.
The meaning is: "because it possesses the specific quality of having a restrictive nature.
This connects with the established probandum (sādhya) obtained from the statement: "the embodied self (śārīra) is not denoted by this word 'Brahman'.
Here, the particle *eva* (only/exclusively) is connected with the word that functions as the predicate (*vidheya*).
Furthermore, the word *brahman* used here with that [specific] suffix signifies the primary sense of Brahman;
and it has already been stated that this is not applicable to the individual soul (*jīva*).
Alternatively, the particle *eva* is connected directly with the term *em*, which denotes the subject, and serves to exclude connection with anything else.
Nor should it be argued that, in this way, the word *brahman* would not attain the status of being restrictive (*sāvadhāraṇatva*).

For when the restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) denoted by the particle *eva*—which is the exclusion of connection with another (*anyayogavyavaccheda*)—is explained as "the exclusion of the connection of Brahmanhood with anything other [than what is denoted by the word *brahman*]," the word *brahman* attains the status of being restrictive because of its connection with the property of Brahmanhood (*brahmatva*), which is the meaning of the word *brahman*. Thus, the word *brahman* itself becomes restrictive.

Although the embodied self (*śārīra*) is not the meaning of this word [“Brahman”], why is that? Because it is specified by the word “Brahman” itself, which denotes the counter-correlative of the sense of the particle *eva*. Such an interpretation of the Sūtra-commentary (*sūtravṛtti*) is indeed possible; nevertheless, because it was not mentioned in the *Ṭīkā*, it has not been presented by anyone.
For they do not declare that the individual soul (*jīva*) alone is Brahman.
To the question, "Even if the word *brahman* is used with restrictive force, why does it not apply to the individual soul?", he says: "For not...
The word *hi* (for) indicates both well-known fact and reason.
The word "poets" is to be supplied as the subject.

If it is asked why, it is because if the individual soul (jīva) were denotable by the word "Brahman" preceded by the restrictive particle *eva*, it would follow that the soul possesses primary Brahmanhood;
and that is not tenable.
The sense is that [the term "Brahman"] is well-known as referring primarily to Brahman.

In this very way, even though the particle *eva* relates to the subject (*uddeśya*) and functions to exclude connection with anything else (*anyayogavyavacchedaka*), it would—under the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)—exclude the status of being Brahman from anyone other than the individual soul (*jīva*) intended here as the referent of the word "this" (*etac-chabda*).
And that is not tenable.

It should also be observed that since the Supreme Self, the primary Brahman, is distinct from the individual soul (*jīva*), and since the secondary Brahman—consisting of genus (*jāti*) and so forth—is also distinct, it is impossible to negate the relationship of "Brahman-hood" with anything other than the Self.

However, in the *Tattvapradīpa*, it is stated: "If the individual soul were Brahman, then its abiding within the elements (*bhūtasthatva*), as expressed in the phrase 'among the elements' (*bhūteṣu*), would be untenable because the soul is itself an element.
[The text continues: "He indeed is Brahman; he indeed is the Self; he indeed is Savitṛ; he indeed is Indra; he indeed is..."
"Thus Hari, the Supreme Bliss, carries away [all else]," so it is said in the Indradyumna-śākhā. // 5 //
To the question, "Why does the term *brahman*, used with restrictive emphasis, apply to Viṣṇu as well? he says: "This... [eṣa iti].
He indeed; or rather, the word "u" refers to Viṣṇu. Thus, the meaning is that this very Viṣṇu is Brahman.

He states that the nature of being the Self (ātmatva) mentioned in the phrase "the Self," as well as the nature of being Savitṛ and so forth mentioned in the phrase "that Savitṛ," belong to Viṣṇu alone, by means of the passage beginning with "This indeed is the Self.
"Ya u" refers to Hari, who is none other than Viṣṇu.
Regarding that, he states the etymological basis: "He takes away" (*harati*).
This means that in the sacrificial halls, he appropriates the portion offered as *iḍā*.
Alternatively, it means that he removes the sin of the virtuous.
Thus, the construction is: "This very one is the supreme, the highest, and full bliss.
The phrase "in the Indradyumna branch" connects with the supplemented passage: "Those called Indradyumna-s call this Viṣṇu, who dwells within all beings, 'Brahman' itself."
And the positive concomitance (anvaya) of this reason with the probandum (sādhya) found in the introduction is:
Sū-oṃ.
And because of the Smṛti. // Oṃ // BBs_1,2.6 //
"I am the Self, O Guḍākeśa, seated in the heart of all beings" (Bhagavad Gītā 10.20);
"And entering the earth, I support all beings by my vital power" (Bhagavad Gītā 15.13),
and so forth.
Having recited the sūtra—"And because of Smṛti"—which establishes Viṣṇu’s omnipresence mentioned here by means of the designation "Smṛti," he cites that Smṛti.

The meaning of the word "and" (ca) in the phrase "from such Smṛti as well" is that Nārāyaṇa alone is the one mentioned everywhere; this is the syntactical connection (anvaya). It is not only because of the reasons already stated.
Even though the Smṛti is [actually] his own statement, its mention here is appropriate because it takes the form of a restatement of what has been said by others.
The same applies to what follows:
"O Agudakesha";
*guḍākā* means sleep, and its lord (*īśa*) refers to one who is free from it.

"He whose hair is like jaggery on all sides" means "one with smooth hair"; the meaning is that I abide within the hearts of all as the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*). Having entered "the earth" (*gām*), having descended there, [I sustain] "beings" (*bhūtāni*).
The meaning of the other statement is: "I sustain the living beings by means of *ojas*, that is, by my power.
And these [words] are from the speech of Kṛṣṇa to Arjuna in the Gītā.

The citation of the second sentence is for the purpose of dispelling the notion of non-difference—that "I am that Self which dwells within the hearts of all beings" as expressed in the preceding sentence.
It is intended that its status as the sustainer is established precisely by its being contained within that [Self];
therefore, there is no inconsistency.
By the word "etcetera" (ādipadāt), other Smṛtis are included;
nor should anything that lacks authoritative basis be postulated. // 6 //

Others, however, having established the siddhānta that in the passage "consisting of mind, having prāṇa as its body, whose form is light, whose resolve is true," the qualities such as being "consisting of mind" belong to the Lord (Īśvara) alone and not to the individual soul (jīva), raise the objection: "Since there is identity between the individual soul and the Lord, how can this be so? and they reply: "There is indeed a distinction."
And this is not a departure from one's established tenet (*apasiddhānta*), because this [position] is not ultimate (*pāramārthika*),
but rather—

Having resolved that it is precisely the falsity [of difference] that was intended by the author of the Sūtra, they describe the purport of the Sūtra as being the falsity of difference; anticipating their view, he refutes it with the words "na ca" (and not).
The suffix *tva* has the sense of "object" (*artha*), and the negative particle *nañ* signifies that which is opposed to or the absence of that [object].
Thus, [the term] *aprāmāṇikaṃ* [means] that which lacks the status of being a means of valid cognition.
"The falsity of difference is not to be postulated";
it should not be imagined as being the intended object of the author of the Sūtras.
Why? Because that [falsity] is unauthoritative, being devoid of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), as in the case of the verse "Two birds... (*dvā suparṇā*).
And because it contradicts such authoritative means of knowledge as these, the construction [of the sentence] is "therefore" (*ataḥ*).
Sūtra: Oṃ.

If it be argued that [the Self] is not [the object of meditation] because of its having a small abode and because of being designated as such, we say no; for it is to be perceived as such, and it is like space.
Om.

If it be argued that [the Self] is not [the Supreme Self] because of the phrase "in all beings" (implying a limited abode) and because of the designation of the individual soul (*jīva*) through such qualities as "consisting of sight," we say no.
Having raised an objection against the stated meaning, the author reads the sūtra which provides the resolution and first explains the part containing the objection: "arbhaka-" (smallness).
The word "in the statement" (*vākya*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. The term *arbhaka* is explained as "small" (*alpa*).
That which has a small abode or place is so called; the state of being such is its essence (*tattva*), and it is from that [essence] [that the inference follows].
And thus, the meaning is "because it is stated to reside in a small place";
the intention is that this is due to the smallness of the cavities within the hearts of all living beings.
Considering that the word *tat* in the Sūtra has the dual sense of both the mode (*prakāra*) and the thing characterized by the mode (*prakārin*), he says: "the eye" and "the living being."
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), qualities such as being composed of hearing are included;
or, by the particle "and" (ca) or from the word "etcetera," the scriptural mention of the sun (āditya-śruti) is also included.
For this very reason, the term "living self" (jīva-pada) was employed as something common to both [the individual soul and] the sun.
The term "jīvavyapadeśaḥ" means the designation or mention of the individual soul (jīva); the phrase "in the Śruti" is to be supplied, as in the passage: "consisting of sight, consisting of hearing.
The particle "ca" is used here for the purpose of conjunction.
"No.
The meaning of "no" is that it is not the case that Nārāyaṇa alone is what is being spoken of everywhere;
the sense is that even in the case of the Supreme Self (paramātman), there exist subverting arguments just as there are in the case of the individual soul (jīva).
He explains the portion concerning the refutation: "No.
The meaning is that it is not the case that Viṣṇu is not spoken of everywhere, because of the aforementioned sublation;
for it is that very Viṣṇu who is to be discerned through His having a small abode and through His being composed of the eye and so forth.

Why is it not so? Because there is no sublation (bādhaka) here; because reasons such as "having a small abode" (arbhakaukastva) and so forth are applicable to Viṣṇu alone and thus do not constitute sublation—having thus supplemented both the reason and the supporting argument for it—one might then suspect that the mention of "having a small abode" and so forth regarding Viṣṇu would be redundant. Anticipating this objection, he explains the portion "because He is to be discerned in this way" (evaṃ-nicāyyatvāt) as the refutation of that, stating: "by virtue of having a small abode" (arbhakaukastvena).
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), he says [it is] by virtue of being composed of mind (*manomayatva*).
By this, the word *eva* in the Sūtra is explained as having the sense of "manner" (*prakāra*).

Regarding the portion concerning the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), he says "of that very one" (*tasyaiva*), intending the connection of the word *tat*—which has the meaning of Viṣṇu, is transposed, and is accompanied by a restrictive particle (*avadhāraṇa*)—with that [portion].
Alternatively, considering that the word *tad* (that), which recurs from the primary sūtra, is repeated here in its transformed form, he says: "of that very Viṣṇu.
The particle *eva* (very/only) has the sense of "also" (*api*).
Thus, the meaning is: "even though He is omnipresent, and even though He is distinct from the individual soul (*jīva*)."
But it does not refer to the individual soul (jīva);
thus, the particle "eva" (only) serves to exclude other [possibilities],
as indicated by the phrase "because it is to be perceived."
Because it is the object of worship;

by this, the objection that the mention of "having a small abode" is inappropriate for that which is unlimited—and that the reasoning regarding "consisting of the eye" and so forth is useless for that which is distinct from the individual soul—is resolved.
Furthermore, even though it is all-pervading, having a small abode is logical, just as in the case of space.

Now, in order to dispel the doubt that it is improper for that which is all-pervading to occupy a small space, he explains—intending a connection with the word "ca" (also) following the illustrative portion taken from the Sūtra, as well as a connection with the repeated word "iti" by supplying the word "api"—the phrase "sarvagatatve" [as follows]: "In the state of being all-pervading... [etc.]

The word "api" (also) is an explanation of the second "ca" (and). As stated in the Skanda Purāṇa: "Viṣṇu consists of all the senses and resides within all living beings; he is denoted by all names and is proclaimed by all the Vedas. // 7 //

As for the objection that it is improper to describe the Lord—who is distinct from the individual soul and possesses eternal knowledge—as being "consisting of the eye" and so forth due to His abundance of the eyes and other organs which are instruments of cognition, he refutes this by means of the Smṛti indicated by the word "ca" (and): "He consists of all the senses."

Viṣṇu is so called because he is established within all living beings (*prāṇin*). "Prāṇas" refers to the sense organs (*indriya*), and those who possess them are "living beings. He is situated among them as the controller of the senses; that is to say, he is the master of all the senses.
Therefore, the meaning is that He is said to consist of all the senses;
the intention is that the sense of "consisting of" (*maya*) here signifies lordship (*svāmitva*).
The word "and" (*ca*) provides the reason for the meaning of the second quarter-verse based on the meaning of the first quarter-verse.

In this way, the second and third quarters [of the verse] should also be explained through the relationship of cause and effect: because [the Self] resides within all living beings such as the sun and others, it is denoted by all names such as "the sun" and so forth.
For this very reason, the word *ca* (and) should be understood as serving to conjoin further qualifications, just like the *ca*s in the second and third quarters.
By this first quarter, [it is stated]: "consisting of sight, consisting of hearing, consisting of mind, consisting of speech."
Thus, it is explained that [the term "Aditya"] is applied to Brahman by way of its being the cause [of the sun] through its lordship over it.

In this manner, by means of the second and third quarters [of the verse], which state that the sun and other entities are denoted by their respective names because they reside within that [Brahman], it is shown that the Vedic scripture concerning Aditya actually denotes the Lord.
By this very [explanation], the contradiction regarding the logical impossibility of the term not applying to the sun is also resolved.

By the fourth quarter [of the verse], it is established as logical that Viṣṇu consists of the *chandas* (Vedic meters), because he is the primary meaning of the Veda as expressed by the word *chandas*.

In the *Aitareya-bhāṣya*, it is stated: "He consists of the eye because his power of vision is complete; he consists of the ear because his power of hearing is complete; he consists of the *chandas* because his desires are true; he consists of the mind because he is the knower of all; he consists of speech because he is the speaker of all; and he is the Self because he is the embodiment of the full fruit [of existence]."
Likewise, in the *Bṛhadbhāṣya*, having proposed the thesis: "The suffix *mayaṭ* has the senses of 'abounding in' (*prācuryārtha*) and 'consisting of its own nature' (*svarūpa*)," it states:
"Because [the Self] is the essential nature of all seers, it is said to be 'consisting of sight' (*cakṣurmaya*)."
"Because he possesses the nature of all hearers, he is declared to be composed of hearing.
Likewise, in the *Bhāgavata-tātparya*:
"Since all things reside in Viṣṇu, he is indeed composed of everything (*sarvamaya*)."
Thus, in another manner, the Lord’s nature of consisting of the eye (*cakṣurmayatva*) and so forth has been explained.
After the words "in the Skanda [Purāṇa]," the phrase "because it was stated" is to be understood as the ellipsis.

The connection with the qualified probandum (*upaskṛtasādhya*) is as follows: even though this [Lord] is distinct from the individual soul (*jīva*), His nature of consisting of the eye and so forth is appropriate by virtue of His being the master of the sense organs and the like; therefore, there is no inconsistency in that.

If it is argued that Nārāyaṇa is not the one spoken of everywhere because of these subverting factors— namely, the statement in the passage beginning with "in all beings" (*sarveṣu bhūteṣu*) that he has his abode in the heart of a child (*arbhakaukastva*), the description of him as "consisting of the eye" (*cakṣurmaya*) and so forth which refers to the individual soul (*jīva*) in that manner, and the designation of him as the Sun (*āditya*)— we reply: no.
In this regard, since there is no subverting evidence and because qualities such as having a small abode are applicable to Viṣṇu alone,

it should not be argued that the mention of a small abode for the unlimited [Brahman] or the mention of being "consisting of the eye" and so forth for one distinct from the individual soul (jīva) are purposeless.

Thus, because it is to be honored (*cāyṛ* means "to worship" and "to observe"); for even that very Viṣṇu, though unlimited, has the purpose of being described in order to be worshipped through such modes as having a small abode or consisting of sight, so that the statement of those [attributes] is meaningful for the sake of meditation (*upāsana*).
Nor should it be said that the description of having a small abode and so forth is inappropriate for Brahman, which is undivided and distinct from the individual soul;
for [the text says] "and thus" (*evaṃ ca*),
meaning even though it is all-pervading, it is "like space" (*vyomavat*).
Therefore, its being "consisting of sight" (*cakṣurmaya*) and so forth is appropriate because it occupies a small space.

Just as the unevolved space (*avyākṛtākāśa*), though all-pervading, resides in a single location such as a hut, so too is the residence of Brahman within the hearts of beings and the like appropriate.

And since this is so, even though Viṣṇu is distinct from the individual soul (*jīva*), the application of terms such as "consisting of sight" is appropriate by virtue of his being the master of the senses and so forth; thus the meaning of the Sūtra has been explained.
Sūtra—Oṃ.
If it is argued that there is the attainment of enjoyment [in the intermediate state], we say no, because of the difference in nature. Om.

If it is argued that since the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*para*) reside in one and the same body, they must experience identical enjoyments, we say: no. Having raised this objection—which is a repetition of a previous point—the author presents the sūtra as a resolution: "sambhoga" and so forth.

Here, carrying over the word "evam" (thus) from the preceding sūtra, he first explains the portion of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), demonstrating the logical consequence (*āpādaka*) indicated by that term, with the words: "jīva" and so forth.
The meaning is "of the individual self (jīva) and the supreme self (paramātman).
"Oneness" (ekatā).

The sense is that since Viṣṇu resides in all bodies, he necessarily comes to reside in the same body as the individual soul (jīva). Relying on the fact that the prefix *sam-* has the meaning of "identical" (*samāna*), as in the rule *avyavahṛpaṇossamarthayoḥ*, he says: "identical" (*samāna*).
Even in the case of the position that [the soul] is the Lord (Īśvara), the remainder of the sentence is "this [soul] is not omnipresent," because the subverting arguments are equal.
He explains the part concerning the refutation: "No" (na).
The meaning is that there is no attainment of identical enjoyment for the Lord.

[The phrase] "because of the distinction of capacity" [is used]. To which [objection] does "no" refer? He applies the portion "because of the distinction" as the reason for that: "sāmarthya... [and so on].

The suffix *ṣyañ* is used in the sense of the base word itself, or it denotes the state (*bhāva*) of that which qualifies. Thus, the meaning is that when another person does not obtain equal enjoyment, [the distinction arises] even from the living being due to a specific excellence of capacity (*sāmarthya-vaiśeṣyāt*).
And it is said in the Gāruḍa:

"Due to the distinction between omniscience and limited knowledge, and due to the distinction between total power and limited power, as well as between independence and dependence, there is no equality in enjoyment between the Lord and the individual soul. Thus [ends verse] 8.
Thus concludes the section on omnipresence.
What is that specific excellence of capacity by which there is no attainment of equal enjoyment? To this, he says: "It has been stated."

The conjunction "ca" (and) has the sense of inclusion, indicating that not only is the absence of equality in enjoyment between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśa) stated in the Sūtra, but their distinction in capacity is also stated there as the reason for it; furthermore, this is also stated in the Gāruḍa Purāṇa.
To address the question "What was said?", he recites the following verse: "O Omniscient One... and so forth.
The meaning is: by means of the two differentiating attributes consisting of omniscience and limited knowledge.

To avoid the objection that [the attribute] has already been established, even though Viṣṇu possesses the capacity [to prevent it], the initial establishment [of the attribute] would nonetheless occur, just as the burning of one who obstructs fire is nonetheless established.
Yet, even that [establishment] is not possible in the case of the Blessed One.
The mention of "omniscience" here is made with the intention that it is possible for Him [the Lord] to ward off future sublation by virtue of His omniscience;

however, even when residing in the same body as the individual soul (*jīva*), independence is not the cause for the soul's experience of pleasure alone while abandoning suffering. Rather, it should be distinguished that the dependence of the *jīva* in experiencing both [pleasure and pain] is due to its lack of autonomy.
"Sambhoga" means equal enjoyment;
"gāruḍa" is the grammatical connection [of the term].
And as for the reading "iti ca," the word "ca" (and) there serves the purpose of conjunction with what was stated previously.

If it is argued: "Just as the Sūtra has stated that the objection—the impossibility of all [souls] experiencing identical enjoyments—is a sublation [of the view] that a single soul resides in all bodies;

likewise, accepting that the Lord (Īśa) is present in all beings, there is a sublation consisting in the Supreme [Lord] attaining enjoyments identical to those of the individual soul (jīva) when both the soul and the Lord reside in one body.
Therefore, the Lord does not reside in all beings"—if this is said, we reply: no.

Why is this so? Because even when that [fire] has not reached him, there is a specific excellence of power compared to a living being, just as there is an absence of burning for one who has paralyzed fire; such is the meaning of the Sūtra as it has been stated. // 1 //
Thus concludes the section on omnipresence.
2. The Section on Non-Selfhood (Attṛtva-adhikaraṇa)
It has been stated: "From which [proceeds] the birth, etc., of this [world].
In that context, the quality of being an eater is described: "Whatever he created, he resolved to eat; because he eats everything, that is the nature of Aditi."
(Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.2.5) — thus it is understood from the case of Aditi.

In this section, the reconciliation of the characteristic mark of being the "begetter" (tṛtva), which is mentioned alongside the word "Aditi" that is well-known in a sense other than [the primary Vedic one], is established with reference to Hari.

Having cited the subject passage, he indicates the connection with the scriptures and so forth, as well as the subject matter, the doubt, and the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) along with its supporting arguments, by the words "janma... (Brahmasūtra 1.3.30).
The meaning is that in the *Janmādi-sūtra*, Viṣṇu’s status as the agent of birth and so forth is stated.
Regarding the word "therein" (*tatra*):
it means among those [entities] possessing the characteristics previously mentioned.
The word "entered" is to be supplied as the ellipsis;
[the phrase] "the state of being an eater" [is explained as follows].
At the time of creation, he creates everything; at the time of dissolution, he consumes it again.
He is the creator, the protector, and likewise the devourer (as stated in the Skanda Purāṇa).

In such passages as these, the meaning is that "it" (tat) refers to the state of being an eater—like a spider and so forth—which is denoted by many words derived from the verbal root *ad* (to eat), and which is understood through terms synonymous with "the absorber" (*saṃhartṛ*).

By this, the doubt that there might be an over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the definition of "absorber" to Aditi—even though she is an eater according to the sense of the root *ad* as "eating"—is refuted.
The first word "iti" is found in the Vedic text itself.
The second view, however, belongs to the author of the Bhāṣya: the word *aditeḥ* is repeated;
therein, one instance has existence (*bhāva*) as its primary meaning.
And likewise, in the passage from the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, that which is perceived as "the state of not perishing" (attṛtva) must belong to Aditi alone, the mother of the gods.
Why? Because of the mention of "Aditi" (aditeḥ).
Likewise, the construction is: "and because of the indicative mark of being Aditi.
And being Aditi is a property residing in Aditi alone, like cowness and so forth;
it has no scope in Viṣṇu.

Because this [sūtra] raises the objection that the definition stated in the *janmādi-sūtra* is either over-extensive (*ativyāpti*) or impossible (*asambhava*), its connection is one of objection (*ākṣepikī saṅgati*).
The subject matter (*viṣaya*) is the quality of being the "eater" (*mattṛtva*) mentioned in the Śruti;
the doubt (*saṃśaya*) is whether this refers to Viṣṇu or to someone else.
The prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that [the one who eats the honey] is Aditi, the mother of the gods;
thus, both the scriptural mention of Aditi and the logical reason of her being Aditi are indicated.
Regarding the meaning of the scripture in the prima facie view, [the word] "he" (*saḥ*)—

Aditi, the mother of the gods, under the name Saṃvatsara, the four-faced one, "resolved to eat whatever she created"; [the word] "mind" follows, and the ellipsis is "she ate. Why does Aditi possess the quality of being the eater of all?
Because she consumes everything and everyone, that very quality constitutes the "Aditi-ness" of Aditi, the divine mother;
it is the basis for her being designated by the word "Aditi," for otherwise that would not be the case.
Even in this view, this is the etymological explanation of the word "iti" from another location.
Here, the word "all" (sarva) refers, according to the *Sudhā* commentary, to all that is fit to be eaten by Aditi;
or, according to the *Ṭīkā*, it refers to a restricted sense of "all."
According to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), the meaning of the Vedic text is as follows:
"He"—the four-faced one named Saṃvatsara—"whatever he created, all that he resolved to eat";
thus Janārdana, bearing the name Mṛtyu, took hold [of it].
And [the word] "āda" [is used].
From what [source] is Viṣṇu's quality of being the destroyer of all [derived]?
From the word "aditeḥ," that is, from the term "aditi."
For in another Vedic text it is said, "Aditi is indeed all this... whatever exists here" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.6), and "Aditi consists of the deities" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 4.7);
that is to say, because the word *aditi* is used for Brahman in these other scriptural passages.
Even by that much, how can Viṣṇu possess omnivorousness?
For "the state of being Aditi" (adititvam) belongs precisely to that which is denoted by the word "Aditi," which is feminine in gender and signifies "she who eats all."
The meaning is that [Viṣṇu's] being denoted by the word "Aditi" would otherwise be without a basis;
by this, it is stated that regarding Viṣṇu’s status as the devourer of all, the word "Aditi" found in another scriptural passage serves as the reason.
For it has been said in the *Candrikā*:

"It is possible to employ the word *Aditi*—which is applied to Brahman in another Vedic passage as being based on the quality of being the devourer of all (*sarvāttṛtva*)—as a reason for the previously stated omnivorousness (*sarvāttṛtā*) expressed by the phrase 'He eats that and that'.
For this very reason, it is stated in the *Ṛgbhāṣya*: "Because He eats the universe, He is Aditi; thus [He is] Viṣṇu.

And in that same work, it is further stated: "The state of being indivisible (*akhaṇḍitatva*), characterized by infinity in terms of qualities (*guṇa*) and time (*kāla*), is the basis for the application of the word *Aditi*."
And the masculine form "sa yadyadevāsṛjata" is used just as in such passages as "He is called the immutable, the unchanging" (Bhagavad Gītā 15.16).
"But surely, if this non-eating belongs to Aditi, how then is the masculine form 'sa' (he) appropriate for her?
Therefore, by that [masculine gender], there would be a contradiction with the Śruti and other authorities. To this, he says: "sa" (he).
The meaning is that [the word] "śrutam" (is heard) occurs in the sentence.
Immediately after the phrase "ityādivat," the words "is joined to Aditi" (*adityāṃ yujyate*) are to be supplied as the remainder.
The particle *ca* has the sense of "but" (*tu*).
By the word "etcetera" (ādipadena), the statement of the Chandogas, "I know Vāyu as the calf of the quarters," is included.
That which stands immutably like a peak (kūṭa)— that is, like space (ākāśa)— is called *kūṭastha*.
The meaning of the Gītā verse is that *prakṛti* is called "imperishable" (*akṣara*) because it is indestructible in relation to the body.
[The word] "calf" (*vatsam*) refers to the arms of the Lord situated in the four directions, beginning with the east, which are designated by the term "directions."
From that, "wind" was born;
"I know" means "I understand" the principal vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa).
This is the speech of Lakṣmī. To this, it is said: Sūtra—Oṃ.
The Self [is the cause], because of the inclusion of both the moving and the non-moving. Om.
He introduces the sūtra that establishes the final position with the words: "In this regard."
To this objection, the solution is stated by the author of the Sūtras—the word "iti" (thus) being understood as the remainder [of the sentence].
By this, it is shown that the remainder of the phrase "it is said here in the Sūtra" is implied.
He recites that Sūtra: "attā" (the self).
The word "that" (tat) is carried over [from the previous context] and is modified;
thus, in this sentence, that which is the "eater" (attā);
He who is called the "Absorber" is Viṣṇu himself.
Why? Because [the text says] "he eats everything" and "of the moving and the unmoving."

The meaning of the sūtra is as follows: because the universe, consisting of both sentient and insentient forms, is not grasped [as its object] due to its being the primordial source and its being subject to dissolution; that is to say, because of the mark (liṅga) of being the devourer of all that is moving and unmoving.
For Aditi does not possess the quality of being the devourer of everything, whether moving or unmoving.

He addresses the doubt that the inferential mark (*liṅga*) might have another possible application—namely, that even if [the Self] is grasped as the primordial cause of the moving and non-moving world, why should it follow that He is the giver of that [fruit]?—with the words "For not... (*na hi*).
The word *hi* indicates what is well-known.
Having cited the words of the sūtra as "of the moving and the non-moving" (*carācarasya*), the commentary explains them as "of all" (*sarvasya*) in accordance with the Śruti.
Nor should it be argued that this explanation by means of a general term is useless.
This is because the purpose [of this passage] is to dispel the perception of contradiction with the Śruti regarding the Sūtra.
"Aditi" refers to the mother of the gods.
He alone is indeed the creator, the protector, and likewise the consumer of everything.
"Vāsudeva is the supreme among men; others are either [supreme] over a small portion or not at all"—thus it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa.
To the question, "How is it established that even Viṣṇu is the devourer of the moving and the unmoving? he says: "The Creator."
"Vāsudeva is the supreme among men"; he is "the highest" (uttama) compared to them;
Kṛṣṇa is "one alone."
He is the sole independent "creator" (sraṣṭā)— the maker of the entire world—
and likewise the "protector" (pātā),
meaning the guardian; the word "tu" has the sense of "and."
And here:
"those other than Vasudeva"; whereas Brahmā and the others are "of the small."
They are the agents of creation and so forth for only one part of the world, not independently;
this is the meaning with respect to their lack of independence.
The phrase "because it is stated immediately after [the words] 'in the Skanda'" is the completion of the sentence.

"He who alone was in the beginning of this world, from whom the protector of the universe arose—he to whom the world returns at the final dissolution, may that Lord Hari consume the clarified butter here for our long life.
Thus says the Śruti (the Ghṛtasūkta). 9.
Because its meaning is clear, having first cited a Smṛti, he also cites a Śruti on this very point: "One... (Ekaḥ).
There is a repetition of the word "one" (eka), and there is also both a repetition and a transformation of the word "this" (idam). And thus, that which is one is "this."
He existed "before" this world during the dissolution; and from whom, at the time of creation, "this" [world] arose.
"The world came into being"; it was born.
Then, he who was the one "gopāḥ"—the protector—of the becoming, he became [the guardian].
And that God Hari, who at the time of liberation and dissolution enters the world like one who has swallowed boiled rice— for our long life.
"Come here for the sake of longevity"; having come to the place of sacrifice, "eat the ghee," which is the form of the oblation.
"May he accept"—this is the meaning of the Taittirīya Śruti.
This is the statement of the seer (ṛṣi) who perceived the mantra.
Following the word "iti" [from the Śruti], the word "yataḥ" (from which) is to be supplied as the remainder.
Therefore, from this also, it is established that Viṣṇu is the devourer of the moving and the unmoving; such is the syntactical connection.
Sūtra—Oṃ.
And because of the context. // Oṃ // BBs 1.2.10 // 10 //

When it is established that the Eater is Viṣṇu alone by the sublation of the indicative marks of being the "Eater of All" (which are without scope) and the indicative marks of being "Aditi" and so forth (which have scope), based merely on the former, then what need is there to mention that this is so when the indicative mark is conjoined with the context which is itself without scope? Having stated this meaning, he reads and explains the Sūtra: "And because of the context" (prakaraṇācca).

The meaning of the Sūtra is that the "Eater" is indeed Viṣṇu alone, on account of the force of the context concerning Viṣṇu which admits of no other possibility, as seen in the passage, "There is nothing here whatsoever" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.2.6),
and because that context is established by [attributes such as] the creation of water, the year, and so forth.
Anticipating the objection that the Vaiṣṇava nature of this section is not established, he says: "By means of [the mention of] water, the year, creation, and so forth."
That which has the creation of the waters and the creation of the four-faced Brahmā named Saṃvatsara as its beginning is described thus.
By the word "beginning" (ādi), the signs such as the rising of the sun from the year are included,
because they belong to that same context.
The meaning is "because it belongs to the section concerning Viṣṇu"; the words "of this section" are to be supplied as the ellipsis. This [term] is an indicator for "understanding."

Therefore, from this context, Viṣṇu alone is what is being spoken of here; thus, there is a syntactical connection with the subject under discussion (*prakṛtasādhya*). The particle *ca* is used for the conjunction of reasons.
A "context" (*prakaraṇa*) consists of multiple sentences that establish a single object of knowledge (*prameya*).
For in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad it is said: "In the beginning, indeed, nothing whatsoever existed here.
This was covered by death alone;
for hunger is death. He [the Self] created the mind, thinking, 'May I have a self.'"
He moved about worshipping. From him, as he was worshipping, water was born. That which was the foam of the waters solidified;

it became the earth. Upon it, he exerted himself. He desired, "May a second self be born from me. Through mind and speech, he entered into union; for hunger is death. That became semen; it became a year. Him—

"Having been born, He opened His mouth; He uttered speech, and that became Vāk. He reflected: 'If indeed I should think of this [universe], I shall create less food. With that speech and with that self, He created all this. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.2).
Thus, many scriptural passages concerning Viṣṇu are heard.
"At the beginning" means at the time of dissolution; "here" refers to the group of dependent beings, or alternatively, to the sky.
"Kiñcana": there was no object whatsoever, whether of the nature of a living being or insentient matter.
But [it may be objected]: "Viṣṇu, the destroyer of all; the Goddess; likewise the individual souls; Time;
the equilibrium of the three qualities (guṇas); actions; the vital breath; and the senses—" [all these existed].
Neither the formative impressions nor the Vedas existed at all in that dissolution, apart from him.
Since this statement might be questioned on the grounds that even eternal individual souls (jīvas) exist—as evidenced by the citation from the *Bṛhadbhāṣya*—it is therefore said: "by Mṛtyu alone.
"This"—referring to the individual soul and so forth—is "enveloped by Mṛtyu," that is, by Janārdana who bears that name.
It was covered.
The reason for Death's state of being a coverer is "by hunger" (*aśanāyayā*); the meaning is: by that which leads the world of food (*aśa*).
He states that death’s nature as hunger is well-known from the Śruti: "For hunger indeed...
Because of being alone, "that" death desired: "May I be embodied," that is, may I possess a body in the form of the world.
Thus that Death, "worshipping"—that is, adoring his own self—proceeded; as he was worshipping, the waters were produced. The sense is that those very waters were the means for his worship.
There, among the waters, that which was the essence of the waters in the form of foam— that was the arrow.
That arrow was struck by Death, who is without seed.
He was brought to a state of aggregation; that which is an aggregate is "earth," and it took the form of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*). "In that [egg],"...
On the earth, in Śvetadvīpa, Death rested; he lay down.
That Death [said], "Me."
"I shall have a self," [he thought]; "Brahmā shall be born as a second from me with respect to Vāyu"—thus he desired. Then there was hunger.
That Death [is associated] with the "mind"; with "speech" according to his own will;
and with Śrī, who presides over the Vedas, as his "mate."
It "became a pair" (dvandvībhāvam asambhavat); that is, it attained union. Through that state of copulation, whatever semen there was, "that became the year";
that is, it became the four-faced one named Saṃvatsara, possessing a body composed of the constituent elements.
Then, aiming at the newborn one-year-old child to devour him,
Death opened his own mouth;
that year, out of fear, made the sound "bhāṇiti," which is the speech that awakens bliss through the splendor of Viṣṇu.
Whatever word he uttered, that very speech, presided over by her, became Sarasvatī by name.
That Mṛtyu reflected; what did he reflect? "If this..."
"I shall disregard the year";
"I shall make it [the year] sluggish"; "then that will be less for me"; "I shall make the food scanty."
Then, having reflected, "May there be abundant food," that Death created all this by means of that speech— Sarasvatī— and by means of that self— the four-faced one.
"Janayāmāsa" (he brought forth) is the meaning of the Vedic text.
"In the beginning, there was nothing whatsoever here; at that time, Death existed as Hari.
That Janārdana, by means of his own mind, drew forth the waters alone."
Lying upon them, the Blessed Lord created a vast cosmic egg;
there, the Sovereign brought forth Brahmā, known as Saṃvatsara.
Opening its mouth to devour him, it then let out a roar;
then Viṣṇu, out of compassion, employed it for the work of creation.
Thus the omnipresent Lord created the entire universe for the sake of Hari’s sustenance today.
Thus, in the Brahmavaivarta [Purāṇa], verse 10.
Thus ends the section concerning the non-eater. // 2 //

Now, one might ask: even though the creation of water, the year, and so forth are mentioned here, how can it be determined that this is a section concerning Viṣṇu? To address this, with the intention that the creation of water, the year, and so forth are marks (liṅga) of Viṣṇu, he cites a Smṛti passage regarding their being such marks: "nehāsīt" (here there was not).
"In the beginning," at the time of dissolution, "here," within this group of dependent beings, "not even anything"— neither a living soul nor the insentient— existed.
Is this not improper, given that the individual soul (*jīva*) and other entities are eternal? To this he says: "Death.
At the time of dissolution (*pralaya*), Hari, named Death, existed as the veiler of the individual soul and the rest.
The intention is that there is no inconsistency in stating "it did not exist" because it was concealed;
thus, the word division is "saḥ ātmanaḥ" (he [was] from himself).
In the case of mantras, there is the elision of the initial *ā* of *ātman* according to the rule "mantreṣvāṅyāderātmanaḥ";
thus, [the form] is "saḥ."
The Lord Viṣṇu, by his own will and without the aid of a mind, created the waters;
in those waters, he [created] that which is greater than the great (mahattara).
The suffix *tarap* is used in its own sense;
he created the "great" (*mahat*) or "vast" (*sthūlam*) egg, the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍam*).

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) here is: "In that egg, he created Brahmā, who is called Saṃvatsara. By the word "named" (*nāma*), it is stated that the term *saṃvatsara* is well-known as referring to the Four-faced One (Brahmā), based on the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) that he "perfectly causes those who have become his children to delight" (*ramayati*). To avoid the charge of lack of capacity [to create], the word "Lord" (*prabhuḥ*) is used.
Viṣṇu opened his mouth wide to devour— that is, to consume— that four-faced one; he gaped.
Then Brahmā "uttered" (avirurāva); the meaning is that he made the sound "bhāṇ.
The particle "ha" indicates that this matter is well-known in the Śruti.
Then, immediately after the act of devouring, "out of compassion for him"— that is,
out of compassion for that four-faced one— Viṣṇu, having not swallowed him, employed him in the work of creation.
"That omnipresent one," the four-faced Brahmā, created the world for Hari, for the sake of Hari's food.

Alternatively, the construction is to be completed by supplying the words "he created the world" and "having created it, he offered it to Hari," following the statement from the *Brahmavaivarta* Purāṇa.
The connection is with the supplied probandum (sādhya): "Therefore, the creation of the waters, the year, and so forth, is established as having Viṣṇu as its characteristic."
Thus ends the section concerning the Eater (Attṛtva). // 2 //
3. The Section on the Cave (Guha-adhikaraṇa)
The One who consumes all is declared to be supreme:
"Drinking the Truth (ṛta) in the world of good deeds, having entered the cave in the highest upper realm,
those who know Brahman and those who have performed the three Nāciketa rites call them Shadow and Light" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.3.1).
Thus, two who are drinking are perceived; but who are they?
In this section, the concordance (*samanvaya*) of the mark of being the enjoyer of the fruits of actions—well-known from worldly usage elsewhere—to Viṣṇu is established.
Having first cited the subject passage (*viṣayavākya*), he indicates the subject matter (*viṣaya*) along with its connection to the preceding section (*pūrvādhikaraṇa*): "All... and so forth.
Because the "Supreme" (paraḥ) is the "Supreme Self" (paramātmā), who is "one" (ekaḥ)—
endowed with the number one— and is the "devourer of all" (sarvāttā).
And he is the destroyer of all;

therefore, because the meanings of the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*) are joined therein, the meaning is that he is expressed by words that indicate the gender of verbal actions such as "the devourer of all" (*sarvāttṛ*).
The intention is that by the very statement "devourer of all," it is also implied by the sense of the matter that he is the "protector" (*pātṛ*).
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "The Truth" (*ṛtam*).
This is to be connected with the beginning of the passage starting with "therein" (*tatra*).
And thus, "therein":
In the Kaṭha Upaniṣad, where the state of being a drinker— which is a specific instance included within the general state of being an eater—
is mentioned in the passage "the two drinking the ṛta," the construction is that two [beings] are perceived as the enjoyers of the essence of the fruits of action.
The intention is that duality is understood through the dual number.
By this, the Blessed One's status as the "Eater" (Matter) is appropriate there, because both the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*) are applicable;

however, here, in the Supreme Self who is free from the bondage of karma, it is not so, because the meaning of the base is impossible in that which is non-dual, and the meaning of the suffix is likewise inapplicable.

The connection of this [adhikaraṇa] with the preceding one arises either from an objection based on a previous discrepancy— namely, that the term *piba* has a dual ending— or from an implied objection (ākṣepa) regarding the impossibility of the previously established sense of "drinker" residing in anything other than [the two], or from the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) if it were to exist in another as well.
And the object designated as "the state of being the enjoyer" (pātṛtva) is also indicated.

In the subject-sentence, the meaning of the genitive case is the relationship between the produced and the producer; thus, in the phrase "in the world of good deeds" (*sukṛtasya loke*), it refers to the body created by good deeds—that is, the body caused by merit—according to the *Tattvapradīpa*. Having entered the cave of the heart within that [body], they are also "supreme" (*parame*) within that cave.

The term *sarvajīvottama* means "the highest among all living beings. *Ā* refers to that which is half-filled (*ārdha*). *Parārdha* means "half of the others," namely half of [the space] belonging to others such as Rudra and so forth.
The word "in that" (*tasmin*) implies "in the wind" (*vāyau*), meaning it is completely full.
Thus, having entered there, they are supported by the wind residing in the cave of the heart (*hṛdayaguhā*). This is the sense.
"He, being distressed, went to his father's side" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.3.4)—

according to this scripture cited in the *Tattvapradīpa*, because it is the abode of the Supreme Brahman and because it is the locus of the individual soul's identification [with the body], the body is called "the other half" (*parārdha*). Likewise, *ṛta* and *satya* are designated as *dharma* and *sukṛta* (meritorious action).

According to the Smṛti cited in the *Gītābhāṣya*, "Ṛta is the dharma of the mind" (*ṛtaṃ tu mānaso dharmaḥ*), the term "Ṛta" is used figuratively to denote the fruit obtained through actions prescribed by the scriptures. Thus, the two specific forms of the Lord known as the Inner Self (*antarātman*) and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), who exist as "drinking the Ṛta"— that is, enjoying it— are called "the knowers of Brahman."
The knowers of Brahman are "those who maintain the five fires," meaning those who perform the five great sacrifices known as the Devayajña, Pitṛyajña, Bhūtayajña, Manuṣyayajña, and Brahma-yajña.
As it is said: "This sacrifice is fivefold: the Agnihotra, the Darśapūrṇamāsa, the Cāturmāsya, the Animal sacrifice, and the Soma sacrifice."
Or, it refers to the five great sacrifices (pañcamahāyajña) taught in the Aitareya [Āraṇyaka];

or it refers to the mastery of the knowledge of the five fires known as heaven, rain, earth, man, and woman. Naciketas is the name of a seer (ṛṣi); that which belongs to Naciketas is "Nāciketa," referring to a specific type of fire-altar construction (agnicayana).
