The meaning is that those who have performed the Nāciketa fire-altar rite three times— those among the wise and those among the sinful— are respectively called "shadow and sunlight," which serve as the causes of happiness and suffering.
This secondary designation as "shadow and sunlight," insofar as it consists in being the cause of happiness and suffering, is not contradictory because the respective correlates differ.
As it is stated in the *Tattvapradīpa*: "The meaning is that they are the ones who gladden the immortals (*amarāḥ*) and cause distress to the demons (*asurāḥ*).
By means of the question and its subject matter, he shows the manner of the doubt rooted therein: "'Those two' refers to the two who drink, as mentioned in the Śruti."
The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "In this sentence, who are those two who are perceived as 'the two drinking'?

By this, the doubt is indicated: "Are the two drinking the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Lord (*para*), or are they both of the nature of the Supreme [Lord] alone? Immediately after the word "iti," the remainder of the sentence is: "When such a doubt exists, and when the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that 'the Lord together with the individual soul drinks'."
It is said: Sū-oṃ.
For by seeing that [Self], the two selves have entered the cave. Om.
"Having entered the cave, they are drinking, being indeed of the nature of Viṣṇu.
Then, introducing the sūtra which establishes the final conclusion, he explains it with the words: "It is said."
The word "iti" (thus) is to be supplied after the sūtra.
The phrase "entered into the cave" is a qualifying attribute containing a reason.
The word "drinking" is an explanation of the term "ātman."
The word "ṛtam" (truth) and so forth is to be supplied [from the preceding verse].
"In the forms of Viṣṇu" is another explanation for the term "the two selves.
And thus: those two selves who drink the truth are indeed the two selves in the forms of Viṣṇu.
Why? Because the construction is "the two who have entered the cave.
By the word "eva" (indeed), the meaning of the particle "tu" (but/however) which recurs [in the verse] is expressed.

Although one should say "Viṣṇū" (the two Viṣṇus), the expression "viṣṇurūpe eva" (indeed the two forms of Viṣṇu) is intended to show that the dual number has scope by intending to express two distinct forms.
This is because that [state] is seen in such passages as: "The two heats have pervaded the threefold on all sides; Mātariśvan has attained their favor" (Ṛgveda 10.114.1).

Now, one might object: since Viṣṇu enters all bodies in only a single form, how can the use of the dual number be justified even with the intention of referring to two forms? To this, he cites the scriptural passage indicated by the portion of the Sūtra beginning with "taddarśanāt" (from the observation thereof):
"gharmeti."
The words "the two Blessed Ones" and "to perform" are to be supplied as ellipses;
the word "trivṛtam" (threefold) is repeated.
And thus: "Gharmāḥ" means the two blazing ones, or the two who rub, or the two who contract.
"Nṛsiṃha is called Gharma because he grinds all the worlds."
This is because of the statement in the *Aitareya-bhāṣya* and because of the statement in the *Tattva-pradīpa*: "And by being pervasive (*ghṛṣṭatvena*), [they are] in the limited (*mitau*).
"Samantau" means the two pervaders; they are those who pervade primordial matter (*prakṛti*), the individual soul (*puruṣa*), and time (*kāla*).

The two Blessed Ones, who are complete in terms of place, time, and power, "entered" (vyāpatuḥ)—that is, they entered specifically—that body composed of the threefold [elements] of fire, water, and food; they reached the abode within the cave of the heart of that body.
Of those two, "the favor" (juṣṭim)...
Even ‘Mātariśvā’, the primary wind, went to the triple-layered [world] to perform service;
[he drank] the milk, the breast-milk, of the goddess ‘Div’, the wife of Vāyu.
‘Didhiṣāṇāḥ’ means desiring to drink;
the gods, thirsting, ‘aveṣan’— that is, they sought— that one who has a twofold form.
The meaning of the Śruti is that they know Him as "arka"— *araṃ* meaning *alam*, sufficient— and as "sahasāman," meaning accompanied by Vāyu.
However, in the *Gurvarthadīpikā*, having made the word division *samantāt* and supplied the words *vidyamānau*, it is explained as "those two who exist everywhere, [that is,] who are all-pervading."
"That is to be considered," and so forth;
the word "by the sentence" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
By the word "etcetera," the second half [of the verse], "The milk of heaven," is included; likewise:
"The single Suparṇa entered the ocean; he beholds this entire world."
I beheld him from nearby with a mature mind; the mother licked him, and he licked the mother.
And such passages as "The wise sages, through their words, fashion the single Suparṇa in many ways" (Ṛgveda 10.114.4, 5) are also included;
[referring to] "the single Suparṇa."
The Blessed One, whose nature is supreme bliss, has entered the ocean;
He beholds—sees—all this world.
With a matured mind, I have seen Him, the Supreme Self.
"She licks him"—because she manifests him, Speech is Sarasvatī;
"she licks" means she licks as it were.
That Supreme Self licks his mother.
Those two are mutually connected;
and thus, the sense is that even the words which manifest the Blessed One possess the quality of being manifested by Him.
[The seers] [perceive] that very one, the single *suparṇa*. "The wise ones" (*viprāḥ*).
The meaning is that eminent poets, through their words— namely, speech— conceive of and contemplate Him who exists in twelve ways, such as Keśava and others, in many forms.
"Because of the observation of that" means because it has been stated that Viṣṇu, by virtue of his dual form, enters all bodies.
Thus, the sense is that even though Viṣṇu is one, the dual number is appropriate with the intention of referring to his two forms.

In this way, according to the method of the *Tattvapradīpa*, this [interpretation] should also be explained as follows: since the dual number is seen in reference to Viṣṇu—who has been determined by the aforementioned qualifiers—through such passages as "one bird" (*ekaḥ suparṇaḥ*) where He is referred to by the singular pronoun *tat*; and since He alone, who dwells in the ocean and beholds all worlds, is shown to have entered the cave in the passage "I saw Him from nearby" (*apaśyam antitaḥ*); and since He alone is shown to possess many names and forms.
The Self and the Inner Self—Hari alone exists in two ways;
eternally established in the heart, He drinks the juice born of karma.
And thus it is stated in the *Bṛhatsaṃhitā*.

Now, one might object: even if the meaning of the suffix is established by intending two forms in Viṣṇu, since it is impossible for Him to be the enjoyer of the fruit of action—which is the meaning of the nominal stem—He cannot be the subject of the sentence "Ṛta. To this, he says: "The Self."
Hari alone, due to the distinction between the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of the body and the individual soul (jīva), exists in two forms as the Self (ātman) and the Inner Self (antarātman);
thus he has become twofold,
being seated within the hearts of both the body and the individual soul.

Alternatively— according to the method of the *Ṭīkā*— without even intending to distinguish between limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), [the Self], residing in the body in a twofold manner, "constantly" (*nityam*) and "regularly" (*niyamena*) "drinks" the "juice born of karma," that is, the fruit.
The meaning is that he "enjoys.
In the reading *smṛtaḥ*, the meaning is "proclaimed.
By the word *rasa*, the Lord is meant as the enjoyer of the qualities that are the objects of enjoyment for the individual soul (*jīva*).
However, it has been indicated that the object of knowledge (*prameya*) is not the enjoyer of those objects of enjoyment;
this is connected with the phrase "because it is seen in the *Bṛhatsaṃhitā*" by means of the recurring statement [in the commentary].
Its meaning is: because the experience of the fruits of karma has already been stated.
And thus—the sense is that there is no inconsistency in this.
Not only in the *Bṛhatsaṃhitā*, but also:
"The ear, the eye, the sense of touch, the tongue, and likewise the nose."
"And having presided over the mind, he experiences the sense objects" (Bhagavad Gītā 15.9);
such is also the meaning in the Gītā.
"He always drinks what is auspicious; that Hari would never drink what is inauspicious."
"The activity of this one who consists of full bliss is not known anywhere," so it is said in the Padma Purāṇa.
Now, does the Lord experience suffering as the fruit of evil karma,
or happiness born of merit?
It is neither the first nor the second case.
Because it is full bliss, he says: "Auspicious."

‘Asau’ refers to ‘Hari’, the Lord who resides within the vital breath (prāṇa) present in all bodies; as the one who accepts the oblation in sacrifice and removes sin, He ‘nityam’— that is, invariably and by rule— ‘pibati’, meaning He partakes of or enjoys only the fruit of auspicious actions.
Hari does not "drink" the fruit of unwholesome karma; the meaning is that he does not experience it.
"Only merit goes to him" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.5.20).
According to the Śruti, "In the highest beyond" (Kaṭha 3.1),
one accepts non-duality regarding the agent who drinks the *ṛta*, as expressed by the word "drinks."
By this reasoning, having accepted the second position, the first position is refuted by non-acceptance.
He refutes the second objection—that there is no possibility of the enjoyment of bliss for one who consists of full bliss—with the words "of that which consists of full bliss" (*pūrṇānandamayasya*).
Here, the suffix *mayaṭ* is used in the sense of identity (*tādātmya*).
As stated in the *Gītā-bhāṣya*: "The suffix *mayaṭ* has three meanings: in the sense of identity (*tādātmya*), in the sense of modification (*vikāra*), and in the sense of abundance (*prācurya*).
And thus, the "activity" (*ceṣṭā*) of this Viṣṇu, whose nature is full bliss (*pūrṇānanda*).
The meaning is that at some time or in some place, sovereignty is not known in its entirety by anyone; nor is it even conceivable.
And thus, the sense is that the enjoyment of happiness is appropriate even for one who is full of bliss through the power of sovereignty.
Alternatively, since accepting Viṣṇu as the enjoyer would contradict the scriptural text, "The other [Self] does not eat" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.1), he says: "The auspicious."
The meaning of that statement is that its subject matter is either the absence of enjoyment dependent on others or the absence of enjoyment of what is unpleasant;
nor is it asserted that "the very state of being low or high constitutes the enjoyment of suffering and so forth," for such a state does not undergo [the condition of] being low or high.
If it is argued that this constitutes a contradiction in statements because the enjoyment of pleasure consists in the form of elevation (*uccatā*), it must be said in response:

since Viṣṇu’s acceptance of the pleasure inherent in the individual soul (*jīva*) is admitted merely as an act of taking possession, no specific modification (*vikriyāviśeṣa*) that would produce such elevation is admitted.

For it is said in the Tattvapradīpa: "Nor is there a contradiction with the scriptural text, 'Another [the Lord] does not eat while not eating,' for enjoyment [on the part of the individual soul] is not dependent on another."
Nor is there for Viṣṇu the experience of what is unpleasant, nor any sense of high or low status caused by that;
rather, it is merely said that he accepts the experience inherent in the individual soul (*jīva*).
Alternatively, "experience" refers to the direct realization [of objects] as one's own, which brings about the state of being high or low.
And that [being] intended [as the subject] is possessed of conceit (abhimāna), whereas this [conceit] does not exist in Īśvara; thus there is no contradiction.
The phrase "because it was stated immediately after [the passage from] the Pādma" is the ellipsis to be supplied.
And thus, the meaning is that there is no contradiction with scripture or reasoning.
By the word "hi" (for/indeed), he shows what is well-known from such passages as, "He who knows [Brahman] hidden in the cave" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1). // 11 //

[Objection: But how can it be determined that the one drinking is Viṣṇu on the basis of the mark of being seated in the cave (guhā), since that [mark] is applicable to the individual soul (jīva) as well? To this he says: "He who knows...
It should also be supplied that here the state of being seated in the cave must be understood as belonging to Viṣṇu alone.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), [the following are included]: "the Self, the inner Self";
"the ear, the eye";
and "having become Vaiśvānara, I [am]..."
The *smṛti* passage beginning with "thus" and so forth is understood here.

Thus, by means of the words "thus" and so forth, the author of the Sūtras indicates through the word "hi" (for/indeed) that what is to be accepted here is the well-known fact that Viṣṇu alone resides in the cave.
Furthermore, although the mere state of residing in the cave of the heart is possible for the individual soul (*jīva*), that is not what is taken as the reason here.

However, the intended meaning is that it is precisely the state of being hidden in the cave (*guhānihitatva*), as established by the Vedas and other authorities, which serves primarily as the mode of the knowledge that produces liberation; and this [state] has no application in the case of the individual soul (*jīva*).
In the Sūtra, only the word "but" (*tu*) is carried over from the Sūtra on Concordance (*samanvaya-sūtra*).
The term "two selves" (ātmānau) is repeated.

Thus, "the two selves" refers to the two enjoyers of the fruits of auspicious karma, as indicated by the word *ātman* through the etymological derivation: "that which experiences (*māti*) the happiness that is to be acquired (*ādeya-sukham*). Therefore, it means "the two selves indeed."
[The two] are indeed the two forms of Viṣṇu known as the Self (ātman) and the Inner Self (antarātman), and not the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara).
Why? Because they have entered the cave of the heart.
For it should not be argued that the mark of being "situated in the cave" (guhāniviṣṭatva) is possible even for the individual soul (jīva);
because that [mark] is not well-known from scripture and other sources,
and because only that which is well-known in such contexts is to be accepted.
The meaning of the word "hi" (for) is that [the drinking] is not well-known in the case of Viṣṇu from such scriptural passages as "He who knows.
Now, an objection is raised: in the case of Viṣṇu, the use of the dual number in the word "pibantau" (the two drinking) would be untenable.
And fearing that the entry [of the self] by means of the two forms through the entrance into *rūpa* is unestablished, he says: "Because of the observation of that" (*taddarśanāt*).

The meaning of the sūtra is: because of the observation of the mark (*liṅga*)—namely, Hari's abiding in the cave of the body and the heart (*hṛdayaguhā*) in his twofold form—as stated in the Śruti passage beginning with "the dharmas" (*gharmā*).

Here, by the recurrence of the word *tat* (that) and by the recurrence of the Vedic term (*śrauta-pada*), the proposition is established—just as in the case of "The one consisting of bliss is that Brahman"—and thus the statement "the two selves" (*ātmānau*) is made. He explains the purpose of the Vedic dual number with the words: "The Self... (*ātmeti*).

This is stated in order to express the designation "Smṛti" (the one who remembers), the application of the term used in the Śruti, and the inferential mark (*liṅga*) consisting of being the enjoyer of the fruits of auspicious actions, based on the etymological derivation that "one who perceives (*māti*) what is to be perceived (*ādeya*).

For it is said in the *Candrikā*: "Based on the etymological derivation that 'one perceives (*māti*) what is to be perceived (*ādeya*'), the state of being the enjoyer of the auspicious, denoted by the word 'Self' (*ātman*), is the fundamental reason.

Nor should one suspect a contradiction with other passages of that [text], on the grounds that this statement is made through the mention of entering the cave as being in grammatical apposition with the state of being the drinker of the immortal (*ṛtapātṛtva*).

For it is accepted that in that Sūtra, [the meaning] is established by way of stating such a qualified subject (viśeṣya), which is capable of being construed with another word ending in the dual number— a mark indicating that [the subject] has necessarily entered the cave. Likewise,

although the state of drinking the *ṛta* (merit) to be connected [to the subject] ought to be stated directly, and thus another sentence [containing that term] would also have to be adopted, it must nevertheless be stated by the very clear expression "two who drink the *ṛta*" (*ṛtaṃ pibantau*), just as [the Self within] is called the "Inner Controller" (*antaryāmī*) even without the etymological derivation [of the term].
However, there is no contradiction because the meaning is based on the word *ātman* [in its conventional sense];
otherwise, it would result in a contradiction with the stated statement.
And thus, in this regard, the explanations by some concerning the intention of the *Candrikā* are otherwise.

Likewise, the claim that there is a contradiction with the *Candrikā* regarding the statement "the word 'that' (tat) also carries over here from the *Samanvaya-sūtra*" is itself to be examined. For it is possible to convey the predicate (*vidheya*) by the very phrase "the two selves" (*ātmānau*), which must necessarily be stated both to justify the dual number in the *sūtra* and to provide the subject (*uddeśya*); thus, in the *īkṣati-sūtra*, the particle *tu* alone serves merely to exclude others.
This is because it is appropriate for that [word] to follow here;

furthermore, there would be a contradiction with the *Sudhā* on the *Samanvaya-adhikaraṇa*, which states that if "that" (*tat*) were not mentioned, the connection of the word "but" (*tu*) could not be understood,
since the intention is that there is no other word serving as the subject or the predicate.
Sūtra—Oṃ.
And because of the qualification.
"He who is the bridge for those performing sacrifices, the imperishable Brahman which is supreme" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.3.2).

Thus, since the inferential mark (*liṅga*) of being situated in a cave that allows no other possibility is stronger than even the dual-numbered scriptural mention (*śruti*) which allows for other possibilities, and since the status of being an enjoyer—which is the primary meaning of the root *pra-kṛ*—is possible only for Viṣṇu, it is established that He alone is the Protector; how much more so when there is also an unconditioned scriptural statement? Demonstrating this point, [the author] recites the sūtra and cites the very scriptural passage intended by it: "And because of the qualification" (*viśeṣaṇācca*).

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is thus: "because of the qualification. In the aphorism, the term *pibatoḥ* is carried over by modification; the particle *ca* is used for the conjunction of logical reasons.
And likewise, in the Śruti passage "He who is the bridge," because the two drinkers are qualified by singularity understood through the singular number, there is only one drinker.

And since he is qualified by being the bridge of the sacrificer, by being Brahman, by being the Imperishable (akṣara), and so forth, and because Brahman is further qualified by being "the highest" (para), it is Viṣṇu alone.
The meaning of the aphorism is that [the soul] is not the living being (jīva).
The word "and" (ca) implies that this is established not only by logical inference (liṅga), but also by scriptural texts such as those concerning the "bridge" (setu) and so forth.

The Blessed One, who possesses the two forms known as the Inner Self (Ātman) and the Supreme Self (Antarātman), is the "bridge"— the support— for those "performing sacrifice" (ijānānām), that is, those performing a sacrifice directed toward Viṣṇu;
He is that which is the Imperishable, the Supreme Brahman.
The meaning of the *Kāṭhaka* scripture is: "We are able"—that is, we are capable—"to state the means for meditating upon Him" with respect to Naciketas.
His qualities cannot be stated separately because of their immeasurability.
Therefore, by the word "Brahma," there would be the inclusion of all [the Vedas].
"Therefore, this word *brahman* is a qualifier of Viṣṇu alone;
for infinite qualities belong to Him, the Lord, and not to others. Thus it is stated in the *Brāhma-purāṇa*.
This recalls that the word *brahman* has the Blessed One as its sole referent—[as shown by the verse beginning with] "separately."
In this context, the word "yataḥ" (because) is repeated;
and thus, because the qualities of that Viṣṇu are "immeasurable."
Because they are innumerable, they cannot be described separately— that is, by distinguishing them individually.
And it is to be understood as the remainder that all these qualities must be known by all qualified aspirants.
Since the word "Brahman" would entail the comprehension of all qualities, the word "Brahman" is applied to that Viṣṇu for the purpose of knowing all his qualities; this is the implied meaning.
For by the word "Brahman," the inclusion of all qualities occurs.
And thus the word *brahman* denotes all qualities;
the sense is that it is impossible for it to produce knowledge of those [qualities] without a specific function (*vṛtti*).
For, apart from that all-pervading Viṣṇu, the qualities of other individual souls (*jīvas*) are not infinite.
However— since this is established by authoritative evidence (pramāṇa) regarding Viṣṇu alone,
for this reason, this word "Brahman" is a "qualifier" specifically of Viṣṇu; the meaning is that it is the primary designator of him and not of others.

The remainder [of the argument] is that immediately after the word "brāhma," it was stated that the word *brahma* refers exclusively to the Blessed Lord (*bhagavat*). Nor is a concordance with the individual soul (*jīva*) being asserted here.

In this regard, when the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) proposed by others—that "the two who drink" are the intellect (*buddhi*) and the individual soul—had been reached, it was explained that they are indeed the individual soul and the Lord (*jīveśvara*).
He refutes that with the words: "And not."
The word "here" (*atra*) is an ellipsis;
its meaning is "in this chapter.

The particle *ca* (and) is used either in the sense of a cause—meaning the refutation of the explanations of others together with one's own exposition—or in the sense of a conjunction. The intended sense is that otherwise there would be a lack of coherence (*asaṅgati*).
The Self is real, the individual soul is real, the distinction is real, the distinction is real, the distinction is real;
let there be no disputing me, let there be no disputing me, let there be no disputing me.

Thus says the Paiṅgi-śruti. Now, one might object: is it not irrelevant here to speak of the concordance [of the Upaniṣads] with respect to the individual soul (jīva)? For, since the distinction between the individual soul and the Lord (īśvara) is unreal, the two are identical.
Because the very connection with the individual soul (jīva) is of the nature of the connection with Brahman, he says: "Truth" (satya).
"Satyam" means that difference (abhidā)—that is, distinction—is real.
Although here, by the statement of the reality of both the Self and the individual soul, the reality of the difference between their essential natures is also implied; [he states it explicitly].
Nevertheless, the statement "Truth is difference" is a repetition of an oath intended to refute the perception of non-difference that arises from [certain] philosophical systems.
Since some claim that difference is unreal, asking how this can be so, the Scripture repeatedly states the refutation of their position: "Not so! (maiva).
‘Āruvaṇyaḥ’: those who possess spokes (arā) are the faults;

or alternatively, ‘āravaḥ’ refers to those who are habitually full of spokes [faults]. Viṣṇu is not at all to be sought after (vanyaḥ)—that is, not to be worshipped—by such people who possess false knowledge of distinctions.
Thus ends the Paiṅgi-Śruti; the word “yataḥ” (because) is to be understood as the ellipsis following this.
The connection with the subsequent [passage] is: "the difference of this is real (nāsatya)," and the same applies to the phrase "thus the Bhāllaveya-śruti.
Here, although it is stated in the *Bhāgavata-tātparya*: "And the reality of difference is declared in the Bhāllaveya-śruti:
'A pillar indeed moved away; he said to Prajāpati: "Who are you? Who are we? Who is he?"'"—
He said, "Whoever I am, whoever you are, whoever he is.
Then he reviled him with the words beginning, "Truth! Split! Truth! Split! Truth! Split! and so forth, ending with "Truth."
This statement is recited as being contained within the Bhāllaveya Śruti;
furthermore, in some manuscripts of the Commentary (Bhāṣya), the statement "It is true" appears as "For the Self... (ātmā hi).
And this statement is recited specifically as belonging to the Bhāllaveya Śruti,
and not as being situated in two separate Śrutis.
Nevertheless, according to their underlying purport (tātparya), these two belong to a single Śruti.
By the force of more numerous readings, there is the Paiṅgi-śruti: "The Self is real";
and the Bhāllaveya-śruti: "For [it is] the Self."
However, there is no fault, as another [name] cited in the *Tātparya* is its designation and form;
"Sthāṇu" refers to Rudra, and "uccakrāma" means he went upwards.
That Rudra reproached Prajāpati—that is, Brahmā—and said:
"What?"—meaning, "Who are you? Of what nature are you?"
The intention is as follows: "Who" are we? Of what nature are we?
"Who" is that Viṣṇu? Of what nature is he? Is he different [from us] or non-different? Such is the inquiry.
He answers in succession: "I" am whatever I was previously, and I remain exactly so at all times; "you" are whatever you are, and you remain exactly so.
The meaning of the Śruti is that Viṣṇu is exactly as He is described by me and by you and others—He is indeed such [the Supreme].

Furthermore, the Bhāllaveya-Śruti states: "For the Self is supreme, independent, and possessed of infinite qualities; whereas the individual soul (jīva) has little power, is dependent, and is inferior."
(12) Just as the distinction between Īśvara and the individual soul is real according to certain conviction,
so indeed you ought to make my word true here.
Just as Īśvara and the individual soul (jīva) are truly distinct from one another,
by that truth may the gods, together with Keśava, protect me.
Thus, there is no unreal difference [between them]. // 12 //
Thus concludes the section on the Cave (Guha-adhikaraṇa). 3.
In this context, the second sentence, "The Self," has been introduced to present contradictory attributes as a means of establishing the aforementioned distinctions.
"The Self" refers to the Supreme Self; "Supreme" (paramaḥ) [qualifies it].

He is independent (*svatantra*), possessed of superior qualities (*adhiguṇa*), and endowed with full power (*pūrṇaśakti*). For this very reason, later on, the properties that are the opposites of supremacy, independence, and full power— such as "limited power" (*alpaśakti*) and so forth— are stated in reverse order by means of those respective terms.
Regarding this very point, he cites a passage from a Purāṇa: "Just as..."
Regarding this, the *Tattvapradīpa* states that the genitive form (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*) is found in the *Padma Purāṇa*, while the nominative form (*prathamānta*) is found in the *Skanda Purāṇa*;
by the words "me" and "mām," the subject under discussion therein is to be understood.
The word "viniścayāt" has this very meaning;
"satyabhedau" is a bahuvrīhi compound.
"Just as there are divisions of truth," means by means of "truth" known without overstepping what actually exists—
that is, by the cause called the knowledge of the reality of division through the divisions of truth.
"Sahakeśavā" is a single word.
"May the gods, together with Keśava, protect us"— the meaning is "may they guard us.
From such a sentence, there is no difference from the Nāsatyas (the Aśvins).
But— this means that it is known to be indeed true.
Here, because the difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśa) was presented as an illustration in the preceding statement, its authoritative status is understood,
since only such a [difference] can serve as an illustration.

In the second [verse], however, since it is stated that the knowledge of the reality of difference (*bhedasatyatva*) is the cause of protection by way of not overstepping the objects [of perception], the reality of difference is also understood; thus, there is a connection with the subject at hand. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the words regarding the object of apprehension (*grāhya*) cited in the *Tattvapradīpa* are intended.
For instance: "There are two types of creation of beings in this world: the divine and the demonic."
The divine has been described by me in detail; now hear from me, O Pārtha, about the demonic.
Beginning with "They say that the world is without truth, without a foundation, and without a Lord," [it continues]:
"These hateful, cruel ones, the lowest of men in the worlds, I [cast]..."
I perpetually cast those who are inauspicious into the very wombs of the asuras.
Thus says the Blessed One (Bhagavad Gītā 16.8, 9): "They say that this world is without truth, without a foundation, and without a Lord;
they are demonic, self-destructive, and bringers of destruction to the world."
Thus says the Vyāsa-smṛti.
"O Indra and Soma, burn the Rakṣasas; cast them down, O Bulls, those who increase the darkness!
Overthrow the senseless ones, consume them, slay them, drive them away, and pierce the Atriṇas! (Ṛgveda 7.104.1).
"O Indra and Soma, drive away the Atriṇas from heaven with your stone-smiting, heat-forged,
fever-slaying, and ageless weapons"—
this is the beginning of the Śruti (Ṛgveda 7.104.5).

"Those for whom there is no distinction between the Lord of the world and the individual soul (jīva) are non-existent," so say the proponents of Māyā, [referring to] the state of the earth being defiled by the duality of the individual soul and the Supreme Lord, both of which are imagined through one's own ignorance.
"Having covered [it], he casts aside his own shimmering nature;
the world-form of the Lord of Life is indeed false," and so forth. Also:
"Three times the demon goes forth with his snare, O Agni, he who strikes with falsehood against the Truth" (Ṛgveda 10.87.11).
"May arrows strike the thief in his vital parts with speech; may the sorcerer fall into the snare of everyone. (Ṛgveda 10.87.15).

Now, beginning with "the afflictions of knowledge," [it is said]: "One should not dwell together with those others who, by means of false reasoning, fallacious examples, and deceptive magic, seek to oppose the Vedic tradition.
For these are revealed to be thieves who lead one away from heaven. (Maitrī Upaniṣad 7.8).
By hundreds of such scriptural passages, it is determined that blind darkness alone is the destination of those possessed by *māyā*.
Likewise, in the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
"Those who know all things to be Brahman, and those who know the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman..."
"Those who recognize Viṣṇu as equal to others, as well as those who hate Viṣṇu—all go to a terrible darkness; for them there is no emergence at any time. Thus it is said.
Thus concludes the section on the Cave (Guha-adhikaraṇa). 3.
4. The Section on Intermediate Matters (Antarādhikaraṇa)
It has been stated that Viṣṇu is in the sun:
"That person who is in the sun, I am he; I am indeed he" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.11).
In such passages as these, it is stated that the fires themselves reside within the sun and so forth.
In this section, the mark (liṅga) of residing within the eye is shown to be consistent with Brahman.

He demonstrates the connection with the scripture (śruti), the subject sentence, the doubt regarding the subject, and the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) along with its reasoning, starting with the words "āditya" (the sun).

The meaning is that in the scriptural passage cited under the *Ānandamaya-ādhikaraṇa*, "And he who is in the sun," as well as in the passage cited under the *Antar-adhikaraṇa*, "Within the sun," it is stated that Viṣṇu, who is the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), exists within the sun.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "He who...
The word "that" and so forth should be joined with the beginning of the following passage:
"I am he; I am indeed he."
This presentation of repetition is for the purpose of demonstrating the arguments of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).
By the word "first" and so forth, [the text says]: "Then the Anvāhāryapacana fire instructed him:
'That person who is seen in the moon...'"
"Therefore, I am He; indeed, I am He.
Then the Āhavanīya fire instructed him:
"That person who is seen in the lightning—that I am; indeed, that very I am. Thus, two statements are understood.
By the second and subsequent terms, the abiding in the moon and lightning is indicated.

Although the mention of abiding in the moon and lightning— unlike the abiding in the sun— is not useful for the present context because it lacks the power to establish that fire abides in the eye, nevertheless, the plural number in "of the fires" (agnīnām) is likewise inappropriate.

In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), it is established that only the Gārhapatya fire resides in the eye, because the three fires beginning with the Gārhapatya are not thereby established [as residing there]. Furthermore, since the moon and lightning do not possess the same nature as the eye, their residence [in the sun] cannot serve as a proof for their residence in the eye.

Nevertheless, the two occurrences of the word "etc. (*ādi*) and the plural number are intended to indicate the reasoning in the prima facie view, namely, the scriptural mention of many fires such as the Gārhapatya and others.
Just as it is stated that the two fires known as the Anvāhāryapacana (the southern fire) and the Āhavanīya reside in the moon and lightning respectively,

so too is it stated that the Gārhapatya fire resides in the sun; thus, for the sake of illustration, since the three fires beginning with the Gārhapatya reside respectively in the triad beginning with the sun, the location of the Gārhapatya itself— which is already well-known— comes to be its location in the eye by way of its location in the sun.
Or rather, that [mention] is for the purpose of demonstrating the logical reasoning; thus, it should be understood that there is no pointlessness.
Therefore, because of the identity of the eye and the sun, [it is said]: "This person who is seen within the eye" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.15.1).
In this case as well, fire alone is being spoken of. To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "Therefore."
This [word "because"] does not connect with the immediately preceding word "on account of identity" (*aikyāt*);
for it is impossible for the quality of being situated within the sun, which is the subject under discussion and referred to by the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*), to serve as the reason for identity.

However, its connection is with the distant phrase, "here too, it is fire alone that is spoken of"; the meaning of the word "api" (also) is that this applies not only to the passage concerning the sun.

And likewise: that state of being situated in the sun, which was stated as residing in Viṣṇu known as Ānandamaya, is perceived in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad— in passages such as "I am that person who is in the sun"— as belonging to the Gārhapatya fire among the sacred fires,
and not to Viṣṇu.
Why? Because here, the state of being situated in the sun and so forth is described sequentially for the three fires—the Gārhapatya, Dakṣiṇāgni, and Āhavanīya—and therefore [the question arises].
What follows from that? Since here it is stated that the fire called Gārhapatya alone is situated in the sun, [it refers to] "this person who is seen within the eye."
Thus, even in this statement, it is the Gārhapatya fire alone that is spoken of as being "located in the eye," and not Viṣṇu;
the construction is that he alone is also spoken of by the word "I" occurring in the Śruti.

And thus, since the word "I" occurring in the scriptural passage of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is primary only with respect to fire, the intention is that it refers to that alone. Now, one might ask: even if fire resides in the sun, how is its presence in the eye established? To this he says: "Of the eye and the sun," [citing] "The sun, having become the eye, entered the two eyes."

The meaning is that, according to this *Aitareya-śruti*, the insentient eye and the solar orb are of one kind because they share a single common attribute: being presided over by the same single sentient being denoted by the terms "Āditya" and "eye.

Alternatively, the meaning is that they are of one kind by virtue of the attribute of being threefold (*trivṛt*), in accordance with the scriptural statement: "The solar orb cited as food is indeed threefold; so too is the eye—white, black, and the pupil."
And thus—the point is that by the statement of [the Self] residing in the sun, its residence in the eye is also necessarily established by implication.

Although the word "sun" (āditya) in the previously cited Taittirīya Śruti passage, "And he who is this... (*sa yaścāyam*), was explained as indicating any exalted conscious being in general; [it nevertheless refers here to the specific deity].
Nevertheless, in this section, the objections and their resolutions have been formulated by accepting that this [term] refers to the solar disc identified with the Sun.
For this very reason, it is stated in the *Ṭīkā* that the eye and the Sun are of one kind.
However, in the *Tattvapradīpa*, it is explained according to the literal text as: "because of the identity between the eye—the sense organ—and the Sun, the impeller."
In the *Candrikā* as well, following the *Tattvapradīpa*, the word "eye" (*akṣi*) refers exclusively to the deity;
for this very reason, both in the *Bhāṣya* and in the *Sannyāyaratnāvalī*, it is stated that the eye and the sun are identical, and not merely that they are of the same kind.

It has also been stated that there is another position according to which the *Ṭīkā*— on the grounds that "the eye and the sun are of one kind"— is intended, following the *Bhāṣya*, to establish the identity of the substratum (*prakārin*) by means of negating a difference in modes (*prakāra-bheda*).
And thus, even if [the passage] refers to a deity, the literal meaning of the words "eye" and "sun" found in the *Bhāṣya* text— "it is said that Viṣṇu is in the sun"— remains exactly as it is heard.

The distinction is this: if [the term] refers to the orb, then the word "Āditya" occurring in that commentary and the word "Āditya" occurring in the previously cited Taittirīya Śruti must both be explained as referring to the orb.

By this means, through the refutation of the location in the eye mentioned in the Chāndogya Śruti by asserting it belongs to something else, the location in the eye—though implicitly stated in the Taittirīya Śruti cited under the Ānandamaya-Adhikaraṇa—is also refuted as belonging to something else; thus, this [present discussion] has an implicit connection (*ākṣepikī*) with the Ānandamaya-Adhikaraṇa.
The connection has been stated;
the subject matter is its presence in the eye.
The doubt is whether it belongs to Agni or to Viṣṇu.
The prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa) is that the fires themselves reside in the eye;
here, the reasoning regarding their residence in the sun is also stated, namely:
"This person who is in the sun."

Having established that the two statements, "This person who is within the eye" and [the other], share a single meaning by means of the statement "The Sun, having become the eye," one should [understand] through that medium the [person] "who is in the sun."

Having established the connection between the sentence "And he who is in the sun" and the preceding statement by means of this [intermediate] sentence, the commencement of this section proceeds through an indirect sequence of connection (*vakrasaṅgati*), whereby the sentence "He who is within the eye" is also connected with it— this being a sentence whose meaning is implied by the meaning of that [former] sentence. This is done for the purpose of establishing the consistent application (*samanvaya*) of even the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of residing in the sun.

Otherwise, in such passages as "Not another, because it is not possible," it is stated that liberation results from the knowledge of Viṣṇu; that liberation [is described] in the passage beginning with "Just as."

It should be noted that by this statement, the commencement of the present section (*adhikaraṇa*) would have been justified through the straightforward connection (*ṛju-saṅgati*) to be explained later—namely, that [the Self] is understood from the knowledge of the one residing in the eye mentioned in the passage, "He who is here within the eye" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 1.7.5).
Therefore, [the text continues]: "Just as water does not cling to a lotus leaf, even so evil action does not cling to one who knows thus" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 4.14.3).
Thus, liberation is established precisely because of the non-adherence of all sins through the knowledge of fire alone.
Not only is the attainment of the nature of bliss (ānandamayatva) for fire established upon proving its location within the eye, but furthermore, as previously stated: "Not the other."
In such passages as these, it is stated that liberation results from the knowledge of Viṣṇu;
however, since that too would be contradicted, he says "therefore" (ataḥ).
"From the knowledge of fire," and "due to the non-adherence of all sins"— by this very [statement], "liberation" [is established].
This also connects with that [preceding statement].
And thus, since fire resides in the eye, liberation would result from the knowledge of that alone, not from the knowledge of Viṣṇu.
Why is this so? Because through the knowledge of the fire residing in the eye, there is no clinging of any sins.
Nor is that [knowledge] unestablished;
for in the explanatory passage beginning with "tadyathā" (just as), it is stated that through the knowledge of fire alone there is no clinging of any sin.
Nor should it be asked how liberation follows merely from the non-clinging of all sins due to that knowledge.

The construction is as follows: since liberation is impossible without the non-attachment of all sins resulting from the knowledge of that [Self], liberation is established precisely through the impossibility of that [liberation] otherwise.

And thus, in the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), because fire resides in the eye, the status of being the object of the knowledge that causes liberation—which was stated regarding the one residing in the eye in the passage "Just as..."—would also accrue to that very [fire] alone; therefore, [the Sūtra says] "Not the other."
The sense is that what was stated is improper;
by this, its direct connection is also demonstrated.
For in the Chāndogya [Upaniṣad], there is this narrative (Chāndogya 4.10.5):
Kāmalāyana, the son of Kamalāyana, was by name Upakośala; he dwelt with a teacher named Satyakāma for the purpose of practicing *brahmacarya*.
He attended upon the teacher’s fires—the Gārhapatya and the others—for twelve years.
While Satyakāma was causing his other students to master their own sacred study (*svādhyāya*), he did not teach him alone.
Although he was told again and again by his own wife, he set out for travel without even mentioning the knowledge.
Then Upakosala, afflicted by disease, did not eat even when told by his teacher’s wife, "Eat," because of his preoccupation with obtaining the knowledge.

While the religious student remained silent and fasting, the three fires—the Gārhapatya and the others—were overcome with compassion and made this vow: "We three shall proclaim the knowledge to this religious student."
Having come together, they spoke the Vidyā:
"Breath is Brahman; Ka is Brahman; Kha is Brahman," and so forth. After this instruction given collectively, it is stated by the Vedapuruṣa that the Fires instructed him individually.
Then the Gārhapatya fire instructed him with the words: "That person who is seen in the sun, I am he; I am indeed he," and so forth.
Having been thus instructed individually by each of the three fires, Upakosala then thought: "What has been told to me by these [fires] is indeed that which is to be known."
"It is not to be attended upon;
however, the Teacher will come and explain it himself"—thus was he told by them.
While this was the case, the teacher Satyakāma arrived.
Having arrived and heard what Upakosala had said, he replied:

"What is it? [He meant: "That which has been taught to you by the fires must indeed be known by you, but it is not to be meditated upon; I shall teach you the Truth. Having thus made this promise, in order to generate reverence, he praised that which was about to be taught: "Just as water does not cling to a lotus leaf, even so evil action does not cling to one who knows this."
Thus, having praised him in this manner, Satyakāma taught the knowledge to Upakosala.
What did he teach? "That person who is seen within the eye, that is the Self," he said.
"This is the immortal, this is the fearless, this is Brahman.
Then, immediately after the instruction given collectively, the Gārhapatya fire instructed Upakośala.
What did it say? "Brahman is that which is called earth, fire, and food."
Having thus explained the Vyāpti-vidyā, he speaks of the Antaryāmin-vidyā with the words "He who...

Since the realization "I am He" involves two agents, it is stated that the Lord, as the inner ruler (antaryāmī) of Gārhapatya and the other fires, declares the identity of Gārhapatya and the others with their respective inner rulers— namely, the inner ruler of the Sun and so forth— with the inner ruler of the Sun and so forth.
And thus: because it is not to be abandoned and because it is the inner self (*pratyak*), "I am the Inner Controller.
Furthermore, by divine vision, this Person within the sun is seen as the Lord endowed with the six full attributes; the meaning is that "I am He.
Between Viṣṇu residing in the sun and my own Inner Controller, there is not merely non-difference—as in the case of Vidura, Dhṛma, and others—[but rather identity].
But he says that there is no distinction [between the two], namely: "He himself [is that].
Thus he states the fruit for the worshiper: "He who, knowing it thus, worships this—[he] destroys evil action, becomes a possessor of the world, reaches a full lifespan, and lives radiantly.
Regarding the term "evil action" (*pāpakṛtyā*):
One who performs evil deeds is "worldly" (lokī); however, the Blessed One is not worldly.
He attains a "complete" (sarva) lifespan.
"Long-lived": meaning he lives as one who is omniscient.
Thus [it is said]: "He who is in the moon";
"He who is in the lightning."
In this way, the meaning of these two should be understood:
"therein" (tatra) refers to that sense; as for the example to be stated later, "just as on a lotus leaf" (puṣkarapalāśe), water does not adhere.

"They do not cling to one who knows thus"—the meaning is that for one who possesses the direct realization of Brahman by virtue of the [Self] residing in the eye as will be described hereafter, sinful action does not adhere after the attainment of knowledge. Satyakāma said to Upakośala: "This person who is seen within the eye by divine vision—this is the Self called Vāmanaka."
"This is the immortal," meaning it is by its own nature devoid of death and eternally liberated;
"this is the fearless."
According to the established doctrine (siddhānta), the meaning of the Śruti is that this Brahman is "void of its own [intrinsic] being" yet "full of qualities";
however, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) considers this context to be concerned with Agni.
Therefore, he says:
Sū-oṃ.
Because of the intermediate state prior to rebirth.
Om.
Viṣṇu alone is the one residing within the eye.
Introducing the sūtra that establishes this conclusion, he explains it with the words "ataḥ" (therefore).
Thus, because a logical connection exists and because doubt arises, the author of the Sūtras spoke the subsequent [sūtra] in order to resolve that; this is the meaning.
By the phrase "residing within the eye," the portion "within" is explained, and by the phrase "Viṣṇu alone," the recurring portion "that indeed" is explained.

Although, in the *Anuvyākhyāna*, for the sake of avoiding the redundancy of the word, it is explained as "one who sports by remaining within," and therefore here too one should say "and one who sports" in accordance with that;

nevertheless, because the word *ātman* (Self), which denotes the act of sporting, is used here as a reason (*hetu*), its meaning cannot logically be connected to the proposition (*pratijñā*). Thus, it is stated simply as "remaining within. In that [other] context, however, since there is no intention to treat the meaning of the word *ātman* as a reason, its connection to the probandum (*sādhya*) is not improper; hence, it is also stated as "one who sports."

In reality, however—since the word *antara* is not mentioned in the Sūtra while the word *antaraḥ* is added, and this addition must be meaningful—it should be understood here by way of indication (*upalakṣaṇā*) that "and the creator of delight" is also implied.
Furthermore, it should be noted that whether the etymological meaning of the word *ātman* is intended or not, its status as the cause for establishing the probandum remains appropriate.
[As stated in Ṛgveda 10.90.3]: "Three-quarters of Him are the immortal in heaven."
Because immortality and other attributes are logically established for that very [Self] by such passages as "three quarters," etc.;

and he explains the word "because of logical establishment" (upapatteḥ) by taking it to refer both to the multiplicity of indicative marks (liṅgas) and to the statement that those indicative marks are not otherwise applicable (niravakāśatva), saying: "three quarters."
The word "of that which" (*tasya*) is the ellipsis to be supplied for the phrase beginning with "by such statements as.
The word "of that" (*tasya*) is repeated in its inflected form.
Furthermore, the term "because of immortality" (*amṛtatvāt*), though appearing in the ablative case here, is mentally construed in the genitive case to connect with the preceding.

By the first word, "fearlessness," [it is meant] as in: "Fearlessness for those desiring to cross to the further shore" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 3.2) and "This deity is indeed immortal. (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.7.5)

The statement, "The Self is ageless, immortal, and fearless— Brahman" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.4.25), and so forth, takes up the quality of fearlessness and the rest by means of the second [quarter].
And thus, by another scriptural passage beginning with "Three-quarters," this very Viṣṇu who was described is referred to as "this is the immortal."

The construction is as follows: because the indicative mark (*liṅga*)—consisting of immortality and so forth, which is stated in the passage as residing within [the heart]—is appropriate for that very Viṣṇu, and inappropriate for any other.
By this, it is shown that the indicative mark possesses superior force due to its being both "unrestricted" (*niravakāśa*) and "multiple" (*aneka*).
"Immortal" (*amṛtam*) means that which removes death; "that which is fearless" (*yadabhayam*).
And that which is free from fear, the "far shore" for those "desiring to cross over"— that is, for those wishing to transcend saṃsāra—

the Supreme Brahman situated on the far side of saṃsāra, residing in Śvetadvīpa and other such places as the ultimate limit of transcendence and attainable by the liberated: we are able to speak of the means for meditating upon that.
"We are capable" is the meaning of the *Kaṭha* Śruti. Furthermore, this is supported by the appropriateness of terms such as "Brahman.

Thus, because it is more powerful due to its lack of alternative application (*niravakāśatva*) and its multiplicity (*anekatva*), there is a certainty that Viṣṇu is the one residing within the eye, on the strength of these indicative marks (*liṅga*).

Thinking, "How much more so [is it established] by both [reasons], namely, because there is no room for an intrinsic nature [of the world] and because of its multiplicity, and even from powerful scriptural testimony," he explains the portion of the Sūtra beginning with "because of reasoning" (*upapatteḥ*) in a different manner—by taking it to refer to another reason in the form of scriptural passages such as "Brahman," and by demonstrating how that [scripture] serves to establish the lack of room for an intrinsic nature, which is necessary for its preeminence: "Brahman... and so forth.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the word "self" (*ātman*) is included.
In the reading "Brahmā, self, etc. (*brahmātmādī*), the word "etcetera" should be understood to include the word "person" (*puruṣa*).
This is to be connected with the phrase beginning "heard here" (*atra śruteti*) and so forth.
The phrase "of that very one" is to be supplied [to the previous statement].
Thus, the meaning is as follows: in this internal context, because the word *brahman* and others heard here are appropriately applicable to Viṣṇu alone and not to any other;

for the word *brahman*, which denotes the fullness of attributes, has its primary sense (*mukhyatva*) in Viṣṇu alone, and the word *ātman* also has its primary sense in him alone, based on the etymological derivation: "that in which the desirable, that which is to be accepted—the happiness—is measured (*māti*) and experienced. This is the intended sense.

By this [reasoning], it is established that the "Inner One" mentioned in the Vedic text, "He who is within the eye," is indeed Viṣṇu—who, by virtue of being the impeller of each respective individual soul, resides within each respective eye—and not Agni.
Why? Because of logical consistency (upapatti).

In this regard, the meaning of the Sūtra has been stated as follows: because of the hearing of indicative marks such as immortality and fearlessness in the passage, "This is the immortal, the fearless; this is Brahman; this is the Self," and because of the hearing of words such as "Brahman," these [marks] are appropriate only for Viṣṇu and are not applicable elsewhere.
The passage beginning with "So, I am that" (so 'hamasmi) refers, however, to the Inner Controller (antaryāmin).

[Objection: But if, by the force of unambiguous scriptural statements (śruti) and indicative marks (liṅga), Viṣṇu alone is the one residing in the eye, then he must also be the one residing in the sun.
In that case, [the mantra] would read: "So, I am that; he indeed is I."
To the question, "What is the status of such scriptural passages as 'I am He'? he replies: "By the words 'so 'hamasmi' (I am He) and so forth.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), terms such as "Gārhapatya" and others are included;
thus, the meaning is the entire collection of words beginning with "I" found within such sentences.
The word "in relation to" (*apekṣayā*) implies that [the following] proceeds immediately thereafter; namely,
that all words such as "I," "you," and so forth are employed even when there is a difference between entities, in relation to the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*), the Lord of Lords (*īśeśa*).
Thus it is said in the Mahākaurma Purāṇa.
He recalls the application of words such as "I" to the Inner Controller (antaryāmin) with the words: "the Inner Controller."
The first [particle *api*] is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*).
The second is used in the sense of "even though" (*yadyapi*) and "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*).
The term *īśām* refers to the lords, such as Brahmā and others; the word *īśam* serves to establish their status as internal rulers (*antaryāmin*).
And thus: "In objects"—that is, even though there is a difference between fire and other such things and the individual souls (jīvas), the words "I" and "you" convey their non-difference.
What need is there for more? All various words are employed as proving that very non-difference.

How so? Because these words are employed specifically with reference to the Inner Controller (antaryāmin), one should not suspect on that basis a non-difference between the Lord and the individual souls such as Agni and others;
for the meaning is that this Inner Controller is the Lord of lords, the highest even above Brahmā and the rest.
This connects with the preceding sentence "So 'ham" by supplying the phrase "because it is stated thus in the Mahākaurma."
Sūtra—Oṃ.
And because of the designation of place and so forth. Om.
"The fact that when one pours either clarified butter or water upon this [eye], it flows away along the eyelids" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.15) refers to the power of the location;
"Vāmanirbhāmaniḥ" and so forth refer to the power of the self.

For this is its indicative mark. Introducing and explaining the sūtra which establishes by another argument that Viṣṇu resides within the eye, [the author] says: "On account of the place and so forth. Before the word "clarified butter" (*sarpiḥ*), [the text reads]: "That which is in this... (*tadyadasmin*).
Such is the reading of the scriptural passage;
however, in the *Tattvapradīpa*, the preceding sentence is cited with a different reading as "yad idaṃ cakṣuṣi" (that which is here in the eye).
The term "ityādi" (and so forth) has its case-ending elided; it means "in such passages as these.
The same applies in all subsequent instances.
By the phrase "and so forth," expressions such as "he goes only on the path" are included.
This refers to the power of location (*sthāna-śakti*).

The meaning is that the power called "non-attachment" (asaṅgatva) arises from the connection of the two eyes—which have become the abode of Brahman—with the Supreme Person residing within those eyes; the word "is said" (ucyate) also connects here [with this].
By this, the term *sthāna* (abode) in the Sūtra is explained as indicating the power of the abode of the Supreme Self.
By the phrase "is said," the meaning of the word *vyapadeśa* (designation), which serves to avoid the charge of unestablished proof (*asiddhi*), is shown.
By the word "etcetera," [the text refers to]: "They call him *saṃyadvāma*, for all blessings (*vāmāni*) converge upon him... He is indeed *vāmanī*, for he leads all blessings;
he is indeed *bhāmanī*, for he shines in all worlds."
Thus, the entire sentence is taken [as a single unit].
"Self-power" (ātmaśakti) means the capacity of the Self, characterized by its quality of being the center of all blessings (saṃyadvāmatva).
By this, it is explained that the word *sautrādi* (and so forth), referring to the presiding Supreme Self (*adhiṣṭhātṛ-paramātman*), is indicative of His power (*tacchaktyupalakṣaka*).
The particle *ca* serves both to aggregate reasons and to aggregate powers; the first [conjunction] is displaced in its position.
The ellipsis is to be supplied as "it is said because... (*ucyate yataḥ*).
Therefore, this [statement] is also connected with the previously stated proposition: "Viṣṇu alone resides within the eye.
Since this unattached Puruṣa is present in the eye by way of being the controller, therefore, if "clarified butter" (*sarpiḥ*) [is poured] into this eye...

"He sprinkles either clarified butter or water"; the meaning is that even if someone were to sprinkle [them], they would go toward both paths—that is, along the two tracks—and would not touch the eye.
In this way, the wise call Viṣṇu, who is the "Short One" (Vāmana) and pertains to the eye, "the one in whom all things desirable meet" (saṃyadvāma).
Why? Because all "desirable things" (vāmāni)—that is, forms of women—converge upon him;
thus, the analysis of the compound is shown as: "desirable things converge upon him."
"He indeed" is primarily called Vāmanī when he has entered the eye;
why? Because "he leads"—that is, impels—"all beautiful things," such as the forms of women endowed with beauty, pleasure, and so forth.
This very person in the eye is "the one whose light is not in the light";
he is primarily denoted by that term. Why? Because [it is said] "in all worlds."

The meaning is that His splendor shines among men as its illuminator; it blazes there. As it is stated in the *Tattvapradīpa*: "Vāma is beauty and bhāma is splendor; because they are predominant [in them], women and men are designated by the words *vāma* and *bhāma*, and He who leads them is *vāmanirbhāmaniṣṭha*. To the question, "Even though these two marks are present, how is the certainty established that the one residing in the eye is Viṣṇu?", he says: "Of Him... (tasya).
For this reason: "of Him," that is,

of Viṣṇu, "this"— namely, the quality of causing non-attachment to the eyes through His own association, as well as His leadership of women who are the locus of all beauty— is the "liṅga" (inferential mark).

The phrase "the uncommon attribute" implies that there is no lack of logical necessity; thus, the remainder of the sentence is that the determination of Viṣṇu-hood is established by this. [As it is said: "He is the Lord, he is without rival, he is Hari, he is the Supreme, he is the highest of the high;
for whatever one pours, whether clarified butter or water, into the eye, it goes only to the eyelids; he is Vāmana, he is Bhāmana, he is Ānanda, he is Acyuta."
Thus it is stated in the Caturvedaśikhā.
From what is it known that this has that characteristic? To this he says: "He" (sa).
The mention of the phrase "He is Hari" and so forth, as well as the portion "He is Acyuta," is for the purpose of making known that the *liṅga* resides in Viṣṇu.
The word "idaṃcakṣuṣī" (these two eyes) is a compound;
otherwise, it would be understood as a qualifier for "clarified butter" (*sarpiḥ*) and so forth,
and consequently, its status as a qualifier for the cow's eyes— which are established by direct perception— would not be known.

Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the scriptural statement occurring in this very context, namely, "In this [body], the eyes... If that is the case, then the word "yasmāt" (because of which) must be supplied;
and thus it means: "Because of whom," that is to say, because of the power of the proximate presiding Lord.
Regarding the phrase "in this eye":
if someone were to pour clarified butter or water into this eye, it would simply run along the eyelashes; thus he is "without a rival," meaning free from enemies.
‘Saparaḥ’ means distinct from the world; ‘parovarīyān’—
this is one word.
The meaning is that he alone is superior to Rudra and others, superior to Vāṇī (Sarasvatī), superior to the Four-faced One (Brahmā), and even superior to the Śrī-tattva.
He is designated by the words Vāmana, Bhāma, Ānanda, and Acyuta.
Because there are multiple predicates, the word "he" (sa) is repeated more than once.
In the phrase "parovarīyān," the word "tat" (that) should also be supplied by ellipsis.

Alternatively, because a modification of a single part does not alter the identity of the whole, the meaning of the words *vāmana* and *bhāmana* is precisely the same as the meaning of the words *vāmanibha* and *bhāmanibha*.
The phrase "because it was stated immediately after [the passage] in the *Caturvedaśikhā*" is the required supplement.
"This is the sign of that" is understood; this connects with what precedes it.
"Because it is His abode, this eye is unattached to all things;
one should contemplate thus: 'He is Vāmana, the Supreme, our goal. Thus [it is said] in the Vāmana Purāṇa, verse 14.

Since the nature of that *liṅga* and its subsistence in a particular manifestation of the form of Viṣṇu are not explicit in the Śruti, he cites a Smṛti regarding this matter for that purpose, beginning with "yat".
The meaning is "because it is the locus" (*sthānatvāt*) of that [which is referred to by the pronoun *yasya*]. This pronoun *yasya* is syntactically connected with the pronoun *saḥ*.
[This refers to] "by all things" (*sarvavastubhiḥ*).
By means of ghee and other [remedies];
"Vāmana" refers to Viṣṇu himself, known as Vāmana because he measured out the eyes of beautiful women; "of us" means of the devotees; "supreme."
The meaning is that one should contemplate [Him] as "the supreme goal" (*parā gatiḥ*) to be attained;
or else, by the word "Vāmana," the word "supreme" (*paraḥ*) is used to ward off any suspicion that He might be small in size.
It has been stated "Pūrṇa. Regarding "Vāmana," the meaning is the Purāṇa known as the Vāmana.
The connection [of this] with the *Caturvedaśikhā* is as stated; the meaning of the aphorism is clear. Sūtra: Oṃ.
And precisely because it is designated as being distinguished by bliss.
"Breath is Brahman, Ka is Brahman, Kha is Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.10.5).
Having introduced the sūtra which establishes that Viṣṇu resides within the eye by the force of the context, he cites the very scriptural passage it employs: "Sukha... and so forth.

The connection of the portion ending with "Space is Brahman" is with the Sūtra; for although Prāṇa was mentioned at the beginning, this section does not have that as its primary subject, because there exist subverting factors such as the scriptural citations and indicative marks (liṅga) of Viṣṇu mentioned in the preceding Sūtra. This is to be demonstrated, and for the sake of indicating that both Prāṇa and Brahman will be taken up together (tantra) by the word "karma" in the subsequent Śruti, [the author says] "Prāṇo..."
This is an illustration of a partial [application].
In the sūtra, the word "ca" (and) serves to conjoin the previously stated reason with the reason supplied here by the force of the context;
furthermore, the reason cited in the sūtra is to be construed with the probandum that has been supplied.
It is both distinguished and blissful, hence "distinguished-bliss" (*sukhaviśiṣṭa*).
The adjective is placed last [in the compound] by rule;
or alternatively, it means "distinguished by bliss."
Alternatively, the analysis [of the compound] is "distinguished among pleasures" (*sukheṣu viśiṣṭa*).

In that case, in the second [interpretation], the quality of distinction (*vaiśiṣṭya*) in the form of preeminence (*śraiṣṭhya*) follows from the sense [of the context] as applying to pleasure as well.

For in this section, having stated the fullness (*pūrṇatva*) of the principal vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*)—namely, that the principal vital breath is Brahman and is more complete than all living beings—it says: "Ka is Brahman, Kha is Brahman."
By this [it is shown that] "kaṃ" is bliss, "brahma" is the full, and "khaṃ" is the ether.
Since knowledge is full, the fullness of both bliss and consciousness is also stated.
Thus, Viṣṇu is not only within the eye by the force of the aforementioned reason,
but also by the force of the context.

Nor is it the case that the Vaiṣṇava nature of this section is not established; for the meaning of the sūtra is that at its beginning there is the mention of "one distinguished by bliss," which refers to the declaration of full bliss.

Since the Vaiṣṇava nature of this section is established by the very mention of "Ka is Brahman"—which denotes full bliss—at the outset, how much more so when there is also "Akha is Brahman," which denotes full knowledge? It is for the purpose of indicating this *kaimutya* (a fortiori) logic that the word "eva" (only/itself) is used in the Sūtra.
Although in the *Chāndogya-bhāṣya* it is stated that "Prāṇa is Brahman"...
"Bala" is Brahman in the form of strength;
"Kaṃ" is Brahman in the form of full bliss;
"Khaṃ" is Brahman in the form of full knowledge.
It has already been explained that [the term] refers to the Supreme Brahman.
Nevertheless, there is no fault in providing this alternative explanation based on the conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) of the word *brahman* for both the supreme and the non-supreme; thus it is said:
"Brahman is consciousness and bliss" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.9.28).
"Ānanda is Brahman"—
from such passages as this, that very [bliss] indeed possesses its defining characteristic.
Now, one might object: "Even though perfect bliss and consciousness are mentioned at the beginning [of the Upaniṣad], on what basis does this treatise belong to the Vaiṣṇava tradition?

Anticipating this doubt, and with the intention that since those two (bliss and consciousness) are the defining characteristics of Brahman and are its very nature, if they were mentioned at the outset, it would be Brahman itself that had been introduced, the author demonstrates through scripture that perfect bliss and knowledge are the characteristics of Brahman: "Vijñānam... [and so forth].
The meaning is that Brahman has the form of consciousness and so forth.
Here, the term "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) and the others denote complete knowledge and the rest, because there is no reason for restriction; this is the connection with the subject at hand.
This is heard in the Vājasaneyi [Brāhmaṇa]:
"Bliss is Brahman";
this is the remainder [of the sentence], referring to the statement from the Taittirīya.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), passages such as "Now this is indeed the supreme bliss" and "Truth, knowledge... and so forth are included.
And thus, from the sentence beginning with "tathā ca," the word "tasya" refers to Brahman, and "tat" refers to its "lakṣaṇa," namely perfect bliss and so forth.
The meaning is that its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is known.

And thus, since full knowledge and bliss—which are understood in another Vedic scripture (*śruti*) as the characteristics of Brahman—are mentioned here in this context, the intention is that its status as Vaiṣṇava is established.
"The characteristic is supreme bliss; it belongs to Viṣṇu alone, there is no doubt."
From the unmanifest (avyakta) down to the blades of grass, all share in the bliss of a single drop.
Thus it is stated in the *Brahmavaivarta*.

Now, one might object: "Since all sentient beings are also possessed of complete bliss (*pūrṇānanda*), how can this be a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of Viṣṇu? To this, he says: "The defining characteristic... [and so forth].
This term "supreme bliss" (*paramānanda*) has both the meanings of essential nature (*svarūpa*) and attribute (*dharma*);
indeed, the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is precisely limitless, perfect bliss.
Here, what is intended as the defining characteristic is not mere full bliss alone;
and that [characteristic] belongs to Viṣṇu alone, and not to others.
For others, however, there is only relative fullness of happiness, not an unlimited fullness like that of Viṣṇu—this is the meaning.
Why is this so? To this he says: "Because they have the unmanifest as their beginning" (*avyaktādi*).
Śrī is the unmanifest; those whose beginning is that very [Śrī] are described in that way.
Grass-living beings and the best of men are mentioned at the end for the sake of distinction.
"Partakers of the bliss of the droplets" means that they possess relative bliss by virtue of being reflections of the bliss of Brahman according to a gradation;
the word "conscious beings" (cetanaḥ) is to be supplied as the subject.

He states the restrictive nature of the meaning of the phrase "there is no doubt" by supplying the words "because it has been stated in the *Brahmavaivarta*," [thus forming the sentence]: "that alone has that characteristic."
Thus, the connection is with the preceding sentence which contains an emphatic restriction; and when the primary meaning is possible, a secondary meaning is not appropriate. // 15 //
Now, one might object: "Since even the happiness of fire and other such things possesses fullness in a relative sense, why should this not be their perfect happiness?
Likewise, why should it not have that as its characteristic? And why should this treatise not belong to them alone? To this, he says: "And not... (na ca).
The meaning is that since the definition [of Brahman] is possible as the sense of the Vedic scripture "Kaṃ brahma" (Brahman is bliss) when there is primary, limitless fullness, a secondary,
relative, and dependent fullness is not tenable.
Sūtra—Oṃ.
And because the scripture describes the path for one who has heard the Upaniṣads. Om.
"He leads them to Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.15).
Now, even though bliss and knowledge are mentioned at the beginning of this [section], it is not appropriate for the section concerning that which resides in the eye to belong to Viṣṇu;
for in the Chāndogya, it says, "Prāṇa is Brahman, Ka is Brahman."

Having thus stated the knowledge [of the Self] as "This person who is in the sun," and having further stated the knowledge [of the Self] to Upakośala by means of the fires with the words, "Upakośala, my dear, this knowledge of the Self has been told to you by us," [the text asks] "Whom? (kam).
This is because it is logical that the first [passage] refers to Viṣṇu as the object of ignorance, while the second, beginning with "He who is this," refers specifically to Agni as its object;
nor does the phrase "our knowledge" [apply here].

It should not be argued that, although the aforementioned Āditya-vidyā has fire as its object, this does not apply to the vidyā concerning what resides in the eye; for the vidyā concerning what resides in the eye—
expressed as "He who is within the eye"—
has the same meaning as the Āditya-vidyā.
Nor is there a contradiction with the opening [of the hymn];
just as in the case of "I invoke Agni first for well-being," even though Agni is mentioned at the outset, [the hymn continues] with "Savitar for aid."

Just as the context [of the preceding passage] is identified as pertaining to Savitṛ by means of the scriptural mention and indicative marks of Savitṛ, such as "Savitṛ with his golden chariot," thereby breaking the continuity of the context,
so too here, despite the initial introduction of Brahman, there is the phrase "our own knowledge."
Thus, since the word "us" (asmat) refers to Agni, this context pertains only to the fires and not to Viṣṇu;
nor should the phrase "our knowledge" (asmad-vidyā) be interpreted as referring to the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin).
If that were the case, the separate mention of "knowledge of the Self" (ātmavidyā) would be untenable.

Therefore, having read the Sūtra which dispels the doubt that the knowledge residing within the eye has fire as its sole object, he cites the very scriptural passage contained therein: "It is heard. (Śruta).
The connection with this [phrase] is through the sūtra.
In this sūtra, "heard" (śruta) is an indicative mark; it should also be understood as including "thought" (mata) and "meditated upon" (dhyāta).
"Ke" refers to wind,
because of the definition: "Wind is designated by the word 'ke'."
By repeating the word *ka*, it is also connected with the word *gati*; thus, "the destination of *ka*" (*kagati*) refers to the destination of the Supreme Brahman.
This meaning is determined because the context concerns the Supreme Brahman as taught in the passage, "Brahman is *ka*.
And so: for those men who have heard the Upanishads and have meditated upon this knowledge after hearing it, by what wind (*kena vāyunā*) is there a destination of *ka*—that is, "Brahman is *ka*"?

The meaning of the Sūtra is that because the attainment of Brahman— made known by the statement "He leads them to Brahman"— is mentioned in the concluding summary, the knowledge of the one situated in the eye has Viṣṇu as its object, and not Agni.

Alternatively, the meaning is that because the Agnis, in response to Upakośala who has heard the Upaniṣads, declare the attainment of Brahman as the fruit of this knowledge, this section concerns Viṣṇu alone and does not concern the Agnis.
However, in the *Tattvapradīpa*, it is stated: "He leads them to Brahman."
Thus, because it is stated that those who have heard the Upaniṣads—that is, those who have heard the meditations contained within the Upaniṣads—attain Brahman, Viṣṇu alone is the internal [object].

"Upaniṣad" refers to meditation (*upāsanā*), in the sense that "Brahman sits near (*upaniṣīdati*) by means of this," or "Brahman causes [the practitioner] to sit near through this. This is what has been taught.

The meaning is: for those who possess the *upaniṣad*—which is the meditative worship (*upāsanā*) consisting of reflection (*mati*) and meditation (*dhyāna*) directed toward what has been heard—and who possess that meditation directed toward [Brahman] as its object;
by this, it is stated that the word *upaniṣad* refers to meditative worship in the form of reflection and meditation.
By the word "brahma," it is indicated that the syllable *ka*, which is a constituent part of the *bahuvrīhi* compound, is repeated and functions as a designation for Brahman.
For this very reason, the author of the *Ṭīkā* says: "The word 'śruta' (heard) is indicative of both reflection (*manana*) and meditative concentration (*nididhyāsana*)," and so forth.
In the view of the *Tattvapradīpa*, the word "Upaniṣad" refers to worship (*upāsanā*);
in the view of the *Ṭīkā*-author, it refers to knowledge (*vidyā*).
In the commentary (*ṭīkā*), the word "or" (*vā*) has the sense of "and" (*ca*).

Although this sūtra is intended to state a mark (*liṅga*) located in the concluding section in order to dispel the suspicion of a break in the context (*prakaraṇaviccheda*), and since it does not establish another argument for the ultimate thesis (*paramasādhya*), the word "and" (*ca*) should not have been employed here.

Nevertheless, because the mark (*liṅga*) consisting of the attainment of Brahman by those who know this vidyā— as found in the concluding statement, "He leads them to Brahman"— is directly connected to the ultimate probandum (*paramasādhya*) that "the one within the eye is Viṣṇu alone," and because this mark [is stronger] than both the mark of immortality mentioned in the first sūtra and the mark mentioned in the second sūtra located in the subsequent passage;

Some say that the use of the word "and" (ca) in the Sūtra is justified because it intends to present a different argument with respect to the section mentioned in the third Sūtra. However, in reality— even though the suspicion of a break in the context has been removed here— the use of "and" is justified because this intermediate thesis, which was supplied as being Vaiṣṇava in nature, is one and the same in both the previous Sūtra and this one, and thus another argument is stated therein by means of this [present] reasoning.
Now, whether they perform the funeral rites for him here or not, they all pass into the light (arcis).
From the light, they go to the day; from the day, to the waxing fortnight; from the waxing fortnight, to those six months during which the sun moves northward;
from those months, to the year; from the year, to the sun; from the sun, to the moon; from the moon, to lightning. There, a person belonging to Manu (mānava) awaits them.
"He leads them to Brahman"—this is the meaning of the Chāndogya Śruti. Here, "atha" (then) signifies a transition to another topic;
