"atha" refers to one whose ritual duties have been completed, and "asmin" (in this).
Regarding the subject of the knower (jñānin), if his sons and others perform the funeral rites suitable for a corpse, such as cremation and so forth— 'if they do,' that is;
or 'if they do not'— then [he goes] to the light (arciṣam).
The connection [of the words] is to be understood through the modification [of the verb]: "these knowers indeed arise," meaning they attain the divine world named Arcis.
Furthermore, the reading of the verbal root *viś* in the singular form *saṃviśati*, as well as the reading *te* (they), is contrary to the *Prameyadīpa* and the *Chāndogya* recensions.
From there, to the world of the day; from there, to the waxing fortnight—
the world of the bright fortnight.
Then, for six months, the sun moves northward; during those months, they reach the world of the gods and the world of the northern course (uttarāyaṇa).
Thereafter, after a year, they successively attain the worlds presided over by Āditya, Candra, and Vidyut.
Then, the "person" (puruṣa) who was the husband of that [goddess] named Vidyut-Bhāratī was "Mānava."

The chief Vāyu, who is dear to Viṣṇu known as Manu, goes to him; that Vāyu leads "these"— those who have attained him by taking the image as their support— to the effected Brahman called the Four-faced One (Caturmukha), while he leads those who do not take the image as their support to the Supreme Brahman.
For it is not logical that there should be a transition to another state by means of a different knowledge.
Granted that this statement regarding the attainment of Brahman is made as the fruit of this knowledge;
nevertheless, why does it not have fire as its object? To this he says: "For not... (na hi).

The word "hi" (for) is used because it is not logical that through the knowledge of one fire there should be a transition to another, nor that through [the knowledge of] one Brahman there should be the attainment of another;
and because here the attainment of the Supreme Brahman is stated as the fruit—this is the meaning.
Therefore, this is not the knowledge of something else, but is indeed the knowledge of Brahman; such is the remainder of the sentence.
By the word "hi" (for/indeed), he indicates the contradiction with the Smṛti in the case of the opposite view: "Those who sacrifice to the gods go to the gods; my devotees go to me as well.
[The phrase] "our knowledge is the knowledge of the Self" [is used].

This contradiction between the two statements is to be resolved by understanding that they refer to two distinct forms of the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin): the one who is all-pervading and the one who is limited.
The sense is that even a scriptural statement with a restricted scope (*sāvakāśa-śruti*) is superseded by a statement that is unrestricted (*niravakāśa-śruti*).
Sūtra: Oṃ.
Because of instability and impossibility, it is not the other.
Om.

Because an infinite regress would result if one living being were the controller of another living being, and because it is impossible on account of their equality, the living being [is not the controller].

Having thus established that Viṣṇu resides in the eye through reasoning and other means, the author recites the sūtra— "On account of non-abiding"— which supports that very point by demonstrating a refutation of the opposing view.

In this context, "the other" (*itaraḥ*)—who exists within each respective eye as the impeller of that particular individual soul—is not a different fire-soul from the Brahman denoted by the word *ka* mentioned previously.

Why? Because, intending the connection between the reason and the probandum—that "he is the other soul"—the author applies the portion of the argument stating "due to the lack of finality" (*anavasthiteḥ*) as a statement of an undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭaprasaṅga*) regarding the opposing view, [beginning with] the words "of the soul" (*jīvasya*).

The word "sāmyāt" (due to equality) is supplied as an elliptical supplement to the sūtra; and according to the method of the *Tattvapradīpa*, this [word] is connected to both [parts of the sūtra] by way of the "lamp on the threshold" (*dehalī-dīpa*) maxim.

Furthermore, the phrase "in the case of one individual soul being the controller of another individual soul"—which is a transformation of the meaning—is also connected with the word "asambhavāt" (due to impossibility).
The word "co" (ca) signifies a conjunction of reasons.

Alternatively, when the meaning of "itara" (the other) is to be expressed as "fire," the general term "jīva" is used in order to express both the probandum and the reason simultaneously through a single mention (*tantra*).
The phrase "not jīva" is to be construed with the recurring term "internal" (*āntara*), which serves to present the subject (*uddeśya*).
By this [reasoning], because He is the impeller of each respective individual soul (jīva), He is neither another nor fire.
Why? Because that other, namely the individual soul, is [not the impeller] precisely because he is a living being (jīvatvāt).
Nor is there a lack of a subverting argument (bādhaka) against the contrary position.

If one jīva were the controller and impeller of another jīva, then since the inner jīva would likewise possess the same nature as a jīva, yet another jīva would have to be posited as its controller; thus, because of the resulting infinite regress—an undesirable consequence known as *anavasthā*, consisting in the postulation of an unestablished series—it follows that the other [fire] is not the internal [controller]. This has been stated on the basis of a concession; however, in reality, the other [fire] is not the internal [controller] because it is impossible for a jīva to be the controller of another jīva.
Whence is this impossibility?
It is because fire and the individual soul possess a commonality of being dependent souls with respect to another soul that impels them; thus the commentary on the Sūtra is shown.
[This is so] because there is no authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for such a restriction.
And because it does not depend upon a Lord (Īśvara). // 17 //
Thus ends the section on the intermediate [state]. 4.

[Objection: "Surely there is no infinite regress because we admit the independence of the fire that impels the individual soul (jīva). Nor should it be argued that, by parity of reasoning regarding their status as souls, other individual souls would likewise possess independence; for we admit a restrictive rule that even though there is equality in their being souls, independence belongs to fire alone and not to others. To this, he says: "niyama... [etc.].
The meaning is that even though there is a commonality in being living beings, there is no evidence for a restrictive rule (niyama) that independence belongs to fire alone and not to others.
Therefore, the sense is that since independence is untenable for fire, the [objection regarding] infinite regress remains firmly established.
Now, one might object: let it be that fire lacks independence; [but what of it?]
Nevertheless, since the independence of God, who impels that [atom], is possible, there is no infinite regress; to this he says: "not depending on a Lord" (*anīśvarāpekṣa*).
One who expects or accepts a Lord as the impeller of the world is "one who depends on a Lord";
one who does not do so is "one who does not depend on a Lord."
The meaning is: "tattva" is the state of being that [nature]; therefore, from that.
The word "pūrvavādinaḥ" (of the proponent) is to be supplied as the remainder.
And the word "ca" (and) is used for the conjunction of reasons.

Or rather, [the objection]: "Granted that there is equality in being dependent (*paratantra*), since individual souls (*jīva*) exercise control over other individual souls, how can that [control] be impossible? To this he says: "anīśvarāḥ" (they are not lords).

The explanation is as before. And thus: just as in our own position, when there is a king who is the lord of the realm, the relationship of the ruled and the ruler among subjects exists through the king's power; so too, through the power of the Lord (*īśvara*), the possibility of one soul exercising control over another soul is established.
The meaning is that this is not possible in the case of the opponent's position, because the opponent does not admit the existence of a Lord (īśvara).
And this constitutes two ways of construing the two sentences.
In the *Ṭīkā*, exactly what was stated in the *Tattvapradīpa* has been said.
For it is stated in the *Tattvapradīpa*: "The absence of a restrictive means of knowledge (*niyamapramāṇa*) and dependence upon a non-Lord (*anīśvara*)—both of these are the reason in both cases.
The meaning of "in both cases" is: in the two instances of infinite regress (*anavasthiti*) and impossibility (*asaṃbhava*).
Thus ends the section on the intermediate [state]. // 4 //
5. The Section Concerning the Inner Ruler (Antaryāmin)
"He who dwells in the earth, yet is within the earth, whom the earth does not know, whose body is the earth,
who controls the earth from within— He is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.7.3).
Thus, and so forth, the Inner Controller is described.
In this section, the mark (*liṅga*) consisting of the activity of controlling, accompanied by the state of being situated within, is shown to be consistently applicable to Brahman.
He demonstrates the subject matter by first citing the scriptural passage that constitutes the topic: "He who... etc.
In the phrase "ityādi," the nominative case is used in the sense of the locative or the instrumental,
according to the rule *saptasu prathamā*.
The reading "ityādinā" is contrary to the statement in the *Tattvapradīpa*: "'kriyāviśeṣaṇaṃ vā'."
The remainder [of the construction] is either "in the sentence" (*vākye*) or "by means of the sentence" (*vākyena*): namely,
"He who dwells in the waters" and "He who dwells in the elements."
The word "etcetera" (*ādi*) includes such passages as these. By the term "the Inner Controller" (*antaryāmī*), the subject matter is indicated;
this is the statement spoken by Yājñavalkya to Uddālaka in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.
"He who is in the earth":

the earth (*pṛthivī*) is so called because it moves or goes having mounted upon Viṣṇu, who is broad (*pṛthu*); standing in that [earth], he is "within" (*antaraḥ*), distinct from the conscious being who identifies with it.
The conscious being who identifies with "that which is the earth" does not know it in its entirety;
yet, he is "he to whom the earth belongs."
Because it is caused by being under its control, it has become the body;
not merely its abiding therein, but that which is "internal."
Abiding within and delighting without regard for external objects,
he is eternally satisfied by himself— “He who delights without dependence on the external is known as the internal one.”
Thus it is stated in the *Bṛhadbhāṣya*; or else, because of His extreme dearness, Hari’s state of being internal has been illustrated.
For it is stated in that very same place:
because, according to such scriptural passages as "More dear than a son," it is of the nature of the supreme object of love, it is "innermost" (antaraḥ).
Being exceedingly dear, he "controls the earth"; that is, he restrains Garuḍa.
This "Self within you" (antaryāmyātmā)— the governing Person— is "immortal," meaning eternal; such is the meaning of the Śruti.
By this, the contradiction with the *Bṛhadbhāṣya* regarding the commentary’s statement "interior and secluded" is refuted;
for the *Bṛhadbhāṣya*, in the passage beginning "the Self which," refers to the word "interior" (*antara*) as its subject matter.
For this very reason, there is no tautology in the scripture,
because the two [passages] have different meanings;
however, the proponent of the prima facie view considers this sentence to be intended for something else.
And therein, the immortality stated in the passage "This is the immortal" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.15.1) is declared;
and that [immortal] is he "whose body is the earth."
By such statements as these, because [the Self] consists of all things, it is logical that either primordial matter (prakṛti) or each respective individual soul (jīva) [is the subject].
He shows the connection with the preceding section and its subject matter by saying "therein" (tatra).
The interpretation stated here in the *Tattvapradīpa* is as follows: in passages such as "He who dwells in the earth," the Inner Ruler (*antaryāmin*) is spoken of;
and in those very same passages, regarding that very Inner Ruler, it is said: "This is the immortal, this is the fearless."

Thus, the immortality stated regarding the Person in the Eye in the previously cited Chāndogya passage— “This is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal”— is what is being expressed here. By this, through the refutation of the idea that the Inner Controller mentioned in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka is other than Viṣṇu, it is shown that the immortality mentioned therein must also reside in another [than Viṣṇu].

By establishing that the state of being "located in the eye" mentioned in the preceding section (pūrvādhikaraṇa) serves as a proof for Viṣṇu's identity, the introductory connection (*saṅgati*) has been stated through an objection (*ākṣepikī*).
To the question "What follows from this?", the author states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) along with its supporting arguments, beginning with the words "And he... (*sa ca*).
The word "ca" (and) serves to collect the reasons;
by the phrase "etcetera," there is an inclusion of such [scriptural passages] as "whose body is water."
The word "tat" (that) is connected to the causal statement through grammatical modification (*vipariṇāma*).

The word "ātman" signifies both one's own nature (*svarūpa*) and the body (*śarīra*). Thus, that Inner Controller (*antaryāmī*) is appropriately identified as either *prakṛti*—which consists of both the insentient and the sentient—or as the respective individual soul (*jīva*) of the earth and other elements.

Why? Because the word *śarīra* (body) used in the revealed scripture (*śruti*) has the meaning of "essential nature" (*svarūpa*), as in the phrase "this is the body of the prima facie view" (*idaṃ pūrvapakṣaśarīram*).
Furthermore, because insentient primordial matter (*jaḍaprakṛti*) is the material cause of everything, it constitutes the self of all;

and because sentient primordial matter (*citprakṛti*) is the presiding agent of all, it constitutes the self of all; and because the individual soul (*jīva*) of earth and so forth has earth and so forth as its entire body—such is the construction [of the argument].

"For Viṣṇu’s having the earth and so forth as his body is not accepted. [Objection: "But just as their status as inner rulers (antaryāmin) is established by the mark of being primordial nature (prakṛti) and so on, why should that same status for Viṣṇu not be established by the mark of immortality? To this he says: "For... and so forth.

He whose body consists of earth and so forth is described as such; the state of being that is "tattva," and if the suffix *tva* is not recited, then the connection (*anvaya*) is straightforward and is accepted.
The word "by the Siddhāntin" is to be understood as the ellipsis [of the agent].
The intention of the word "hi" (for) is that he [the Antaryāmī] has consciousness as his body, which is distinct from inert matter such as earth and the like.

And thus—the sense is that, because the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) characteristic is more powerful than the Siddhāntin’s characteristic due to its lack of any other possible application (niravakāśatayā), the latter sublates the former; therefore, Viṣṇu is not the Antaryāmī.
Therefore, he says: Sūtra—Oṃ.
The Inner Ruler (Antaryāmin) [is Brahman] because His attributes are designated in relation to the divine and other spheres.
Om.
"Whom the earth does not know, who is within the earth," and so forth (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.7.3).
Because His attributes are designated in relation to the deities and so forth, Viṣṇu alone is the Inner Ruler (antaryāmī).
Introducing the aphorism that establishes this conclusion, he explains it with the words "ataḥ" (therefore).
The phrase "by such a statement" is to be understood as the ellipsis [of the sentence].

In that regard, although the statement intended by the term "designation in the Sūtra"—namely, "He whom the earth does not know, who from within rules the earth"—should indeed have been cited as the example; [it was not].
Because here it is precisely the state of being internal as stated [in the previous context] that constitutes the meaning of the word *dharma* in the Sūtra,
and not the sentence "internal in the earth";
for in this case, the word *atyantara* has the sense of "distinct," and thus what was stated there does not serve as a reason.

And thus, that example is not applicable to the subject at hand; nevertheless, there is no fault, as it was cited merely as a representative illustration (*pratīka*). By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the statements from the three sections are included.
"In the sections concerning the deities and so forth"—
the word "in the sections" (prakaraṇeṣu) is to be understood as the ellipsis [of the sentence].
A "section" (prakaraṇa), by definition, consists of multiple sentences that establish a single object of knowledge.
In this regard, "He who dwells in the earth" refers to the section concerning the deities (adhidaivata);
"He who dwells in all beings" [refers to the section concerning the self (adhyātma)].
The section beginning with "Thus [regarding] the elements" is the section on the elements;
the section beginning with "He who dwells in the vital breath" is the section on the inner self (adhyātma).

By the statement "with reference to the deities" (*adhidaiva*) in both the Sūtra and the Bhāṣya, the doubt that the earth and so forth— being insentient— are incapable of such knowledge by anyone has been dispelled;
for since the earth and others mentioned here are sentient as presiding deities (*adhidaivata*),
the word "Prāṇa" in the Śruti passage refers to the deity of the vital air (*prāṇavāyu*).
That very [power], by way of being the light of the object of knowledge, is the deity of the vital breath and the senses;

by the inclusion of various sections such as "among the presiding deities" and so forth, it is indicated that the statement of its attributes is not found in only one place, but rather in many locations.

He states the meaning of the word "that" (*tat*), which follows [the previous discussion], as "Viṣṇu alone. Although the word "that" is neuter, it is explained as "Viṣṇu alone" in accordance with the sūtra-word "the Inner Controller" (*antaryāmī*), which provides the subject (*uddeśya*).
By this, [it is shown that] "this is your Self" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.7.3).
Thus, the Inner Controller (antaryāmī) is indeed Viṣṇu.

Why? Because "His attributes are designated" within the contexts concerning the deities and so forth; for the attributes of that Viṣṇu, such as being unknown and being internal, are declared in the passage: "Whom the earth does not know."
The meaning of the Sūtra has thus been stated by the words "because it has been declared [in passages] such as these.
For that [Self] is indeed described [in the Śruti]: "O Viṣṇu, neither one being born nor one already born is equal to Thee" (Ṛgveda 7.99.2);
and "He who is unheard from this, ungone, unmeasured, unlimited, unseen, unknown, undirected, [the Self] of all... etc.
He is the inner person within all beings; thus, as stated in passages such as *Aitareya Āraṇyaka* 3.2.4, he is both unknown and internal. // 18 //
To the question, "From what [reason] does the state of being unknown and so forth constitute a property of Viṣṇu?", he says: "For he... (sa hi).

"He" refers to Viṣṇu; the phrase "by the sentence beginning with" is to be understood as the ellipsis. By the word "etcetera," the passage "The divine, singular God Nārāyaṇa" (Subāla Upaniṣad 7) is included.

Having begun with the passage, "He whose body is the earth, who moves within the earth, whom the earth does not know—this is the inner self of all beings, free from evil, divine, the one god Nārāyaṇa," another Śruti text is cited as its conclusion:
"Unknown" means not known in its entirety; "inner" (antaraḥ) [refers to the one who dwells within].
The phrase "having remained within, he is renowned for providing delight" is the understood sense. The particle *ca* (and) is used as a conjunction.

Furthermore, the sentence "not you" (*na te*) has been explained in every section in accordance with the context as: "you have not reached the ultimate limit—the full extent—of the greatness of that God by means of the ears and other senses."
The statement "He" (saḥ) has also been explained in that very same place. Sūtra: Oṃ.
And it is not based on Smṛti, because of the description of that which does not possess those attributes.
Om.
Because the attributes of the Pradhāna, such as consisting of the three guṇas, are not mentioned, the Pradhāna described in Smṛti is not the Inner Controller (Antaryāmī). // 19 //

Having thus established Viṣṇu’s status as the inner ruler (antaryāmin) through an indicative mark that allows no other possibility, the author presents the sūtra— "And not [so]"— which refutes by means of reasoning the claim made by the opponent that the status of being the inner ruler belongs to primordial matter (prakṛti) and so forth, which is common to both matter and the individual soul (jīva).
In this context, the expression "ataddharmābhilāpāt" is an avyayībhāva compound, just like the expression "atacchabdāt."

For this very reason, with the intention that it is "indestructible" (avyaya) and with the aim of showing there is no fixed rule, he first explains the causal statement as "because of being composed of the three qualities" (triguṇatvāt).
That which has the three qualities—sattva and the others—as its effects is "composed of the three qualities" (triguṇa);
the state of being that is "the quality of being composed of the three" (triguṇatva). Those things which have that and so forth as their [attributes] are described in that way.

The attributes of *pradhāna*, which is *prakṛti*—such as being composed of the three *guṇas* and so forth—are here referred to as "attributes of *pradhāna*"; this includes qualities such as insentience (*jaḍatva*) and being subject to transmigratory existence (*saṃsāritva*).
The term *pradhāna* also serves as an indicator for the individual soul (*jīva*).
Alternatively, the word "etc. (*ādi*) should be supplied here.

He explains the term "smārta" (based on tradition), which is employed both to indicate the counter-positive of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) and to suggest the underlying reasoning: "stated in the Smṛti.
The meaning is that it is presented in the *Sāṃkhya* Smṛti as having the nature of earth and so forth.
This is stated to make it known that this is indeed declared by Smṛti and not by Śruti. He states the established meaning: "the Pradhāna.
This also serves as an indicator for the individual soul (jīva).
By the phrase "and the embodied one" (śārīraśca), it is shown that what will be stated later is also connected here.
In this sutra, which is intended to negate that the Inner Ruler (antaryāmī) is anything other than [the Self], he indicates the subject of the thesis required for the argument: "the Inner Ruler.
The construction is: "The Inner Ruler is not the Pradhāna."
By the phrase "not the Pradhāna, [but] the Antaryāmī," the word *tu* (but) in the Sūtra signifies that the Antaryāmī is Viṣṇu alone and not the Pradhāna;

and this does not merely serve to negate the opposing view— as in the case of the passage beginning with "nor the embodied soul" (*sa ca na śārīraḥ*)— but rather, [it establishes a positive conclusion].

By stating "the affirmation of one's own position as well," it is indicated that the negation of the opposing position has the specific character of being preceded by the affirmation of one's own position. By this, it is shown that the Inner Controller is Viṣṇu alone, and not the Pradhāna (primordial matter) propounded in the Smṛtis as consisting of earth and other elements.

The embodied one is the individual soul (jīva). Why? Because "there is a description of what is not its nature"; that is, because there is an absence of any mention of the attributes of primordial matter (pradhāna) or the individual soul, such as being composed of the three qualities (triguṇa) or being subject to transmigratory existence (saṃsāritva), as shown in the commentary on the Sūtra.

In the *Tattvapradīpa*, however, another interpretation of the statement of the reason—"because of the description of non-attributes such as selfhood, immortality, non-seenness, and seer-ness"—is also shown by relying on the fact that the negative particle (*nañ*) has the meaning of "contrary to that. Sūtra: Oṃ.
And the embodied self as well; for both [recensions] study this [self] separately.
Om.

"He who, dwelling in the self, is within the self, whom the self does not know, whose body is the self, who controls the self from within—he is your self, the inner controller, the immortal. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, Mādhyandina recension) "He who, dwelling in consciousness, is within consciousness, whom consciousness does not know, whose body is consciousness... (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.7.22)

Thus, both classes of Vedic schools indeed study this individual soul (jīva) as distinct [from Brahman]. That which was stated—that the individual soul is the inner controller (antaryāmī)—has been refuted due to a lack of supporting evidence; now, setting forth and explaining the Sūtra which refutes it again by means of a specific argument termed a "refuting reason" (bādhaka), he says: "The embodied one" (śārīra).
The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "it is thus called.
He shows the substantive (*viśeṣya-pada*) for the term "both" by saying "the followers of the branches" (*śākhinaḥ*); the meaning is "the Kāṇvas and the Mādhyandinas."

The Mādhyandinas [read] "within the self," while the Kāṇvas [read] "within consciousness. The word "api" (also) serves to include both recensions. The term "antaryāmiṇaḥ" (of the inner ruler), having been modified here, is understood to carry over from the previous context.
Having referred back to this [Self] with the word "enam," it has been explained that [the Self] is the living being (jīva).

Therefore, the remainder of the sense is that the embodied self (śārīra) is not the inner controller (antaryāmī). Consequently, the word "ca" (and) in the Sūtra draws back the negative particle (nañ).
It is stated that this is not only non-scriptural (non-smārta), but also bodily; thus, the word "also" (*api*) is used for the purpose of conjunction.

However, in the *Tattvapradīpa*, it is maintained that even the conscious nature (*citprakṛti*), by being taken as the subject of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) here, refers to her in the forms of Śrī, Bhū, and Durgā, [as in the passage] "He who dwells in fire" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 5.7.14).

Because the text "He who dwells in darkness" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.7.13) and others study [the Self] as distinct from the Inner Ruler (Antaryāmin), it has been stated that the Antaryāmin is not that [Self] either; and the word "and" (ca) is used for the purpose of conjunction.
By this [word "for" (hi)], [it is meant] because "both" [of these].
The followers of the Śākha recite— meaning they record— in their texts that "this" [Self] is distinct from the inner ruler (antaryāmin), who is the living self (jīva).
Therefore, because of this sublation, the inner ruler is not the embodied self (śārīra).
The meaning of the Sūtra has thus been stated: that the individual soul (jīva) is one who identifies with the body.

Although the scriptural passage beginning with "He who [is] of the earth" comes first, setting it aside, two passages concerning the knowledge of the Self—which refer to the conscious principle and possess both meanings and a single purport—are cited here as examples of the study of differences between the agents of both.
"Internal to the self" means distinct from the individual soul (*jīva*).
Likewise, the word "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) also refers generally to the individual soul, based on the scriptural designation "he who is in the self."

Although, because the *Bṛhadbhāṣya* explains the word "Self" (*ātman*) and so forth as referring to the individual soul (*jīva*) named Caturmukha, this sūtra is intended to refute that a particular yogin is the inner ruler (*antaryāmin*); and for this very reason, it is stated in the *Tattvapradīpa* that [this sūtra] refutes the inner rulership of a yogin;
nevertheless, when the inner ruler is distinct even from Caturmukha—the one who presides over all individual souls—by virtue of being their controller and so forth, then...

Since it is stated in the *Candrikā* that the expression used there is for the purpose of highlighting the *kaimutya* (a fortiori) argument—namely, "how much more so than all individual living beings (*jīva*) who identify with Him"—there is no contradiction between this commentary on the Sūtra, which proceeds with the aim of negating the status of being the inner ruler (*antaryāmin*) of the general class of *jīvas*, and the *Bṛhadbhāṣya-tattvapradīpa*.
For it is said: "From this Viṣṇu, such a world as this always proceeds."
And because of the statement, "The world is his body, for he delights in it," there is no contradiction with its being a body. // 20 //
Thus ends the section concerning the Inner Ruler (Antaryāmin). // 5 //
[Objection: Is it not the case that Viṣṇu’s being the inner ruler (antaryāmin) is not tenable?
For here, the state of having the earth and so forth as a body—which is a characteristic of Pradhāna—is stated, and that [state] is impossible in Viṣṇu.

[Reply: How is it that the characteristic of Pradhāna is not mentioned? Since the state of having the earth and so forth as a body is indeed its characteristic, [the author] says: "It perishes" (śīryate).
The word "tu" (but) is used for emphasis.
And thus, "hi" means because; "īdṛśam" means like the present world, or a world that is uncontradicted throughout the three periods of time; "jagat" means the world.
The earth and other elements "perish"— that is, they are destroyed— every kalpa, eternally and invariably, from this very Viṣṇu.
Even for sentient beings such as the self, destruction occurs indeed by way of the body.
And because the Supreme Self, being situated "in this" world, "rejoices," therefore He is called "the Other."
Therefore, for that very reason, the "world"— consisting of the earth and so forth— is said to be the body of "Him," Viṣṇu.
The meaning is "not by way of conventional usage.
Regarding the phrase "there is no contradiction with having a body," the meaning is that there is no contradiction with having earth and so forth as one's body.
The remainder [of the argument] is: "Or because of the statement that attributes not belonging to Him are predicated of Viṣṇu’s state as the inner controller (antaryāmitā).

For although it is impossible for Viṣṇu to have earth and so forth as His body—given that He is the very self of earth and so forth—the designation of Him as having earth and so forth as His body is possible in the other case, by relying on the etymological (yogavṛtti) application of the word "body" to earth and the rest.
The intended meaning is that such [a thing] is untenable.
As for what is stated in the *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣya*:
"But the deities, beginning with Earth, are like the body because they are subject to its control."
And they are said to be the bodies of that great-souled Viṣṇu.

Thus, it has been stated that, according to the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the status of earth and so forth as the body of Brahman is figurative (*gauṇa*). This is for the purpose of supporting the reasoning regarding the world (*prapañca*) being the body of Brahman in the Purāṇas and other texts; therefore, there is no contradiction with those [scriptures]. // 5 //
Thus concludes the section concerning the Inner Ruler (Antaryāmin). // 5 //
// 6. The Section on Being Invisible //
The qualities such as invisibility have been stated [in the previous section] as belonging to Viṣṇu.
In this present section, the mark (liṅga) known as the absence of visibility and so forth is shown to be consistently applicable (samanvaya) to Brahman.

By means of the preceding section, its subject matter, the connection, and the citation of the scriptural passage (viṣayavākya), [the author] indicates the subject matter, the doubt, and the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) along with its supporting arguments, beginning with the words "adṛśyatvādi."
"Qualities" (guṇāḥ) refers to wholesome phenomena (śubhadharmāḥ). By the word "etc. (ādi), [factors] such as selflessness (anātmya) are included. They are said to be "taught" (uktāḥ).
The phrase "of the one consisting of bliss" is to be understood as being connected with the statement "in the invisible," and this is an elliptical indication.
By the passage "those within do not perceive" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 3.11), [the Lord] who dwells within is indicated;

by the passage "he who is unheard from this" (Aitareya Āraṇyaka 3.2.4), the omnipresent one is indicated; and by the passage "this earth does not know him" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.7.3), the Inner Ruler (Antaryāmin) is indicated.
It should also be understood that this is supported by the passage cited in the immediately preceding section:

"That which is invisible, ungraspable, without lineage, without color, without eyes or ears, without hands or feet— that eternal, all-pervading, omnipresent, and immutable source of beings, they behold."

Having said, "the wise" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.6), the word "spoken" (uktāḥ) is understood to recur [from the previous context]. Immediately after the word "having said," the word "it was declared" (āmnātaḥ) is to be supplied as the remainder.
Therefore, the formation of the *ktvā* suffix is justified.

However, in the *Candrikā*, it is stated that regarding the commentary’s remark, "having said this, it is understood," the *ktvā* suffix should be viewed as being like the example, "Having heard the lineage of Yadu, a man is liberated from all sins," even in the absence of a common agent for the two actions; this is precisely the intended meaning here as well.
The word "iti" is followed by the word "vākya" as a necessary supplement.

The two words "tasmāt ca" belong to the author of the Bhāṣya. Thus, the construction is as follows: those qualities such as invisibility previously stated of Viṣṇu are mentioned in relation to a certain Akṣara; regarding that Akṣara possessing qualities such as invisibility in the Atharvaṇa [Upaniṣad], it says: "That which is invisible, ungraspable... and so forth.

Having spoken thus, and having likewise recited in that very same place the passage beginning with "Just as a spider... and ending with "the universe," immediately thereafter [the following] is recorded:
For the divine Person is formless; he is both outside and inside, unborn, without breath, without mind, pure, and higher than the high Imperishable.
Thus, in the subsequent statement,
"higher than that imperishable," it is understood that [the Self] is "higher" (para) than even the imperishable under discussion;
that is, it is the most excellent (uttama).
"It is known as that which is to be established.

By this, since the invisibility mentioned previously is implied to reside in none other than Viṣṇu, there is an introductory connection (*ākṣepikī saṅgati*) between this [section] and the preceding sections such as the *Ānandamaya-ādhikaraṇa*.
The subject matter (*viṣaya*) consists of the qualities of invisibility and so forth.
There is a doubt as to whether [the one described] is Viṣṇu or someone else.
The prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that it is not Viṣṇu, because of the qualities such as invisibility (adṛśyatva).
[The sūtra states: "From the Imperishable (akṣara), which is characterized by invisibility and so forth, [the world] comes into being."

Thus, by hearing the word "akṣara" and by the statement that it refers to that [akṣara], the reasoning for the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa)—namely, that Viṣṇu is the subject because he alone is without other scope—is indicated. As for the meaning of the scripture: "That which" is the imperishable (akṣara) accessible through higher knowledge (paravidyā), "that is invisible."
"Different from that which is designated as visible" means distinct from the objects of cognition such as the eye and so forth.
"Ungraspable" means distinct from that which is graspable by the mind.
"Without lineage" (agotra) means that which has no lineage and so forth; thus, according to the *Sudhokti*, it is devoid of lineages such as those of Vasiṣṭha and others.
‘Avarṇam’ means devoid of ordinary colors such as white and so forth.

According to the statement in the *Sudhā* that the words ‘invisible’ (*adṛśya*) and so on denote the mutual absence of being visible and so forth, the meaning is also the state of being distinct from lineage and color.
That which is ‘without eyes or ears’;
It is devoid of the ordinary organs of knowledge and so forth;
it is "without hands or feet," meaning it is devoid of the ordinary organs of action; and it is "eternal."
"Omnipresent" (vibhum) means devoid of the destruction of its own nature;
"all-pervading" (sarvagatam) means capable and pervasive; "extremely subtle" (susūkṣmam).
The wise, that is, the knowers, perceive that which is absolutely unmanifest as the "source of beings," and that is the "Imperishable."
"Imperishable" means devoid of destruction in terms of its body.
Here, the word "that" (tat) is repeated three times so that it may apply to every instance.

Furthermore, the term *bhūtayoni* is explained in the *Sattarkadīpāvalī* as that which brings about the production of certain beings—whether they be the elements such as space (*ākāśa*) or sentient beings such as Brahmā and others—from their own respective bodies alone, without the mediation of a female.
By the word "wise" (dhīrāḥ), the contradiction between invisibility and visibility is resolved.
Just as a spider emits and reabsorbs [its web],
and just as herbs arise from the earth;
Having stated, "Just as hair and body hair arise from a living man, so does this universe arise from the Imperishable" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.7),
[the text] subsequently indicates a further reality beyond that, saying, "And higher than that Imperishable is the Supreme" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.2).
He clarifies this very point by means of an illustration, beginning with "Just as": *yathā*.
"Just as a spider," that is,
a weaver, "emits" its own consumed materials, which have been transformed into the nature of threads, drawing them out from its own body.
‘Gṛhṇate’: it takes back into its own belly the object that was previously projected outward in the form of a wheel and so forth;
likewise, the universe, having been swallowed at the time of dissolution, emerges from the Imperishable (akṣara) at the time of creation.
He states another illustration with the word ‘yathā’ (just as).
‘Herbs’ refers to sprouts and the like.
He states another illustration with the word ‘just as’:
from a ‘living’ person—that is, from a man possessing life—the hair on the head [grows] from the body.
Other than those hairs,
it is in this world that the "universe"— that is, various kinds of effects— comes into being.
The meaning is that [Brahman] is born.
Here, the first example is given to state that Brahman’s status as the cause of the elements consists in its being their agent (*kartṛ*), and not in its being their material cause (*upādāna*).

The second example is given to state that, in the creation of the universe, Brahman depends upon those actions (karma), just as the earth depends upon the seed in the production of a sprout and so forth.
The third [verse] is intended to state that creation occurs without effort;
as for the statement beginning with "divya," "divya" means wonderful, and "amūrta" means formless.
It is devoid of any fixed or delimited measure;
rather, it is both external and internal.
By the two terms "without breath" (*aprāṇa*) and "without mind" (*amanas*), the absence of the sixteen parts (*ṣoḍaśakalā*) is expressed.
"Śubhraḥ" means pure; "beyond the insentient," that is, beyond the imperishable [matter], meaning beyond the material nature (citprakṛti)—so it is explained in the *Karmanirṇaya-ṭīkā*.
Therefore, he says:
Sū - Oṃ.
That which possesses the qualities of invisibility and so forth [is Brahman], because of the statement of its attributes. Om.
He introduces the sūtra that establishes the final position with the words "ataḥ" (therefore).
The meaning is that Bādarāyaṇa spoke this sūtra, which serves as a response, because of the possibility of a connection [with the previous topic] and because of the existence of such a doubt.
He recites that sūtra: "Because of invisibility and so forth" (adṛśyatvādīti).

Having stated the analogies of earth and so forth, and because the text following "From the Imperishable, the universe arises here" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.7) speaks of that which is higher than the highest, and because of the Smṛti statement, "The immutable is called the Imperishable" (Bhagavad Gītā 15.16), there is the possibility [of interpreting the source] as Prakṛti.

If invisibility and other such qualities do not belong to Viṣṇu, then the sentence would lack a subject matter and thus be invalid; therefore, he clarifies the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) with the words "the earth and so forth."

Although the example of the spider (*ūrṇanābhi*) appears first in the scripture, since the word "creating" (*sṛjate*) therein conveys only agency (*kartṛtva*) and does not convey the causality of the world as its material cause (*upādānatā*), which is favorable to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*),
that [example] is set aside and the phrase "earth and so forth" is stated.
The particle *ca* is used for conjunction (*samuccaye*).

And thus, the construction [of the argument] is as follows: after stating the examples of earth and so forth, and immediately following the statement, "From the Imperishable (akṣara), the universe originates here," there is the phrase, "higher than that";
and by the passage studied immediately thereafter, "Higher than the Imperishable is another."

By this statement, "beyond that" (*tatparataḥ*); because it has been declared that there is one who is higher than that cause, the Imperishable (*akṣara*), which is the Supreme; likewise, [it is said]: "The Immutable is called the Unchanging (*kūṭastha*)."
And because of this Smṛti, both the insentient *prakṛti* and the sentient *prakṛti* obtain the qualities of being "unseen" and so forth.

Herein is the distinction: when the insentient *prakṛti* is the subject of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), then the word "Akṣara" refers to that, the reason is directed toward it, and the expression "higher than that" (*parataḥ para*) also refers to it.
Since there is no other scope for it, the two ablative cases in "higher than the Akṣara" (*akṣarāt parataḥ*) are in different grammatical relations (*vyadhikaraṇa*).
And when [the cause] is the conscious nature (citprakṛti), then the word "imperishable" (akṣara) has that as its referent;
the two ablative cases are in grammatical apposition.
Furthermore, "and because of tradition" (smṛteśca) is also a reason.
And *smṛti* has been explained in this section.
Furthermore, because of the word "Brahman" and because it is designated as being beyond that [the individual soul], [it refers] to Hiraṇyagarbha.
He states another prima facie view: "because of the word 'Brahman'."
The meaning is: "from the word *brahman* heard in such passages as 'He [taught] the knowledge of Brahman' (*sa brahmavidyām*).

Since the word *brahman* is used in its primary sense only for Viṣṇu, He alone is the one who accomplishes that [knowledge], and not anyone else; therefore, he states another reason: "because it is beyond" (*parataḥ*).
The two ablative endings are in different grammatical cases (*vyadhikaraṇa*).
Thus, the meaning is: because Viṣṇu, who is beyond the principle of Śrī, is designated as being "beyond" (*parataḥ*) the imperishable one (*akṣara*) known as Hiraṇyagarbha.
The word *eva* (only/just) indicates that the reason [stated] here leaves no room for doubt and that no other reason need be sought;
the grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is "the attainment of Hiraṇyagarbha.
This is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*).

Regarding the phrase "the agent, the Lord" (*kartāram īśam*), because of the hearing of the word "Lord" (*īśa*), one should also consider here what will be stated later: that Rudra attains the qualities of invisibility and so forth.

In this view, even the suspicion that the word "Lord" might have an alternative application in Viṣṇu should be addressed immediately thereafter by the statement, "because of the subsequent mention of Him who is beyond that."
Here too, there are two fifth-case endings in different grammatical relations:
"Knowing Him thus, one becomes immortal here" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 3.12.7).
That action which pleases Hari is true knowledge; that by which His mind is attained is wisdom.
Now, indeed, there are two kinds of knowledge to be known: the higher (parā) and the lower (aparā).
Of these, that which consists of the Vedas, the auxiliary sciences (aṅgas), the secondary sciences (upāṅgas), and the sub-auxiliaries (pratyaṅgas) is the lower.
But the higher is that by which that Hari is to be known—He who is invisible, devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), the supreme, the Supreme Self.

Because of the statement that He is the object of the highest knowledge (paravidyā) understood as His own nature through such passages, Viṣṇu alone possesses the attributes of being invisible and so forth. // 21 //
Thus, in order to refute the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) that has been reached, he explains the Sūtra: "To him, thus... (tamevam iti).
"'Tat' (That)"; thus is one scriptural statement (*śrutivākya*). "'Tat' (That)"; thus is another traditional statement (*smṛtivākya*). "'Atha' (Now/Then)"; thus is yet another scriptural statement.
By the phrase "and so forth," passages such as "This is that Brahman" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.19) and "Three-quarters of it are the immortal" (Ṛgveda 10.90.3) are included.

The analysis of the compound is as follows: *tasya* (of him) refers to Viṣṇu; *dharmaḥ* is his nature (*taddharmaḥ*); *bhāvasatattvam* is its true essence; [the phrase] "by that" (*tena*) is the analysis.
The third case ending is used in the sense of "manner. *Avagatatvam* (the state of being understood) means well-knownness, which is a qualification of the object (*viṣayatva*).
This [term] is an indicator (upalakṣaka) of immortality and so forth;
the word "here" (atra) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].
The meaning of the term "that" (tat), which recurs from the Sūtra, is Viṣṇu alone. Here, "invisibility" (adṛśyatva) means being distinct from that which is visible (dṛśya).

And that essential nature is not distinct from Brahman, as is the case with the absolute non-existence of lineage (*gotra*) and so forth; rather, its possession of those [qualities] constitutes the very nature of Brahman. To express this distinction—that it possesses such qualities—and to indicate the use of the *bahuvrīhi* compound "that which has qualities" (*yasya guṇāḥ*), the word *guṇa* is employed in the sense of auspicious attributes (*śubhadharma*).
Thus, the coordination of this passage with the Sūtra and its Commentary is as follows: That which possesses the qualities of being invisible and so forth is indeed Viṣṇu.

Why? Because in this context, it is said: "Now, the higher [knowledge] by which that Imperishable is attained" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.5), and "This very Imperishable is Brahman" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.2).

In the passage, "The Person alone is all this—the work, austerity, Brahman, and the supreme immortal" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.10), there is the mention of the attribute that He, who possesses qualities such as being invisible, is the object of higher knowledge (*paravidyā*).
Nor should it be asked: "Even if He is stated to be the object of higher knowledge, how is it that He is Viṣṇu?"
Since that [Brahman] has been understood as having those attributes by means of the passage beginning with "him thus" (*tam evam*);
herein, "him thus" (*tam evam*).
Thus, by the statement in the Śruti that [Viṣṇu] is the object of the knowledge which is the means to liberation, it is stated that Viṣṇu is the object of the higher knowledge (paravidyā);
for the very knowledge that is the means to liberation is the higher knowledge.
Furthermore, in the Smṛti, regarding the phrase "that action" (tatkarma), it means that action alone which brings satisfaction to Hari.
Since it has been stated that "that by which the knowledge of Hari arises is itself called *vidyā*," it is thereby declared that He is the object of *paravidyā*.

In the passage, "Two sciences are to be known" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.4), it is also stated that Viṣṇu is the object of the higher science; thus, there is no lack of proof regarding the qualification of the reason.
The word "atha" (now) marks the commencement of the section.
The word *vāva* is used for emphasis;
*ca* signifies mutual conjunction.
Thus, two kinds of knowledge are to be known: the higher (*parā*) and the lower (*aparā*).
In that context, "among the higher and lower," "the Vedas" refers to the *Ṛgveda* and so forth; "the six ancillaries" refers to the *Śikṣā* and the other five;
and "the subsidiary sciences" refers to *Āyurveda*, *Gāndharvaveda*, and the rest.
"Those which are the subsidiary limbs";
the remaining arts and sciences are the lower [knowledge].
Now, the word "atha" (now) signifies a different topic.
That which is "invisible" is other than the visible; "devoid of qualities" means lacking the qualities such as *sattva* and so forth; it is "supreme."

The meaning of the Śruti is as follows: Hari, who is the "supreme self" (paramātmā), distinct in nature, the highest of all, and all-pervading, is to be known through that which is the Veda consisting of the Ṛg and other branches; thus, she (the Veda) alone is the supreme means.

Just as a single action, due to the distinction of limiting conditions (upādhi) such as being performed with desire or without desire, is designated by the terms "active" (pravṛtta) or "desisting" (nivṛtta).

The point is that the status of the *Ṛgveda* and so forth as either higher (*parā*) or lower (*aparā*) knowledge is established precisely through the distinction of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), namely whether their subject matter is Viṣṇu or whether it concerns ritual action (*karman*) and the like.
Nor is there any contradiction with the statement in the *Anuvyākhyāna* that the *Brahmasūtra* is a higher knowledge;

for while the *Ṛgveda* and so forth function as the objects to be assisted (*anugrāhya*), the *Brahmasūtra* functions as the agent of assistance (*anugrāhaka*), and thus both are appropriately designated as higher knowledge.
Sūtra—Oṃ.
And because of the distinction [of attributes] and the designation [of difference], it is neither of the other two. Om.

It has been stated that Prakṛti and Viriñci possess qualities such as being invisible; therefore, because the Sūtra’s function extends even to the refutation of the opponent's position on the grounds of that established doctrine, [the author] reads and explains the Sūtra— beginning with "viśeṣaṇa"— while refuting by means of specific reasoning that which was already refuted by the fact that the status of being the object of higher knowledge (paravidyā), as mentioned in the Sūtra by the phrase "because its attributes are mentioned," finds no other possible application than Viṣṇu.
With the intention that the word "designation" (vyapadeśa) applies to both, he states the scriptural passage concerning both: "yaḥ" (He who...).
"Difference" (bheda) means otherness.
By the word "and" (ca), it is indicated that it is not merely a statement of attributes.

The word "but" (tu) implies that the meaning of the term "conjunction" (*samuccaya*)—expressed by the phrase "on account of the distinction of attributes and designations"—is already clear, and thus its specific meaning has not been stated here.
By the expression "the source is Viriñca," the meaning of the word "other" (*itara*) is indicated through the analysis of the compound as "the other [female] and the other [male].
In both cases, the phrase "possessing qualities such as invisibility" (*adṛśyatvādiguṇaka*) is to be supplied.
In the view that [the term] refers to *prakṛti*, there is a change of gender;
and thus, in the sentence "He who is omniscient," there is a qualification of that [entity] which possesses qualities such as invisibility.
Because of the mention of specific attributes such as omniscience (*sārvajñya*), the insentient primordial nature (*jaḍaprakṛti*) does not possess qualities such as invisibility (*adṛśyatva*).

Likewise, in the sentence "Therefore" (*tasmāt*), since there is a designation of difference through the statement of a distinguishing attribute— namely, that Viriñca (Brahmā) is produced from that Imperishable (*akṣara*)— the construction is that Viriñca does not possess qualities such as invisibility.
Because of the qualifying attributes, "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving, whose austerity consists of knowledge" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.9), it is not primordial matter (prakṛti).
Furthermore: "From Him is born this Brahman—name, form, and food" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.9).
Thus, because of the designation of difference, Viriñca is not [the one referred to];
for in the Atharvaṇa, prior to the statement "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving" (Muṇḍaka 1.1.9), there is the passage: "Brahman is built up by austerity" (Muṇḍaka 1.1.8).
In this context, it has been stated that [the Self] is connected with the austerity of the Supreme Brahman.

Since the word "austerity" (tapas) signifies contemplation, it brings about the cognition of ignorance; therefore, another scriptural passage, "His austerity consists of knowledge," was introduced in order to dispel that [notion].
The meaning is that for him, "austerity" is the act of discernment; it consists of knowledge alone, and not of doubt and so forth.

In response to the inquiry as to how austerity—which consists of distress and incomplete, non-accurate knowledge—can possess the nature of omniscience, the preceding statement, "He who is all-knowing," is introduced to demonstrate the reasons for this, namely, his being all-knowing and having all desires fulfilled.
Its meaning, however, is: "He who is all-knowing."
One who possesses general knowledge of all objects is "all-knowing" (*sarvavit*);
one who possesses specific knowledge of all objects is likewise [all-knowing].
Furthermore, he is the attainer of everything, the fulfiller of all desires, and the originator of all things.
In the *Tattvapradīpa*, however, it is stated that because the verbal root *vid* is explained as "to exist" (*sattāyām*), one who exists everywhere is called "all-knowing" (*sarvavit*).
Regarding the two occurrences of the word *yat* in the phrase "of whom [is] which" (*yasya yaḥ*), [it refers to] "from that syllable" (*akṣarāt*) and "this Brahman" (*etad brahma*).
The phrase "that which is named the four-faced [Brahmā]— name, form, and food"—
is connected with the word "that" (tat) occurring in the subsequent sentence, meaning that both he and the presiding deity arise.
Furthermore, the other is the Imperishable (akṣara), which is Prakṛti, whose nature is insentient.
Śrī is declared to be the supreme primordial nature (prakṛti), the consciousness that rests upon Viṣṇu.
They declare that to be the supreme imperishable (akṣara), the imperishable beyond the beyond; it is Hari himself, possessed of all attributes, who is described as the threefold imperishable.

Thus, in the *Skanda Purāṇa*, because of the mention of the "three-syllabled" [name], the phrase "higher than the high Imperishable" (*akṣarāt parataḥ paraḥ*) is also merely a qualifying attribute. Now, one might object: Viṣṇu cannot possess qualities such as invisibility (*adṛśyatva*), because the scriptural mention of the "Imperishable" (*akṣara-śruti*)—by virtue of being designated as "higher than the high"—has no other scope there. To this, the author states another meaning of the portion of the Sūtra beginning with "on account of the difference in designations of attributes" (*viśeṣaṇabhedavyapadeśāt*): "the lower" (*aparam*).
The word *tu* is used for emphasis. "Three syllables" means the triad of syllables that has been proclaimed.

The phrase "the syllable is said to be threefold" means that he demonstrates the three modes by first specifying their individual manifestations— namely, "the lower. That which is the lower syllable is indeed *prakṛti*, whose nature is insentient (*jaḍa*).

That which is declared by the elders to be the "supreme imperishable" (paramakṣara)—that supreme, highest consciousness, the primordial nature (prakṛti), Śrī, Lakṣmī, who has Viṣṇu as her refuge—they call that.

The meaning of the Smṛti is: they declare that Hari alone, who possesses all attributes, is the one beyond that which is called the "supreme imperishable," [and] who is higher than the insentient primordial nature (jaḍaprakṛti) and the principle of Śrī (śrītattva).
Thus, the phrase from the Skanda Purāṇa, "because of the mention of three syllables," connects with the statement that "the threefold nature of the syllable has been declared.
This also applies to the passage beginning, "higher than the high Imperishable (akṣara)."
It should not be argued that the state of being "higher than the Imperishable" (akṣarāt parataḥ paraḥ) as stated in the aforementioned sentence is contradictory;

for in the *Skanda Purāṇa*, the term "the lower" (*aparam*) is used as a three-syllable designation, and thus it is logically consistent that this Imperishable is higher than another, distinct Imperishable. This is the interpretation.

By mentioning three Imperishables, it is shown that in the phrase "higher than the Imperishable," there is a grammatical connection either through apposition (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) or through different substrates (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*).

In the *Prameyadīpa*, however, the meaning of the scripture is stated according to the method of its commentary: "Because he is beyond the Imperishable (*akṣara*) and beyond the Śrī-tattva, he is the highest of the high.
By this, even the phrase "beyond the Imperishable, higher than the high" is a qualification of that very [Śrī-tattva] alone, and not of anything else.
Nor should it be argued that being "higher than the Imperishable" (akṣara) is contradictory;
for there is a designation of difference [between them], as it is said:
"The triad of imperishables has been declared."

By stating this internal distinction among the syllables (*akṣara*), another interpretation of the portion of the Sūtra is offered: that for Arjuna the Pāṇḍava, just as there is a distinction from Kārtavīryārjuna—who was his own inferior—there is the logical possibility of this *akṣara* being superior to other *akṣaras*, namely the Supreme *akṣara*.
[This is supported by the verse: "When he beholds the beloved greatness of the Lord as distinct [from himself], he is freed from sorrow."
Thus, because of the designation of difference [from Him], even though he has attained the status of the Lord, he is not Rudra. // 22 //

Now, one might object: "Since the word 'another' (*anya*) is heard, could it not be Rudra who possesses the qualities of invisibility and so forth? As an answer to this doubt, he explains the portion of the Sūtra, "On account of the designation of difference, it is not the other," as follows:
although the word *api* in the phrase "juṣṭam api" has the sense of "nevertheless," or it may be used in the sense of conjunction, meaning "even Rudra."
It is not only for the reason stated previously, but also because of the designation of difference; this "or" (vā) indicates a conjunction.
The term "Rudra" expresses a different meaning from the word "the other" (itara).

It should not be argued that if the word *itara* refers to the insentient primordial nature (*jaḍaprakṛti*), Viriñca, and Rudra, the use of the dual number would be untenable; for Viriñca and Rudra are unified by virtue of their being sentient.
And thus, although Rudra is also reached from the word *īśa* as possessing qualities such as invisibility and so forth, [he is nonetheless excluded].

Nevertheless, because in the sentence "juṣṭam" (enjoyed) there is a designation of the imperishable named Viṣṇu— which is engaged therein— as being distinct from Rudra, who is denoted by the word "Īśa," the construction is that Rudra does not possess the qualities of invisibility and so forth.
This Śruti passage has been explained in the *Ānandamayādhikaraṇa*.
Sūtra — Oṃ.
And because of the placement of the forms:
Oṃ.
"When the seer sees the golden-hued one, the maker, the Lord, the Person, the source of Brahman" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.3).

Having cited the sūtra which establishes that Viṣṇu alone possesses the qualities of being invisible and so forth by means of another argument, he quotes the very scripture mentioned therein: "On account of the presentation of form."
Thus, the grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is "because of the presentation of form.
In the Sūtra, the word "and" (*ca*) serves to collect logical reasons.
And so—it is not only because of the statement of the qualities (*dharma*).

However, because the one possessing qualities such as invisibility is described in the scripture [Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad] as having the nature of pure gold in the phrase "when," the construction is that the one possessing qualities such as invisibility is Viṣṇu alone.
Here, the sentence beginning with "when" [is connected to]: "Then the wise man, having shaken off merit and sin, stainless, attains the highest equality" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.3).
The connection is with the remainder of the sentence as follows:
"paśya" means the seer, the individual soul (jīva);
"when [he sees] the golden-colored [Self]"—so it is said.
The one of pure golden color, the "source of Brahman" (brahmayoni)—
the cause of Hiraṇyagarbha— and therefore the "Puruṣa," the creator of the world.
When he sees Viṣṇu, the Lord of himself, who possesses the six perfections in their entirety,
then he is a "knower."

The one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), having shaken off uncommenced merit and demerit—both undesirable merit and sin—is "stainless" (*nirañjana*); that is, free from defects such as impurity caused by actions subsequent to knowledge, or, according to the *Sudhā* commentary, free from ignorance (*avidyā*) known as "stain" (*añjana*), or simply devoid of nescience (*ajñāna*). Thus, he attains "supreme equality" (*paramaṃ sāmyam*).

The meaning of the Śruti is that [the individual soul] "attains" (upaiti), that is, reaches, equality with [Brahman] in terms of full bliss and so forth, or equality in terms of freedom from suffering and so forth.
However, in the *Tattvodyota-ṭīkā*, this Śruti is explained as referring to the liberated soul (*mukta*).
The term "supreme" has been explained as that which is manifested; [as it is said]:
"Nārāyaṇa alone existed, neither Brahmā nor Śaṅkara; he, having become a sage..."
He reflected;
from that, these were born: Viśva, Hiraṇyagarbha, Agni, Yama, Varuṇa, Rudra, and Indra.
Of this very supreme Nārāyaṇa, there are four forms: white, red, golden, and black.

He fashioned these [elements] from those [entities], intermingling what was mixed. Now, since even Brahmā and others possess the existence of form, how can his status as Viṣṇu be determined merely by the mention of form? To this he says: "The One."
The phrase "this was at the beginning" is supplied [to complete the sense].
For this very reason, it is stated in the *Nyāyadīpikā* that "[at] the beginning of the world.
[The term] *hetu* is used in the sense of tasting.
The word "etebhyaḥ" (from these) is in the dative case in the sense of purpose (*tādarthye*).
Thus, at the beginning of this world— that is, during the dissolution (*pralaya*)— Nārāyaṇa alone was independent.
At that time, neither the four-faced Brahmā nor Śaṅkara existed, nor did their respective functions;
at that time, "he," Viṣṇu, was "the Sage."
"Having become either contemplative or silent, he reflected";
that is, he formed a thought in the form of meditation, thinking, "Let these be born. "Then," from his reflection, these were born.
Who are they? The meaning is: "he who is non-universal," namely Vāyu; and Hiraṇyagarbha; and those beginning with Agni—these are they.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "of that";
of this one, well-known from the Vedas and other sources; "of this";
who dwells within the bodies of all living beings; "of the supreme."
The "forms" (rūpāṇi) of Nārāyaṇa, who is supreme among all, consist of four colors. What are they? They are white and the others.
From what was he born? From these "forms" (rūpa), which were previously "intermingled"— that is, mixed by Nārāyaṇa himself.
For the sake of the deities mentioned beginning with Vāyu, he "fashioned" (*abhyacākḷpat*) them;
that is, he made them ready.
Then, those which had been mixed together, he again "separated" (*vyamiśrayat*).
He especially intermingled [them] among humans and other beings; or rather, the meaning is that he mixed these forms together and fashioned them as a composite from these [elements].
The sense is that he made the pure forms for himself alone.
In this regard, the first interpretation has been stated in both the *Tattvapradīpa* and the *Ṭīkā*;
however, it should be understood that the second [interpretation] is found in the *Ṭīkā*.
Therefore, by saying "such is its form" (*etādṛg etad-rūpam*), the very forms of that [reality] are being denoted. // 23 //
// Thus ends the section concerning invisibility (Adṛśyatvādhikaraṇa) // 6 //
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "Therefore" (ataḥ).
Therefore, due to this mixing, its form— that is, the form of that Viṣṇu— is "of such a kind," meaning it is pure, having a nature such as white and so forth;
the meaning is that it is not mixed like the forms of air and other elements.

Although in this context such passages as "Of that very one" (*tasya haitasya*) and so forth should have been cited as examples, because they are more directly relevant to the subject at hand, [the following is instead presented].
But [it is not] such passages as "There is only one Nārāyaṇa";
nevertheless, an example of that portion was provided for the sake of clarifying the meaning of the word "from these" (etebhyaḥ).
Regarding the word "iti": because, by the cited statement, "forms"— namely,
forms such as pure gold and so forth— are designated as belonging to that very Viṣṇu alone.
It does not apply to others;
therefore, the meaning is that one should not suspect the reason [for the argument] to be inconclusive (*aprayojaka*).
By this, although it was stated generally in the Sūtra, the word "form" (*rūpa*) refers specifically to pure form (*śuddharūpa*).
And that [quality] does not exist elsewhere;

for although the phrase "should always be meditated upon" is well-known in reference to the sun, it is still mixed [with other attributes], and thus it is stated that the indicative mark (liṅga) has no scope elsewhere.
Thus ends the section concerning "the invisibility" (Adṛśyatvādhikaraṇa). 6.
7. The Section on Vaiśvānara.

Regarding the qualities such as invisibility and so forth, omnipresence is stated of Vaiśvānara in the passage: "But he who worships this Vaiśvānara Self, which is of the measure of a span and all-pervading" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.18.1).

In this section, for the purpose of establishing the coordination of numerous attributes such as "being a cooker" (pācakatva) and so forth, the coordination of the name Vaiśvānara with Brahman is undertaken.
He indicates the subject matter and other details, including the connection with the preceding section, by first citing the scriptural passage under discussion: "The invisible, etc. (adṛśyatvādi).
The word "stated" (*uktam*) is repeated [in the commentary], with the ellipsis "in the Śruti" (*śrutau*) to be supplied.

Thus, among the attributes such as invisibility (*adṛśyatva*) mentioned in the Muṇḍaka Śruti cited in the preceding section, that "all-pervasiveness" (*sarvagatatva*) which was stated by the passage "eternal, omnipresent, all-pervading" (*nityaṃ vibhuṃ sarvagatam*, Muṇḍaka 1.1.6) is [referred to] in the Chāndogya Śruti by the words "But he who... (*yastvetam*).
The construction is: "By this [sūtra], that which was stated regarding Vaiśvānara is [addressed].
