Having asserted that there is no room for the presentation of a supplied reason— on the grounds that [the word "Self"] begins by setting aside that [other meaning]— and having demonstrated the supplied reason through the force of the context (*prakaraṇabala*), the subsequent portion, "because it is impossible to establish that the word 'Self' and the context are without scope," has been explained.
Thus, as in the case of "because of the teaching of such a vision" or "because of impossibility," the supplied reason does not connect with a subordinate probandum (*avāntarasādhya*).

However, the repetition stating that "Viṣṇu alone is Vaiśvānara" is for the purpose of making it known that [the term] refers specifically to the Pradhāna. The reversal of order occurs because the designation of the subject and the predicate is optional.
"Hi" means "because," [referring to] that which is "beyond" Viṣṇu.
Others, because they are not grasped by the qualities (*guṇa*),
because they are not pervasive, or because they are not accepted by the followers of the Veda as being supreme, are "non-selves" (*anātman*); that is,
they are the primary referents of the term *anātman*.
And because they are non-Brahman due to their deficiency in the mass of qualities (*guṇarāśi*),
therefore the meaning is that Viṣṇu alone is established as the primary denotation of the word "Brahmātmā."

For in the Chāndogya, King Aśvapati was questioned by five great sages known as the Mahāśālas—who were engaged in a collective inquiry as to "Who is our Self? What is Brahman?"—and who had been instructed and accompanied by Uddālaka; [the King] taught them Vaiśvānara, [saying], "'Naḥ' means 'our'; [what is] the Self to be meditated upon by us? 'Kaḥ' [means 'who']."
What is its characteristic? "Brahman" and "what"—the meaning is: what is its characteristic?
By such passages as, "The moon was born from his mind;

from his eye the sun was born" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 3.12), that which is designated as the Puruṣa—Viṣṇu—is described; and it is of that very same nature here [in the Chāndogya], as in: "The head indeed is the excellent luster, the eye is the omniform, the breath is the manifold path" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.18.2).
With these and other such passages, they study this Vaiśvānara.

And in order to establish that Vaiśvānara is Viṣṇu on the basis of scriptural designation (*śruti-samākhyā*), he explains the portion beginning with "They also study him as being in the form of a person" (*puruṣavidhamapyenamadhīyate*) as follows: "The moon... (*candramā iti*).
Here, the phrase "the moon" is taken as a representative citation (pratīka),
while the illustrative sentence is "from the eye the sun was born."
Thus it should be meditated upon.
By the first word and others [it is meant]: "From the head the sky evolved;
from the breath the wind was born."

By the second and subsequent words [of the mantra], such passages as "the earth from his feet" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 3.12) and so forth, as well as "the udder is the atmosphere, the penis is indeed wealth, and the feet are indeed the earth" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.18.2) and so forth, are included.
The explanation of the word "etam" (this) is "vaiśvānaram" (the Universal Fire).
And so it is stated in the Puruṣasūkta: "From his head the sky arose;
from his eyes the sun was born."

By such words as these, Viṣṇu— who is designated by the term "Puruṣa" and who is described as having the nature of being the progenitor of heaven, earth, and so forth, and possessing a head and other limbs— is taught here in the Chāndogya by the passage beginning with "His head indeed was the bright light," as being of that very same nature, endowed with the mode of being the progenitor of heaven, earth, etc., and possessing a head and so forth; therefore, even by virtue of the title "Puruṣasūkta," Vaiśvānara is none other than Viṣṇu— this is the logical connection.
By the word "and" (ca), he shows that the Puruṣasūkta has Viṣṇu as its ultimate referent in all the Vedas, Tantras, Purāṇas, and so forth.
Now, one might object: "If the Puruṣasūkta has Viṣṇu as its referent, then this Vidya [the Śrī-sūkta] would have Viṣṇu as its referent by virtue of being associated with it;
but why is that so? To this, he replies: "By the word 'and'."
Because of the superiority of the Śruti, the proposition comes first;
after "of the Puruṣasūkta," the remainder is "it is well-known."
"He shows" means that the author of the Sūtras indicates [this].

The sense is that since the conjunction of context (*prakaraṇa*) with scriptural statement (*śruti*)—just like the conjunction of context with the designation (*samākhyā*), the recollection of the word "Self" (*ātma-śabda-smṛti*), and so on—is already established by the word "also" (*api*) itself, the word "and" (*ca*) is not exhausted there [in that specific connection].
And so it is said in the Brāhma [Purāṇa]:
"Just as the Pauruṣa Sūkta is eternally devoted to Viṣṇu, even so may my mind always be devoted to Viṣṇu. Thus [it is said].

To the question, "What is that [source] beginning with the Veda?", since the Śruti does not directly establish the matter proposed in the thesis, he bypasses the order of the thesis and first cites the Purāṇa statement— beginning with "And so it is"— because it does directly establish the matter proposed in the thesis.
The meaning is that, just as it was stated that the *Puruṣasūkta* in the *Sūtra* is established as being devoted to Viṣṇu, so too has it been stated in the *Brāhma*.
The particle *ca* is used for conjunction (*samuccaye*).
The word "stated" (*uktam*) applies similarly to what follows as well.
Thus, by supplying the appropriate words, the connection of the locative case endings should be understood as follows:
"nityam" means invariably; "viṣṇuparāyaṇam" means having the primary purport directed toward Viṣṇu.
Regarding the second [term], "nityam" (eternally), its meaning is "sadā" (always).

In the phrase "iti brāhma iti," the word "iti" is connected [to the preceding]; since it serves as an illustration of an established fact, the intended meaning is understood through this statement concerning the Brahmanical word.
And in the *Caturvedaśikhā*: "The Puruṣa has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, and a thousand feet.

For it is He indeed who is inconceivable, supreme, the highest, Hari, the beginning, without beginning, infinite, with infinite heads, infinite eyes, infinite arms, infinite qualities, and infinite forms.
To show the scripture that was promised, he first mentions its source, saying: "And in the *Caturvedaśikhā*."
In this regard, the *Caturvedaśikhā-śruti*, having introduced the *Puruṣasūkta* beginning with "A thousand" and ending with "thousand-footed," states: "For he indeed..."

By this [statement], it is established that Hari alone—and no other—is the one spoken of in the verse "The Puruṣa with a thousand heads"; thus, this hymn is explained as having Viṣṇu as its ultimate subject, which constitutes the relevant connection to the present topic.
The form *supaḥ* is a Vedic usage.
Who is this? He who is "supreme," meaning distinct in nature; for that very reason, he is "inconceivable" by the mind, being the "highest."
"Uttama" means the beginning; "anādi" means being the cause;
"ananta" means being devoid of origination.
He says that Hari is neither subject to destruction nor limited by his own nature;
why? Because this Puruṣa has a thousand heads.
Indeed; because he has infinite heads. Why [is he] thousand-eyed?
Because he has infinite eyes.
Why is he called "thousand-footed"?
Because he has infinite arms; this term is also indicative of his having infinite feet.

Thus, he provides the supporting reason for the preceding statement "He [attains] the earth" and also for the subsequent statement, saying: "possessing infinite qualities, infinite forms, and infinite aspects.
The syntactical connection is with the passage from the *Caturvedaśikhā*.
And in the *Bṛhatsaṃhitā*: "O Nārada, just as the *Puruṣasūkta* is the exclusive designator of Viṣṇu, so too are not all the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas," and so forth.

Since the *Puruṣasūkta*—the speech of Brahmā—is ambiguous, whether it refers to Viṣṇu through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) or to another deity, it cannot by itself determine the truth of the proposition [that Viṣṇu is the Supreme]. Therefore, he cites a traditional text (*smṛti-vākya*) that directly establishes the meaning of the proposition, preceded by a reference to its location, stating: "And in the *Bṛhatsaṃhitā*," [without relying on the relationship between the commentary and the commented text].
The word "ca" (and) has the sense of a cumulative conjunction with what precedes.
"The Vedāṅgas," such as Śikṣā and so forth— this is a statement of the Veda,
and so on.
The grammatical connection is that it is stated in the *Bṛhatsaṃhitā*.
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of the *Brahmatarka* and other texts, such as the passage: "In every respect, the qualities of Viṣṇu are proclaimed in the *Puruṣasūkta*."
"Sarvataḥ" means all the qualities;
"in general," is the ellipsis.
Or, it means "in every respect" or "with excellence" compared to all the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences.

Since whatever arises from the limbs of Hari—such as the world, the Vedas, and so forth—is designated by the name of that specific limb; for example, the face [of Hari] is the source of Brahmā and others.
Thus, according to the statement of Nārada, there is no contradiction with the declaration of non-difference. // 26 //
[Objection: But in the Puruṣasūkta, the Puruṣa is said to possess a head and so forth that are the generator of heaven, earth, and the rest;
whereas in the Vaiśvānara-vidyā, the non-difference of Vaiśvānara from that [Puruṣa] is stated.
Since these two have contradictory meanings, this cannot be a common designation (samākhyā). To this, he says: "Because... (yasmāt).
"Loka" refers to heaven and so forth; "Veda" refers to the Ṛgveda and so forth.

Although it might be argued that since non-difference regarding the Vedas is not stated here in this *Chāndogya* passage, its interpretation need not be discussed, nevertheless, this section is undertaken for the purpose of determining the meaning of the statement concerning non-difference found in another scriptural text (*śruti*).
Alternatively— the word "veda" refers to the sacrificial altar mentioned in the passage, "The chest itself is the altar";
the suffix "-tṛtīya" is used in the sense of excellence.
Because it has been stated thus,
the reading "vedyādikam" is the natural one.
And likewise, because whatever— be it the worlds, the Vedas, or other things— is born from whichever limb of Hari, rests depending upon that limb,
and dissolves back into it, that generating limb is designated by that very name.
Whatever name belongs to that world and so forth—that is, the expressive word—by means of it, [the object] becomes the primary denotatum;
for this very reason, it is also perceived as non-different from it.
However, the meaning is that one should not consider there to be an actual identity between the two on that account.
Regarding this, he provides an illustration with the word "yathā" (just as).
The term "mouth" (*mukha*) is used figuratively (*upalakṣaṇa*).
Thus, the face and so forth of the Blessed One are designated by names such as "Brāhmaṇa" because they give rise to the Brāhmaṇa caste and so on, as in the statement: "The Brāhmaṇa was his mouth."
In passages such as *Tai.
Ā. 3.12*, it is for this very reason that [the Self] is perceived as non-different from that [Brahman], due to grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
The meaning is that it is just like that [Brahman].
For in this passage, non-difference of the Brāhmaṇas and others from the face and so forth of Puruṣottama is not being asserted,
because that would contradict the subsequent statement: "From his feet the Śūdra was born" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 3.12).

The meaning is that because it has been stated, "on account of this scriptural statement," there is no contradiction caused by the declaration of non-difference between the limbs of Vaiśvānara and the worlds and so forth—such as "the head itself [is heaven]";

for the intention is that the statement indicating non-difference is preceded by the desire to express a relationship of cause and effect arising from that [non-difference]. This is the underlying sense.

By this [verse], the head of the Blessed One is called "Sutejas" (Possessing Great Splendor) because it is endowed with qualities such as great splendor and because it generates the heaven known by that term.
Likewise, the eye is called "Viśvarūpa" (Universal Form) because it is endowed with the quality of illuminating all things and because it generates the sun known by that term.

The meaning of the Śruti passage, "Prāṇa is the self whose paths are manifold" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.18.2), is indicated as follows: it is designated by that term because it generates the wind (vāyu).
The word *ātman* signifies either its own essential nature (*svarūpa*) or the central part of the body.
In the *Chāndogyabhāṣya*, however, it is stated: "The head of Viṣṇu is the sky, named *dyu*, which is the support of heaven; it is also named *suptejas* because of its extreme brilliance.
It is called the 'all-formed' (*viśvarūpa*) eye, based on the etymological analysis that it has all forms as its objects, since it perceives every form."

Thus, Viṣṇu’s vital breath (prāṇa), known as Nṛsiṃha, is that whose path is distinct—that is, whose course is separate and characterized by a different nature—from that which cannot be accomplished by the vital breaths of air and the other elements; thus the Śruti is explained by means of this further reason.
Similarly, because they are the progenitors of the deities of space, water, and the earth—designated by the words *bahula-rayi* and *pṛthivī*—the terms *sandoha*, *vasti*, and *pāda* are employed.
It should also be understood that the parts of the Lord Vaiśvānara—namely the middle body, the waist, and the feet—are denoted by those respective terms.

If it is argued that, on account of this [sūtra] "Because of words such as ‘fire’" (ŚB 1.2.24)—that is, because of the scriptural mention of fire and so forth, the indicative marks such as having the Gārhapatya and other fires as limbs, and because of being the internal dweller as the digester—it is not logical to conclude that Vaiśvānara is Viṣṇu alone; we say: no.

Because other scriptural passages, indicative marks (*liṅga*), and so forth have scope elsewhere [than Viṣṇu], it is logical that the certainty [of the identity of the Self] arises from the word "Self" (*ātman*) and others alone.
Why do they have scope elsewhere?
[The Sūtra says: "Because there is instruction regarding such a vision."
This is because the instruction for the worship of Viṣṇu is given through the characteristics and activities of Agni and others;
furthermore, there is no scope for the word "Self" (ātman) and so forth to apply elsewhere,
since qualities such as being the Self are impossible in anything other than Him.
The certainty that Vaiśvānara is Viṣṇu alone is established not only from the recollection and designation by the word "Self," but also from the commencement and the force of the context.
Nor is it the case that the Vaiśvānara-vidyā is not established as having Viṣṇu as its subject matter.
Because this [text] was commenced and studied preceded by the inquiry, "Who is the Self? What is Brahman?
Nor can it be asked: even though it begins with the nature of the Self and Brahman, why should it have Viṣṇu as its ultimate purport?
Since attributes such as selfhood (*ātmatva*) and brahmanhood (*brahmatva*) are impossible in fire and other such things,

it is determined that Vaiśvānara is Viṣṇu alone— not only by the force of Smṛti, name, and context— but because this very Viṣṇu, exactly as the Puruṣa is described in the *Puruṣasūkta*, is [identified] here as "the head indeed."
The Chāndogas study [the Puruṣasūkta] with the words beginning "ityādi.

Therefore, the commentary on the Sūtra demonstrates that even from this scriptural designation (śrutisamākhyāna), the word "ca" (and) indicates that the Puruṣasūkta’s focus on Viṣṇu is established by many proofs. Sūtra: Oṃ.
Therefore, it is neither a deity nor an elemental being.
Oṃ.
Although words such as *agnivaiśvānara* are well-known to refer to the element fire and the deity Agni, for the very reasons stated previously, they do not denote those here. // 27 //

One might raise the objection: "Since the word *vaiśvānara* is well-known to denote both a deity and fire, why should it not refer to those here as well? Anticipating this doubt, he presents the sūtra, beginning with the words "ata eva" (for this very reason).
And here, although the word *ca* has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*), he explains the Sūtra by relying on its sense of "even though" (*tathāpi*)—namely, "Agni," etc.
This is a singular form used for a collective group; by the word "etc. (*ādi*), the term "Jātavedas" and others are included.
The two words "fire" (*agni*) and so forth are included as indicators for other branches of knowledge (*vidyā*).
It should not be argued that since the word "fire" and others alone would suffice as indicators, what is the purpose of including both words;
for it is appropriate to include the word "fire" because the word *vaiśvānara* is the subject under investigation here, while the word "fire" is extremely well-known.

Alternatively, since the word "etc. (ādi) connects with both [terms], the mention of "Agni etc. and "Vaiśvānara etc. is for the purpose of indicating other types of knowledge—namely, other *ādhibhautika* (objective/elemental) knowledge and other *ādhyātmika* (subjective/supernatural) knowledge respectively; thus, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the expression "in the element of fire" (*tejasi bhūte*).
The word *ca* is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaye*). By the phrase "not well-known," the reasoning that [the term] is well-known in the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is indicated.
Having restated the word *mataḥ* from the Sūtra, he explains it with the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*).
Regarding the phrase "as previously stated": the meaning is "by means of the reason beginning with the word 'self'.
The intended sense is that no further reason need be sought therein.
In this context— namely, in the Vaiśvānara-vidyā and in other vidyās—
the word "that" (sā) refers to the deity Agni, and "that" (tat) refers to his nature as light; the reversal in the order of these terms is due to the predominance of conventional usage.
The word "ca" (and) signifies conjunction.
The ellipsis [to be supplied] is "it is denoted by that";
the meaning of this is "by means of such words as Vaiśvānara."
If the reading "atra" is absent, that word must also be supplied as an ellipsis. Sūtra—Oṃ.
Jaimini maintains that there is no contradiction even with direct perception. Om.

Jaimini states that there is no contradiction in accepting that words such as "Agni" and so forth—though they denote fire and other such things—nevertheless function elsewhere for the sake of worldly transaction and due to ignorance, by means of words that directly denote Brahman through the principle of non-connection with anything else (*ananya-yoga*). Now, one might object: since we observe in both the world and the Veda that words like "Agni" are well-known to be used elsewhere [than their primary referent], and since there is no other cause for this, the denotation of those other things must be admitted on the grounds of the inexplicability of that usage otherwise (*tad-anyathānupapatti*).
Anticipating the objection that otherwise there would be a contradiction with that [scripture], he sets forth and explains the aphorism: "Directly," etc.
In this context, from the explanation of the word "even" (*api*) in the phrase "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*), the expression "even though" (*yadyapi*) is obtained.
The word "fire" (*agni*) refers to both itself and others.
The analysis of the compound is: those for which the word "fire" is the first are "fire and the rest" (*agnyādayaḥ*).

The word "api" is used in the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), with the intention that it means "directly indeed"; the meaning is "without the intervention of any other object. He states the resultant meaning: "ananyā" (not other).
The meaning is that [the word] functions in its primary sense (mukhyavṛtti) without a connection to anything else that could be possible.

Alternatively, according to the *Tattvapradīpa*, since there is no application of etymological derivation (*yogavṛtti*) elsewhere, the meaning is "by means of perfect yoga" (*samyagyoga*) with respect to Brahman.
The particle *api* ("even") is to be construed with the phrase "even by those words that denote Brahman."

The phrase "by those words such as 'fire' and so forth" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. "For the sake of worldly transaction" means for the sake of establishing transactions such as avoidance; "[because of] non-recognition."
Because there is an absence of knowledge regarding the primary denotation.
The word "ca" (and) is used for conjunction, meaning that it is not only for the sake of conventional usage, but also because of a lack of recognition.
The phrase "elsewhere" refers to fire and so forth; the ellipsis to be supplied in order is: "the wise and the ignorant use those [terms] for them."
In the phrase "ityabhyupagame," the locative case is used in the sense of a cause (nimitta-saptamī); thus,
because of such acceptance, it is "unobstructed" (avaridham).
The meaning is that the teacher Jaimini states that there is no contradiction in the conventional usage of the terms "the knower" and "the ignorant.
It is said that he "states" this because of the expression "there is no occasion for effort."
By this [reasoning], words such as "fire" (agni) and so forth do not denote fire and so forth,
but rather denote Brahman alone;
nevertheless, there is no contradiction with their well-established usage elsewhere.

Nor should the denotability of other [words] be postulated on the grounds of *anyathānupapatti* (otherwise-unaccountability). Why? Because words such as "Agni" and others, which directly denote Brahman through their primary function (*mukhyavṛtti*), do not require secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) or the like, being mediated only by the cognition of the denoted object. For those who know the primary meaning, these words function just as the word "Nārāyaṇa" did for Ajāmila’s son, for the sake of attaining liberation and so forth; whereas for those who do not know it, this is due simply to their lack of recognition.

By accepting that people employ those [terms] in reference to fire and so forth, the meaning of the sūtra is stated as follows: it expresses non-contradiction with respect to other things, the absence of contradiction in conventional usage, and the absence of the loss of established worldly consensus.
Some [beings] emerge as delimited portions from the space that resides within the mind of Vyāsa;
others, accepting these [portions], engage in worldly activity just like houses and other such things.
Thus, according to the words of Skanda, there is no mutual contradiction between the philosophical systems. // 28 //

Now, one might object: if the views of Jaimini and others are not in contradiction with the view of the Blessed One, then the mention of Jaimini and the rest would be redundant; conversely, if they are in contradiction, how can there be a resolution by means of a conclusion that is itself contradictory? To this, he says: "Vyāsa... [and so forth].

The meaning is that, in relation to the "great space" known as gnosis— which resides within the mind of Vyāsa and is synonymous with *matā*— certain others, such as Jaimini and his followers, employ the term "others" (*anye*) by accepting these various cognitions (*matāni*) as being "delimited" (*avacchinnāni*)— like space enclosed within a house— and thus as distinct and having limited objects.

As stated in the *Sattarkadīpāvalī*: Because they are all-pervasive like space and because they are luminous, these views—which are distinct from the "space" called the universal mind (*matākāśa*)—are "delimited" by their respective individual intellects.
Having asserted, "This is mine; this is mine," people engage in worldly transactions regarding those views.
It is just as people, having delimited portions of space by means of houses, cities, and so forth, engage in transactions such as, "This portion is mine; this portion is mine."
The plural number in "of the opinions" (matānām) is used with the intention of referring to the opinions that are about to be stated.
Thus, the meaning is that there is no mutual contradiction between the opinions of Jaimini and others and the opinion of Vyāsa.
Sūtra—Oṃ.
"It is due to manifestation," says Āśmarathya. Om.

Āśmarathya maintains that although Brahman is manifested even in fire and other such things well-known in various contexts, there is a restriction to the hymns dedicated to fire and others because of the manifestation of Brahman therein. // 29 //

Now, one might object: although worldly convention may be explained otherwise because it is rooted in ignorance and the like, the fact that Agni and others are denoted by the words "Agni" and so forth occurring in the *sūktas* and *mantras* of the Veda cannot be explained otherwise;

for since it is impossible to assume that such usage is rooted in ignorance and the like, there is no possibility of explaining it away. Nor can it be explained otherwise on the grounds that it serves merely for practical communication (*vyavahāra*).
Addressing the doubt that [the world] is beginningless, he recites the sūtra: "Because of manifestation."
In this context, the word "api" (also) from the preceding [verse] should also be carried over;
and with the intention that the word "tat" (that), being thus carried over, must be modified in various ways, he explains it by saying "tatra tatra" (in each of those cases).

The meaning is: "even though that very Brahman is well-known at the beginning of the hymn (sūkta)," that is, even though it is the subject to be expounded, while Agni and the others are not the subjects to be expounded.
The phrase "in [the case of] Agni and the others" is used restrictively.
He explains the intended meaning of the word "non-contradiction with the Sūtra" as follows: "Agni, etc.
The word "etc. (*ādi*) is to be applied in both places;
the ellipsis is "it is stated that it is appropriate."

By this also— namely, that even though Brahman alone is the subject to be propounded in various *sūktas* and the like, there is no contradiction even though Agni, Vāyu, and others are not the subjects to be propounded—

the restriction of *sūktas* (such as "this is an Agni-sūkta" or "this is a Vāyu-sūkta") and the restriction of *vidyās* (such as "this is the Agni-vidyā" or "this is the Vāyu-vidyā") are both appropriate.

How so? Because when that meditation on Brahman is performed by means of those hymns (sūkta) dedicated to Agni and others, there is a rule for the manifestation of that very Brahman as "Abhi" within those very deities such as Agni by its own will; thus, the teacher Āśmarathya states that the well-known usage of the Vedic hymns to Agni and others is not contradicted, since their established application is justified with reference to that [Brahman]. This is the meaning of the Sūtra as it has been explained.
Sūtra—Oṃ.
Bādari [maintains that the soul] is led [to Brahman] by means of remembrance.
Om.
Bādari maintains that there is a restriction [to specific deities] because Viṣṇu, who is mentioned in various places, is to be remembered as present within Agni and the other deities.
Presenting the aphorism which explains how the restriction regarding hymns and so forth can be accounted for in another way, he comments: "Because of recollection" (anusmṛteḥ).
Here, as before, there is ellipsis and so forth;
"in each respective case" refers to the vidyās concerning Agni and the others.
He states the intended meaning of the word "non-contradiction" (*avirodham*), which is supplied from the preceding sūtra, as follows: "That restriction" (*tanniyama*).

By this also—namely, even though Viṣṇu alone is the one to be propounded by the Agni-vidyā and other such knowledges, there is no contradiction in the restriction that He is to be meditated upon and realized within those very deities such as Agni, because He is "remembered" (anusmṛti) therein by those practitioners of the respective hymns (sūkta) and so forth; thus, the established order of the Agni-sūkta and others is logical.

Therefore, Bādari maintains that the well-known status of the hymns and so forth is not contradicted, and it is not to be assumed on the grounds of the impossibility of otherwise [explaining them] that other deities are the primary objects of expression.
The son of Badara, the teacher Śuka, speaks; thus the commentary on the Sūtras is shown. Sūtra: Oṃ.
Jaimini [holds that the fruit belongs to the sacrificer] because of the attainment; for thus the scripture shows.
Om.

Jaimini, asserting that there is no contradiction even with direct perception, considers the restriction regarding the *sūkta* and other elements to be due to the attainment [of the status] of Agni and the other deities.
He introduces the aphorism—*sampatteḥ*—which explains how the restriction regarding the *sūkta*s and so forth can be accounted for otherwise, by means of a different method.

Since the view of Jaimini was presented previously, one might wonder for what purpose it is stated again; in order to dispel such a doubt from those of dull intellect, he explains the Sūtra—beginning with the word "directly" (sākṣāt)—by showing the difference in subject matter through a restatement of what was previously mentioned and referred to by the word "both-inclusive" (ubhayānvayī).
The meaning is that he states "non-contradiction"—that is, the absence of contradiction with worldly usage—even though words such as "fire" (agni) primarily denote Brahman.
Here too, he explains the meaning of the recurring term "non-contradiction" with the words "sūkta, etc. (sūktādīti).
*Niyama* means a fixed rule or established order;
the phrase "by means of attainment" (*saṃprāptyā*) is to be understood as "serving as the cause.
As it is said: "In whatever way they worship Him, that very thing they become."
Thus he demonstrates. // 31 //

Now, one might ask: from what source is it known that by worshipping the Lord in the form of Agni and others, the attainment of Agni and others occurs? To this, he cites the scriptural passage indicated by the Sūtra, beginning with the words "tam" (him).
"In whatever manner qualified aspirants worship that Supreme Self, they become that very form in that same manner";
the meaning is that they attain it.
This is also stated in the *Tattvapradīpa*: "In whatever way the Lord is meditated upon, the individual soul becomes like that."
Thus, from the statement of the third intentionality, "that very thing becomes," it follows that it becomes in exactly that way;
the meaning stated is precisely this: in whatever manner one meditates, in that very manner one becomes.
According to the view of the author of the *Tattvapradīpa*, the singular verb form "upāsate" (they worship) is a different verbal root altogether.

By this, there is no contradiction even when the Supreme Brahman alone is primarily intended to be propounded in the hymns (*sūkta*) dedicated to Agni and others; thus, the restriction regarding the specific hymns and so forth becomes appropriate.
Therefore, one should not consider that other [deities] must be denoted by those [Vedic words] on the grounds that [the stated facts] would otherwise be inexplicable.
How is this justified?
Because through those [deities], the worshippers of the Lord attain identification with Agni and the others.
Nor is that unestablished;

for the reason (hi) is that the well-known scripture (prasiddhā śrutiḥ) "shows" (darśayati) that through meditation having fire and so forth as its locus, the attainment of fire and so forth occurs. "In that way" (tathā).
He establishes [this point]:

by stating that there is no contradiction in worldly convention through the word "directly" (*sākṣāt*), Jaimini considers the absence of contradiction— termed "non-restriction" (*aniyama*)— to be a "restriction" (*niyama*) within the Sūtras.
Thus, the meaning of the Sūtra has been explained as "he describes.

Although it might be argued that in the two subsequent Sūtras, because they speak of the activity of the agent (*sādhaka*) and because of their brevity of syllables, one should say "of seeing" (*dṛṣṭeḥ*) rather than "of manifestation" (*abhivyakteḥ*), [the author] does not do so.

Because that [attainment] is the operation of the Lord (*īśvara*), even so, since perception is impossible without manifestation, both are obtained by mentioning that [attainment]; thus, out of prominence, only the operation of the Lord is stated. Although manifestation occurs immediately after the meditation (*upāsanā*) denoted by the term "recollection" (*anusmṛti*), and its attainment follows immediately thereafter, it should have been said that recollection comes first.

Nevertheless, it should be understood that the placement of *anusmṛti* (remembrance) in the middle [of the sequence] is intended to show that worship (*upāsti*) must be performed even after both manifestation (*abhivyakti*) and perfection (*sampatti*).

Although it is stated in the *Ṛgbhāṣya*: "The distinct forms of Viṣṇu residing in other deities are denoted by words such as 'Agni' and so forth; the distinction of the hymns (*sūkta*) occurs by name."
Thus, the application of words such as "Agni" and so forth—which denote Viṣṇu who is contained within Agni and the others—is stated to be the determining factor for the hymn (*sūkta*).
Accordingly, words such as "Agni" and those respective hymns are primary (*mukhya*) only with respect to the forms of Brahman residing within Agni and the others.

Likewise, even with respect to external forms, they are to be recollected by the worshippers of the hymns of Agni and the others—as being present within Agni and the rest—pertaining to the past, future, and present.

Alternatively, it may be that the specific arrangement of various *sūktas*—such as the *Saura*, *Sāvitra*, *Vāmana*, *Viṣṇu*, and so forth—is established for the sake of their utility in specific ritual performances (*anuṣṭhāna*).
Thus, another factor of arrangement has been stated, and there is no contradiction.

As for the reason why the terms "worldly" and "Vedic" are applied metaphorically (*upacarita*) to Agni and others in those two contexts: it is because, if one were to accept their primary (*mukhya*) application there, [the scripture] would not teach them as being seen in such a manner.

It has been stated in the *Ṭīkā* itself that by this [statement], the aforementioned inconsistency—consisting of contradictions with such scriptural passages as "the name for all" (*sarvanāma*) and so forth—is indicated.
For it is not logical that a worshiper of one [deity] should attain another; therefore, he says:
Sū - Oṃ.
And they enjoin this [Self] in this [body]:
Om.
They declare this Viṣṇu to be within this fire and so forth.

As for what was said—that through hymns dedicated to Agni and others, one who meditates on Brahman attains Agni and the rest—even though that is stated in the Śruti, it is not logical, because [the Lord has declared]:
"My devotees come to Me alone."
Thinking that it is impossible for a worshiper of one [deity] to attain another—as in the passage beginning "Because of the declaration of the path for one who has heard the Upaniṣads" (Chāndogya Up.
8.6.6)—and considering that such a view is not accepted in those passages, he introduces and explains the Sūtra as a refutation of that objection, saying: "Not indeed... (na hi).
The syntactical connection [in the commentary] is "having raised a doubt and introduced [the sūtra].
The meaning is: having demonstrated the introduction to the sūtra in the form of a doubt.
For [it is indicated by] "hi" (because), since it is not tenable that a worshiper of one [deity] attains another, as this contradicts authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*).
Therefore, the meaning is that what was stated is incorrect.
By the restatement "this one" (*enam*), it is explained as "Viṣṇu.
The explanation of "in this" (*asmin*) is "in fire and so forth."
"They enjoin" means "the Śrutis establish," as the ellipsis requires.
The word "ca" (and) serves to dispel the opponent's doubt that it is improper for a worshiper of Viṣṇu to attain Agni and the other deities.
By this, the proposition of the proponent [of the Siddhānta] is established.
The direct reason is also indicated by the phrase "attaining Agni and so forth," because what is intended is precisely the attainment of the Lord contained within them.

However, in the *Tattvapradīpa*, it is stated: "The Vājasaneyins do not merely record or recite this in one place alone; rather, they do so elsewhere as well, in passages such as 'He who is here in this... etc.
Thus others recite "he who is in this," and so forth;
others recite "in this [intellect]," and so forth; and others recite "having created that."
In passages such as "He entered into that very [Self]," and so forth,
the authors of the Smṛtis also record statements such as "That which is in the moon and that which is in the fire.
It has already been stated that the word "ca" (and) has the sense of conjunction.
"Who, dwelling in the fire... (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.7.5);
"This person who is in this fire, consisting of splendor, consisting of immortality... (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.3), and so forth. // 32 //
Thus concludes the section concerning Vaiśvānara. // 7 //
Thus ends the second quarter of the first chapter in the Brahmasūtrabhāṣya composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda. Om!
He shows those scriptural passages with the words: "ya" (he who).
"Who dwells in fire"—
this is one statement from the Vājasaneyi;
"He who is this"— this is another statement from the Chāndogya.
In both instances, the relative pronoun *yat* is connected with the corresponding correlative pronoun *tat*.
"Consisting of light" (*tejomaya*) means having the nature of light; "consisting of immortality" (*amṛtamaya*) means the eternal Self.
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), [the passage] "this [Self], the Adhvaryu priests [place] in the fire... is included.
[The passage] beginning with "ityādikam" is understood; the grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is that they "teach" by means of such [statements].
By this, it is shown that the statement regarding the attainment of Agni and others by a worshiper of Viṣṇu is not improper.
Why? Because by the phrase "attaining Agni and the others," the attainment of the Blessed Lord who is contained within them is intended.
Nor is it unestablished that Viṣṇu is contained within Agni and the others; for [the text says] "him"—that is, Viṣṇu—"in this."
The meaning of the sūtra—"For [the scriptures] declare [it] thus with respect to fire and so forth"—has now been explained.
Thus ends the section concerning Vaiśvānara (Adhikaraṇa 7).

Thus ends [the section] from the *Śrīmad-Brahmasūtra-Bhāṣya-Dīpikā* composed by the illustrious ascetic Jagannātha, disciple of the venerable feet of the holy Raghunāthatīrtha— the revered teachers of the wandering mendicants of the supreme order (*paramahaṃsa-parivrājaka*), who are independent masters of all philosophical systems (*sarvatantra-svatantra*).
The second quarter of the first chapter. Om.
